🎯 What matters most for your 3.9 YOE interviews

If you have limited revision time, don't give equal time to all 23 sections.

Tier 1 — Master

C# Fundamentals → OOP → Collections → Generics → Delegates → LINQ → Exceptions → Async → Concurrency → Memory → SOLID → DI

Tier 2 — Strong Senior knowledge

EF Core → Advanced Memory → Expression Trees → Records/Modern C# → GC → Performance → Design Patterns

Tier 3 — Be able to explain clearly

Reflection → Attributes → dynamic → Iterators → CLR/JIT → advanced C# features

That gives you a strong path from:

C# language → .NET runtime → performance → clean code → architecture.

Yes. Since you've now completed all 23 C# sections, I would prioritize them specifically for your ~3.9 YOE Senior .NET / Full Stack interviews.

This is interview priority, not a recommendation to change the roadmap order.

1. C# Fundamentals — Basic → Advanced

Part A — Variables

Q1. What is a variable in C#?

Interview-ready answer:

A variable is a named storage location used to hold a value during program execution. Every variable has a type, which determines what kind of data it can store and what operations can be performed on it.
int age = 25;
string name = "Saurabh";
bool isActive = true;

Here:

  • int, string, bool → types
  • age, name, isActive → variables
  • 25, "Saurabh", true → values

Real-world example:

int userId = 101;
string userName = "John";
bool isAdmin = true;

These could represent information received from a user request.

Q2. What is the difference between var, object, and dynamic?

This is a very common interview question.

Featurevarobjectdynamic
Type determinedCompile timeobject typeRuntime
Strongly typedYesYesNo compile-time checking
Can change type?NoCan hold different typesYes
Member checkingCompile timeRequires castingRuntime
Typical useLocal variablesGeneral base typeDynamic scenarios

var

var name = "John";

The compiler determines:

string name = "John";

But you cannot later do:

name = 100; // Compile-time error

Interview statement:

var is not dynamically typed. The compiler infers the type at compile time.

object

object value = "Hello";

object is the base type of all C# types.

object value = 100;
value = "Hello";

The variable can hold different types, but when accessing type-specific members, you generally need casting.

object value = "Hello";

string text = (string)value;
Console.WriteLine(text.Length);

dynamic

dynamic value = "Hello";

Console.WriteLine(value.Length);

The member lookup happens at runtime.

dynamic value = 10;

Console.WriteLine(value.Length); // Runtime exception

The compiler doesn't catch that invalid member access.

Real-world example

dynamic can sometimes be used when interacting with data whose structure is determined at runtime, but in normal ASP.NET Core application development, strongly typed models are generally preferred.

Follow-up

Q: Is var the same as dynamic?

No. var is statically typed with compile-time type inference, whereas dynamic defers type checking and member binding to runtime.

Part B — Types

Q3. What are the main types in C#?

At a high level, C# types include:

  • Value types
  • Reference types

Examples:

Value Types
├── int
├── double
├── bool
├── char
├── struct
└── enum

Reference Types
├── class
├── interface
├── delegate
├── array
└── string

We'll study the memory implications of value vs reference types in detail in Section #5 — Memory, so for now focus on the conceptual difference.

Q4. What is the difference between value types and reference types?

Interview-ready answer:

A value type directly contains its value, while a reference type contains a reference to an object. Assigning a value type generally copies the value, whereas assigning a reference type copies the reference.

Example:

int a = 10;
int b = a;

b = 20;

Console.WriteLine(a); // 10
Console.WriteLine(b); // 20

The values are independent.

Reference type:

class Person
{
    public string Name { get; set; }
}

Person p1 = new Person { Name = "John" };
Person p2 = p1;

p2.Name = "Mike";

Console.WriteLine(p1.Name); // Mike

Both variables refer to the same object.

Important: Don't say simply "value types are always stored on stack and reference types are always stored on heap." That's an oversimplification. We'll cover the actual memory model in Section #5.

Q5. What is const in C#?

const defines a value that cannot be changed after declaration.

const double Pi = 3.14159;

This is invalid:

Pi = 4; // Compile-time error

A const value must be known at compile time.

Real-world example

public const int MaxRetryCount = 3;

Used when the value is a true compile-time constant.

Follow-up: const vs readonly is an important question, but we'll cover readonly more appropriately when we reach the type/class-related sections.

Part C — Nullability

Q6. What is a nullable value type?

Normally:

int age = 25;

An int cannot contain null.

But:

int? age = null;

int? is shorthand for:

Nullable<int>

This is useful when a value may be absent.

Real-world example

Consider an API response:

public int? Age { get; set; }

If the database doesn't contain the person's age:

Age = null

instead of forcing a default value like 0.

Q7. What are nullable reference types?

Modern C# allows you to indicate whether a reference is expected to be nullable.

string name = "John";
string? middleName = null;

string? tells the compiler:

This reference may contain null.

This enables compiler warnings that help prevent NullReferenceException.

Q8. What are ??, ?., and !?

These are extremely useful in modern C#.

?? — Null-coalescing operator

string? name = null;

string displayName = name ?? "Guest";

Meaning:

If name is null, use "Guest".

Real-world API example:

var city = customer?.Address?.City ?? "Unknown";

?. — Null-conditional operator

string? name = null;

int? length = name?.Length;

Instead of throwing a NullReferenceException, the expression evaluates to null.

Real-world:

var city = customer?.Address?.City;

If customer or Address is null, it safely returns null.

! — Null-forgiving operator

string? name = GetName();

Console.WriteLine(name!.Length);

It tells the compiler:

I know this isn't null; don't warn me.

Important: ! does not perform a runtime null check.

If name actually is null, you can still get a NullReferenceException.

Part D — Type Conversion

Q9. What is implicit vs explicit conversion?

Implicit conversion

The conversion happens automatically when there is no risk of losing information.

int number = 100;
long value = number;

int → long is allowed implicitly.

Explicit conversion

You explicitly tell C# to convert the value.

double price = 99.99;

int value = (int)price;

Result:

99

The decimal portion is lost.

Interview statement:

Implicit conversion is performed automatically when the conversion is safe, while explicit conversion requires casting and may involve data loss.

Q10. What is the difference between Parse, TryParse, and Convert?

Very common practical question.

Parse

int age = int.Parse("25");

If the input is invalid:

int.Parse("abc");

it throws an exception.

TryParse

if (int.TryParse("25", out int age))
{
    Console.WriteLine(age);
}

Instead of throwing an exception for invalid input, it returns false.

For user/API input validation, TryParse is generally preferable.

Convert

int age = Convert.ToInt32("25");

Convert provides conversion methods for various types and has particular handling for null depending on the target conversion.

Interview summary

Parse expects valid input and throws when parsing fails. TryParse safely reports success or failure without using exceptions for normal invalid input. Convert provides a broader set of conversion utilities.

Part E — Operators

Q11. What are the major types of operators in C#?

Common categories:

Arithmetic
+  -  *  /  %

Comparison
==  !=  >  <  >=  <=

Logical
&&  ||  !

Assignment
=  +=  -=  *=  /=  ??=

Conditional
?:

Null-related
??  ?.

Type-related
is  as  typeof

Bitwise
&  |  ^  ~  <<  >>

You don't need to memorize them as a list only; you should understand the frequently used ones.

Q12. What is the difference between && and &?

This is a good interview follow-up.

&& is logical AND and uses short-circuit evaluation.

if (user != null && user.IsActive)
{
}

If user == null, the second condition isn't evaluated.

& is a bitwise AND operator for integral types, and it can also operate on booleans without short-circuiting.

Q13. What is the difference between || and |?

Similarly:

A || B

uses logical OR with short-circuiting.

A | B

is primarily a bitwise OR operator and does not provide the same short-circuit behavior.

Q14. What is the ternary operator?

The conditional operator:

condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse

Example:

int age = 20;

string result = age >= 18 ? "Adult" : "Minor";

Real-world:

string status = user.IsActive ? "Active" : "Inactive";

It is useful for simple conditional assignments.

Q15. What is is vs as?

is

Checks whether an object is compatible with a particular type.

if (obj is string)
{
    // obj is a string
}

Modern pattern matching can combine checking and assignment:

if (obj is string text)
{
    Console.WriteLine(text.Length);
}

as

Attempts a reference/nullable conversion and returns null if it can't be performed.

string? text = obj as string;

Interview answer

is is primarily used to test type compatibility, while as attempts a compatible reference or nullable conversion and returns null when it fails.

Part F — Control Flow

Q16. What control-flow statements are available in C#?

Main ones:

if / else
switch
for
foreach
while
do-while
break
continue
return

Q17. for vs foreach?

for is useful when you need an index or precise iteration control.

for (int i = 0; i < users.Count; i++)
{
    Console.WriteLine(users[i]);
}

foreach is cleaner when you simply want to iterate through elements.

foreach (var user in users)
{
    Console.WriteLine(user.Name);
}

Real-world example

Processing API results:

foreach (var order in orders)
{
    ProcessOrder(order);
}

If you don't need the index, foreach is usually clearer.

Part G — switch

Q18. When would you use switch instead of if-else?

Use switch when you're comparing one value against multiple possible cases.

switch (status)
{
    case "Pending":
        ProcessPending();
        break;

    case "Approved":
        ProcessApproved();
        break;

    case "Rejected":
        ProcessRejected();
        break;

    default:
        HandleUnknown();
        break;
}

This is often clearer than a long chain of if/else if.

Q19. What is a switch expression?

Modern C# provides a more concise expression form:

string message = status switch
{
    "Pending"  => "Order is pending",
    "Approved" => "Order is approved",
    "Rejected" => "Order was rejected",
    _          => "Unknown status"
};

This is particularly useful when you're producing a value from a set of cases.

  1. is vs as
  1. Implicit vs explicit conversion

  1. && vs &
  1. || vs |
  1. for vs foreach
  1. switch statement vs switch expression
  1. const
  1. Ternary operator
  1. ! null-forgiving operator

2. Methods in C# — Basic → Advanced

Part A — Methods & Parameters

Q1. What is a method in C#?

Interview-ready answer:

A method is a reusable block of code that performs a specific operation. It can accept input through parameters and optionally return a value.
public int Add(int a, int b)
{
    return a + b;
}

Here:

  • public → access modifier
  • int → return type
  • Add → method name
  • int a, int b → parameters
  • return → returns the result

Real-world example

In an ASP.NET Core service:

public User GetUserById(int id)
{
    return _repository.GetById(id);
}

The method encapsulates the business operation of retrieving a user.

Q2. What is the difference between a parameter and an argument?

This is a simple but common question.

Parameter

A variable declared in the method definition:

public int Add(int a, int b)

a and b are parameters.

Argument

The actual value passed when calling the method:

Add(10, 20);

10 and 20 are arguments.

Interview answer

A parameter is defined in the method declaration, while an argument is the actual value supplied when the method is called.

Q3. What are the different ways of passing parameters in C#?

The important parameter-passing mechanisms are:

  1. Value parameters
  1. ref
  1. out
  1. in
  1. Parameter arrays using params

Example:

void Method(
    int value,
    ref int refValue,
    out int outValue,
    in int inValue)
{
}

For your roadmap, we'll focus deeply on ref, out, and in.

Q4. What is pass-by-value in C#?

By default, C# passes parameters by value.

void Change(int number)
{
    number = 100;
}

int x = 10;

Change(x);

Console.WriteLine(x); // 10

A copy of x is passed to the method.

Changing the parameter doesn't change the original variable.

Interview-ready answer

By default, C# passes parameters by value, meaning the method receives a copy of the argument.

Q5. Does C# pass reference types by reference?

This is a very important interview trap.

The answer is:

No. Reference types are also passed by value by default. The value being copied is the reference to the object.

Example:

class Person
{
    public string Name { get; set; }
}

void ChangeName(Person person)
{
    person.Name = "Mike";
}

Person p = new Person
{
    Name = "John"
};

ChangeName(p);

Console.WriteLine(p.Name); // Mike

Why did the original object change?

Because both references point to the same object.

But:

void ChangePerson(Person person)
{
    person = new Person
    {
        Name = "Mike"
    };
}

Calling:

Person p = new Person
{
    Name = "John"
};

ChangePerson(p);

Console.WriteLine(p.Name);

still gives:

John

because the method only changed its local copy of the reference.

Strong interview statement

Reference types are not automatically passed by reference. They are passed by value, where the value being copied is the object reference.

This is a must-know concept.

Part B — ref

Q6. What is ref in C#?

ref allows a method to receive a reference to an existing variable.

void Change(ref int number)
{
    number = 100;
}

int x = 10;

Change(ref x);

Console.WriteLine(x); // 100

Both the method parameter and the original variable refer to the same storage location.

Important rule

The variable must already be initialized:

int x = 10;

Change(ref x);

You cannot do:

int x;

Change(ref x); // Error

because ref requires the variable to already have a value.

Q7. Why would you use ref?

Use ref when a method needs to read and potentially modify the caller's existing variable.

Example:

void Increment(ref int value)
{
    value++;
}

Real-world scenario:

Suppose you have a method that modifies a calculated value:

void ApplyDiscount(ref decimal price)
{
    price *= 0.9m;
}

Q8. What is the difference between normal parameter and ref?

Normal parameter

void Update(int value)
{
    value = 100;
}

Original value doesn't change.

ref

void Update(ref int value)
{
    value = 100;
}

Original value changes.

Interview answer

A normal parameter receives a copy of the value. A ref parameter allows the method to operate directly on the caller's variable.

Part C — out

Q9. What is out in C#?

out allows a method to return additional values through parameters.

bool TryGetAge(string input, out int age)
{
    return int.TryParse(input, out age);
}

Usage:

if (TryGetAge("25", out int age))
{
    Console.WriteLine(age);
}

Important rule

Unlike ref, the variable doesn't need to be initialized before calling the method.

int age;

GetAge(out age);

The method is responsible for assigning it.

Q10. What is the difference between ref and out?

This is one of the most frequently asked C# questions.

refout
Variable must be initialized before callDoesn't need initialization
Method can read existing valueMethod must assign a value
Used to modify existing valueUsed to return a value
ref required at declaration and callout required at declaration and call

Example:

void RefExample(ref int value)
{
    value += 10;
}
void OutExample(out int value)
{
    value = 100;
}

Easy way to remember

ref = input + output

out = output

Q11. Why does TryParse use out?

For example:

if (int.TryParse("123", out int number))
{
    Console.WriteLine(number);
}

TryParse needs to communicate two pieces of information:

  1. Did the conversion succeed?
  1. What was the converted value?

The bool return value communicates success/failure.

The out parameter communicates the converted value.

So:

bool → success/failure
out → actual result

This is a very good practical example to mention in interviews.

Part D — in

Q12. What is in parameter?

in passes an argument by reference but makes it read-only inside the method.

void Print(in int number)
{
    Console.WriteLine(number);
}

You cannot modify it:

void Print(in int number)
{
    number = 100; // Compile-time error
}

Why use it?

It can be useful when passing larger value types where you want to avoid copying while ensuring the method doesn't modify the value.

For example:

public struct OrderDetails
{
    public int Id;
    public decimal Amount;
}
void Process(in OrderDetails order)
{
    Console.WriteLine(order.Amount);
}

Interview answer

in passes an argument by reference for read-only access. It's useful particularly when passing larger value types without making a copy.

Q13. Difference between ref, out, and in

This is a must-prepare table.

Featurerefoutin
Passed by referenceYesYesYes
Must initialize before callYesNoYes
Method can readYesAfter assigningYes
Method can modifyYesYesNo
Main purposeRead/writeReturn valueRead-only reference
Common exampleModify variableTryParseLarge readonly struct

Interview-ready answer

ref is for read/write access to an existing variable, out is primarily for returning an additional value and doesn't require prior initialization, and in provides read-only reference access.

Part E — params

Although not explicitly one of the three highlighted items in your roadmap, it's an important parameter concept.

Q14. What is params?

params allows a method to accept a variable number of arguments.

int Add(params int[] numbers)
{
    int total = 0;

    foreach (int number in numbers)
    {
        total += number;
    }

    return total;
}

You can call:

Add(1, 2);
Add(1, 2, 3);
Add(1, 2, 3, 4, 5);

Real-world example

A logging or utility method might accept multiple values without requiring the caller to manually create an array.

Part F — Optional & Named Parameters

Q15. What are optional parameters?

You can provide a default value:

void CreateUser(string name, string role = "User")
{
}

You can call:

CreateUser("John");

or:

CreateUser("John", "Admin");

Q16. What are named arguments?

Instead of relying on parameter order:

CreateUser(
    name: "John",
    role: "Admin"
);

This improves readability, especially when methods have multiple parameters of the same type.

Part G — Method Overloading

Q17. What is method overloading?

Method overloading means defining multiple methods with the same name but different parameter signatures.

int Add(int a, int b)
{
    return a + b;
}

int Add(int a, int b, int c)
{
    return a + b + c;
}

The compiler determines which method to call based on the arguments.

Important

You cannot overload a method only by changing the return type.

This is invalid:

int GetValue()
{
    return 10;
}

string GetValue()
{
    return "Hello";
}

The compiler cannot distinguish them based only on return type.

Part H — Recursion

Q18. What is recursion?

Recursion occurs when a method calls itself to solve a smaller version of the same problem.

A recursive method normally needs:

  1. Base case
  1. Recursive case

Example:

int Factorial(int n)
{
    // Base case
    if (n == 0)
        return 1;

    // Recursive case
    return n * Factorial(n - 1);
}

For:

Factorial(5)

the calls are:

5 × Factorial(4)
        ↓
4 × Factorial(3)
        ↓
3 × Factorial(2)
        ↓
2 × Factorial(1)
        ↓
1 × Factorial(0)
        ↓
1

Result:

120

Q19. Why is the base case important?

Without a base case, recursion continues indefinitely until the call stack is exhausted.

Bad example:

void Print()
{
    Print();
}

This eventually results in a StackOverflowException.

Interview answer

The base case defines when recursion should stop. Without it, recursive calls continue indefinitely and can exhaust the call stack.

Q20. What are real-world uses of recursion?

Common examples:

1. Tree traversal

        10
       /  \
      5    20
     / \
    2   7

You can recursively traverse:

  • Binary trees
  • File/directory structures
  • XML/JSON hierarchical structures

2. Backtracking

Examples:

  • Permutations
  • Subsets
  • N-Queens
  • Generate Parentheses
  • Maze problems

3. Divide and conquer

Examples:

  • Merge Sort
  • Quick Sort
  • Binary Search

This connects directly with the DSA preparation you're doing.

Q21. Recursion vs iteration — which is better?

There isn't one universal answer.

Recursion

Advantages:

  • Natural for tree/hierarchical problems
  • Often simpler and easier to express
  • Useful for backtracking

Disadvantages:

  • Uses call stack
  • Can cause stack overflow for deep recursion
  • May have additional overhead

Iteration

Advantages:

  • Usually more memory-efficient for straightforward repetition
  • Doesn't create a new stack frame for every iteration

Example:

for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++)
{
    Console.WriteLine(i);
}

Interview answer

I prefer recursion when the problem naturally has a recursive structure, such as tree traversal or backtracking. For simple repetitive operations, iteration is generally more straightforward and avoids deep call-stack usage.

🔥 Top Methods Questions You Should Master

For your 3.9 YOE .NET interviews, prioritize these:

Must know

  1. What is a method?
  1. Parameter vs argument
  1. Pass-by-value
  1. Are reference types passed by reference?
  1. ref
  1. out
  1. ref vs out
  1. in
  1. ref vs out vs in
  1. Why does TryParse use out?
  1. Method overloading
  1. Why can't methods be overloaded only by return type?
  1. Recursion
  1. Base case
  1. Recursion vs iteration

Very likely follow-ups

Be ready for an interviewer to go:

"Explain ref."

↓

"How is ref different from out?"

↓

"What about in?"

↓

↓

"Are reference types passed by reference?"

That entire chain is worth knowing extremely well.

🎯 One-line revision sheet

Parameter → Input defined in method
Argument  → Actual value passed

Default  → Pass by value
ref      → Read + Write existing variable
out      → Produce a value
in       → Read-only reference
params   → Variable number of arguments

Overloading → Same method name, different parameter signature

Recursion → Method calls itself
Base case → Stops recursion

3. OOP in C# — Basic → Advanced

Part A — Encapsulation

Q1. What is encapsulation?

Interview-ready answer:

Encapsulation is the principle of bundling data and the methods that operate on that data together, while controlling access to the internal state through access modifiers and controlled interfaces.

Example:

public class BankAccount
{
    private decimal _balance;

    public decimal GetBalance()
    {
        return _balance;
    }

    public void Deposit(decimal amount)
    {
        if (amount > 0)
        {
            _balance += amount;
        }
    }
}

Here _balance is private, so outside code cannot directly modify it.

Instead:

account.Deposit(1000);

The class controls how its internal state changes.

Real-world scenario

In an e-commerce application:

public class Order
{
    private decimal _total;

    public void AddItem(decimal price)
    {
        if (price > 0)
            _total += price;
    }

    public decimal GetTotal()
    {
        return _total;
    }
}

The caller doesn't directly manipulate _total.

Strong interview statement

Encapsulation protects an object's internal state and ensures that changes happen through controlled operations.

Q2. How do you achieve encapsulation in C#?

Main mechanisms:

  • Access modifiers
  • Properties
  • Methods
  • Private fields
  • Interfaces

Example:

public class Employee
{
    private decimal _salary;

    public decimal Salary
    {
        get { return _salary; }
        private set { _salary = value; }
    }

    public void UpdateSalary(decimal salary)
    {
        if (salary > 0)
            Salary = salary;
    }
}

External code can read Salary, but cannot directly set it.

Q3. What are access modifiers in C#?

The important access modifiers are:

ModifierAccessibility
publicAccessible from anywhere
privateOnly within the containing type
protectedContaining type + derived types
internalSame assembly
protected internalSame assembly OR derived type
private protectedSame assembly AND derived type

Common example

public class Employee
{
    private decimal salary;

    protected void CalculateBonus()
    {
    }

    public void Process()
    {
    }
}

Interview tip

For most application code:

Keep members as restrictive as possible and expose only what consumers actually need.

Part B — Inheritance

Q4. What is inheritance?

Interview-ready answer:

Inheritance allows a class to derive from another class and reuse or extend its behavior and members.

Example:

public class Animal
{
    public void Eat()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Eating");
    }
}

public class Dog : Animal
{
    public void Bark()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Barking");
    }
}

Now:

Dog dog = new Dog();

dog.Eat();
dog.Bark();

Dog inherits Eat() from Animal.

Q5. Why is inheritance useful?

Inheritance can provide:

  • Code reuse
  • Common behavior
  • Hierarchical relationships
  • Polymorphic behavior

Example:

Animal
  |
  +-- Dog
  |
  +-- Cat

Common behavior can be placed in Animal, while specialized behavior belongs to derived classes.

Q6. Does C# support multiple inheritance?

No, C# doesn't support multiple inheritance between classes.

This is not allowed:

class C : A, B
{
}

However, a class can implement multiple interfaces:

class PaymentService : IPayment, ILogging
{
}

Interview-ready answer

C# supports single class inheritance but allows multiple interface implementations. This avoids many of the ambiguity problems associated with multiple class inheritance.

Q7. What is the difference between is-a and has-a relationships?

is-a → inheritance

Dog is an Animal
class Dog : Animal
{
}

has-a → composition

Order has a PaymentService
class OrderService
{
    private readonly IPaymentService _paymentService;
}

Important design point

In modern application design, composition is often preferred over inheritance when there isn't a strong true is-a relationship.

Example:

Instead of:

OrderService
    ↓ inherits
PaymentService

prefer:

OrderService
    ↓ uses
IPaymentService

This also works naturally with dependency injection in ASP.NET Core.

Part C — Polymorphism

Q8. What is polymorphism?

Interview-ready answer:

Polymorphism means one interface or base type can represent different implementations, allowing the same operation to behave differently depending on the actual object.

There are two major forms commonly discussed in C#:

  1. Compile-time polymorphism
  1. Runtime polymorphism

Q9. What is compile-time polymorphism?

Method overloading is a common example.

public class Calculator
{
    public int Add(int a, int b)
    {
        return a + b;
    }

    public int Add(int a, int b, int c)
    {
        return a + b + c;
    }
}

The compiler determines which method to call based on the method signature.

So:

Add(10, 20);

calls one overload, while:

Add(10, 20, 30);

calls another.

Q10. What is runtime polymorphism?

Runtime polymorphism is commonly achieved using:

  • Base classes
  • virtual
  • override
  • Interfaces

Example:

public class Animal
{
    public virtual void MakeSound()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Animal sound");
    }
}

public class Dog : Animal
{
    public override void MakeSound()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Bark");
    }
}

Now:

Animal animal = new Dog();

animal.MakeSound();

Output:

Bark

Although the variable type is Animal, the actual object is Dog.

The overridden implementation is selected at runtime.

Q11. What is virtual and override?

virtual

Allows a derived class to replace the implementation.

public virtual void Process()
{
}

override

Provides the derived implementation.

public override void Process()
{
}

Example:

class Payment
{
    public virtual void ProcessPayment()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Generic payment");
    }
}

class CreditCardPayment : Payment
{
    public override void ProcessPayment()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Credit card payment");
    }
}

Q12. What is the difference between override and new?

This is a good Senior-level follow-up.

override

Overrides a virtual method and participates in runtime polymorphism.

class Dog : Animal
{
    public override void MakeSound()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Bark");
    }
}

new

Hides the base member.

class Dog : Animal
{
    public new void MakeSound()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Bark");
    }
}

Consider:

Animal animal = new Dog();

animal.MakeSound();

With override, the derived implementation executes.

With new, the behavior depends on the reference type, so the base implementation can execute.

Interview answer

override provides runtime polymorphism by replacing a virtual member, while new hides the base member rather than overriding it.

Q13. Can you override a private method?

No.

A private member isn't accessible to derived classes, so it cannot be overridden.

Also, a method must be appropriately declared, such as virtual, abstract, or already override, to be overridden.

Q14. Can you override a static method?

No.

Static members belong to the type rather than an object instance and don't participate in runtime polymorphism.

You can hide static members using new, but that isn't overriding.

Part D — Abstraction

Q15. What is abstraction?

Interview-ready answer:

Abstraction means exposing the essential behavior of an object while hiding unnecessary implementation details.

For example, a payment service might expose:

public interface IPaymentService
{
    void ProcessPayment(decimal amount);
}

The caller only knows:

_paymentService.ProcessPayment(1000);

It doesn't need to know whether the implementation uses:

  • Stripe
  • Razorpay
  • PayPal
  • a bank API

The implementation details are hidden.

Q16. How do you achieve abstraction in C#?

The two primary mechanisms are:

1. Abstract classes

public abstract class Payment
{
    public abstract void ProcessPayment();

    public void LogPayment()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Payment logged");
    }
}

2. Interfaces

public interface IPayment
{
    void ProcessPayment();
}

Q17. Abstract class vs interface?

This is a must-know interview question.

Abstract ClassInterface
Can contain implementationPrimarily defines a contract
Can contain fieldsCannot have instance fields like a class
Can have constructorsNo instance constructors
Supports abstract + concrete membersDefines contracts; modern C# also supports default interface implementations
Class can inherit only one classClass can implement multiple interfaces
Useful for closely related typesUseful for capabilities/contracts

Example abstract class:

public abstract class Employee
{
    public string Name { get; set; }

    public abstract decimal CalculateSalary();

    public void PrintName()
    {
        Console.WriteLine(Name);
    }
}

Interface:

public interface INotificationService
{
    void Send(string message);
}

Q18. When would you use an interface vs abstract class?

Use an interface when:

You want to define a contract/capability.

public interface IEmailSender
{
    Task SendAsync(string message);
}

Different implementations:

IEmailSender
    ├── SmtpEmailSender
    ├── SendGridEmailSender
    └── AwsEmailSender

Use an abstract class when:

The derived classes share common state or implementation.

public abstract class Employee
{
    protected decimal BaseSalary;

    public abstract decimal CalculateSalary();

    public void LogEmployee()
    {
    }
}

Strong interview answer

I use an interface when I mainly need a contract and multiple unrelated implementations may exist. I use an abstract class when related types share common state or implementation in addition to requiring specialized behavior.

Q19. Can an abstract class have a constructor?

Yes.

public abstract class Employee
{
    protected Employee(string name)
    {
        Name = name;
    }

    public string Name { get; }
}

The abstract class itself cannot be instantiated:

new Employee("John"); // Invalid

But its constructor is called when a derived class is created.

public class Developer : Employee
{
    public Developer(string name)
        : base(name)
    {
    }
}

Q20. Can an abstract class contain non-abstract methods?

Yes.

public abstract class Payment
{
    public abstract void Process();

    public void Log()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Payment logged");
    }
}

An abstract class can contain both:

  • Abstract members
  • Concrete members

Q21. Can an interface contain implementation?

In modern C#, interfaces can contain default implementations.

Example:

public interface ILogger
{
    void Log(string message);

    void LogError(string message)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"ERROR: {message}");
    }
}

However, in typical application architecture, interfaces are commonly used primarily as contracts, while implementation lives in implementing classes.

🔥 Q22. Explain all four pillars of OOP

This is one of the most important questions.

1. Encapsulation

Protect internal state.

Private data + controlled access

2. Inheritance

Reuse/extend behavior.

Dog → Animal

3. Polymorphism

Same contract, different behavior.

IPayment
 ├── CardPayment
 └── UpiPayment

4. Abstraction

Hide implementation details and expose essential behavior.

IPayment.ProcessPayment()

Interview-ready answer

The four pillars are encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, and abstraction. Encapsulation protects internal state, inheritance allows reuse and extension, polymorphism allows the same contract to have different implementations, and abstraction hides implementation details behind a simpler interface.

🔥 Q23. Give a real-world example combining all four pillars

Imagine an e-commerce payment system.

Abstraction

public interface IPaymentService
{
    void Pay(decimal amount);
}

The application only knows the payment contract.

Inheritance

public abstract class Payment
{
    protected decimal Amount;

    protected Payment(decimal amount)
    {
        Amount = amount;
    }
}

Polymorphism

public class CreditCardPayment : Payment, IPaymentService
{
    public CreditCardPayment(decimal amount)
        : base(amount)
    {
    }

    public void Pay(decimal amount)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Processing credit card");
    }
}

Another implementation:

public class UpiPayment : Payment, IPaymentService
{
    public UpiPayment(decimal amount)
        : base(amount)
    {
    }

    public void Pay(decimal amount)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Processing UPI");
    }
}

The application can work with:

IPaymentService payment = new UpiPayment(1000);

payment.Pay(1000);

Encapsulation

Amount is protected rather than exposed for arbitrary modification.

  1. Can you override a static method?

🎯 Interview Revision Sheet

ENCAPSULATION
→ Protect internal state
→ private fields + controlled methods/properties

INHERITANCE
→ Reuse/extend behavior
→ class Dog : Animal

POLYMORPHISM
→ One contract, different behavior
→ overload = compile time
→ override = runtime

ABSTRACTION
→ Hide implementation details
→ interfaces / abstract classes

INTERFACE
→ Contract/capability
→ Multiple interfaces possible

ABSTRACT CLASS
→ Shared state + shared implementation + abstract behavior

override
→ Runtime polymorphism

new
→ Member hiding

COMPOSITION
→ HAS-A relationship
→ Often preferable when inheritance isn't a true IS-A relationship

The most important chain to practice aloud

What is OOP?

→ Explain the four pillars.

→ What is polymorphism?

→ virtual vs override vs new?

→ Abstract class vs interface?

→ When would you choose one in an ASP.NET Core application?

4. Types in C# — Classes → Structs → Records → Enums

This is a high-priority interview topic because interviewers frequently ask you to compare class, struct, and record, especially for Senior .NET roles.

A useful mental model is:

Class = object with identity/behavior

Struct = small value

Record = data with value-based equality

Enum = named set of values

Microsoft also frames classes, structs, and records as different ways to define types, with different semantics around inheritance, equality, mutability, and copying. Microsoft Learn

Part A — Classes

Q1. What is a class in C#?

Interview-ready answer:

A class is a reference type that acts as a blueprint for creating objects. It can contain data and behavior through fields, properties, methods, constructors, events, and other members.

Example:

public class Employee
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Name { get; set; }

    public void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{Name} is working.");
    }
}

Creating an object:

Employee employee = new Employee
{
    Id = 1,
    Name = "John"
};

employee.Work();

A class can encapsulate both state and behavior. Microsoft Learn

Q2. What is an object?

An object is an instance of a class created at runtime. It represents a concrete entity containing the state and behavior defined by the class.
Employee employee = new Employee();

Here:

Employee → class/type
employee → variable/reference
new Employee() → object/instance

Q3. What happens when you assign one class object to another variable?

This is a very important interview question.

Employee e1 = new Employee
{
    Name = "John"
};

Employee e2 = e1;

e2.Name = "Mike";

Console.WriteLine(e1.Name);

Output:

Mike

Why?

Because Employee is a reference type. Assignment copies the reference, not an independent copy of the object. GitHub

Conceptually:

e1 ─────┐
        ↓
     Employee
     Name = Mike
        ↑
e2 ─────┘

The deeper memory implications will come in Topic #5 — Memory.

Q4. What are the important members of a class?

A class can contain:

  • Fields
  • Constants
  • Properties
  • Methods
  • Constructors
  • Events
  • Finalizers
  • Indexers
  • Operators
  • Nested types Microsoft Learn

Example:

public class Employee
{
    // Field
    private int _id;

    // Property
    public string Name { get; set; }

    // Constructor
    public Employee(int id)
    {
        _id = id;
    }

    // Method
    public void Work()
    {
    }
}

Q5. What is a constructor?

A constructor is a special member of a class that is automatically called when an object is created. It is mainly used to initialize the object's state.
public class Employee
{
    public int Id { get; }
    public string Name { get; }

    public Employee(int id, string name)
    {
        Id = id;
        Name = name;
    }
}

Usage:

var employee = new Employee(101, "John");

Q6. Can a class have multiple constructors?

Yes.

This is called constructor overloading.

public class Employee
{
    public int Id { get; }
    public string Name { get; }

    public Employee()
    {
    }

    public Employee(int id, string name)
    {
        Id = id;
        Name = name;
    }
}

Q7. What is a static class?

A static class:

  • Cannot be instantiated.
  • Can contain only static members.
  • Cannot be used as a base class.
public static class MathHelper
{
    public static int Add(int a, int b)
    {
        return a + b;
    }
}

Usage:

int result = MathHelper.Add(10, 20);

You don't write:

var helper = new MathHelper(); // Invalid

Microsoft documents static classes as classes that cannot be instantiated and can contain only static members. Microsoft Learn

Q8. What is a sealed class?

A sealed class cannot be inherited.

public sealed class PaymentProcessor
{
}

This is invalid:

public class CustomProcessor : PaymentProcessor
{
}

Why use it?

When you explicitly want to prevent inheritance.

For example, if a class's behavior should not be extended through inheritance.

Part B — Structs

Q9. What is a struct?

Interview-ready answer:

A struct is a value type that can encapsulate data and related functionality. It is generally appropriate for small, logically value-like data.

Example:

public struct Point
{
    public int X { get; set; }
    public int Y { get; set; }
}

Usage:

Point p1 = new Point();

p1.X = 10;
p1.Y = 20;

Structs are value types. Microsoft Learn

Q10. What is the difference between class and struct?

This is a must-know interview question.

ClassStruct
Reference typeValue type
Supports inheritanceDoesn't support class inheritance
Can have finalizerCannot have finalizer
Suitable for objects with identitySuitable for value-like data
Assignment copies referenceAssignment copies value
Can be null by defaultNon-nullable unless Nullable<T>
Can have parameterless constructorsModern C# supports them
Can implement interfacesCan implement interfaces

Example:

Class

class Person
{
    public string Name { get; set; }
}
Person p1 = new Person();
Person p2 = p1;

p2.Name = "John";

Both refer to the same object.

Struct

struct Point
{
    public int X;
}
Point p1 = new Point { X = 10 };
Point p2 = p1;

p2.X = 20;

Now:

p1.X = 10
p2.X = 20

The value was copied.

Q11. Should every small object be a struct?

No.

This is an important design question.

Structs are generally best for small, value-like types where copying makes sense.

Good examples:

Point
Coordinates
Temperature
Money-like value objects
Date/time-like values

Poor candidates are typically large, mutable objects with complex identity and behavior.

Microsoft's guidance similarly recommends structs for small value-like data and classes for mutable state/behavior or reference identity. Microsoft Learn

Interview answer

I wouldn't choose a struct merely because the object is small. I first consider whether the type has value semantics, whether copying it makes sense, and whether its size and mutability make a value type appropriate.

Q12. What is a readonly struct?

A readonly struct is a struct designed to be immutable.

public readonly struct Point
{
    public int X { get; }
    public int Y { get; }

    public Point(int x, int y)
    {
        X = x;
        Y = y;
    }
}

Its instance members can't mutate the struct's state.

This becomes particularly relevant later when we discuss performance and readonly behavior.

Part C — Records

Q13. What is a record in C#?

Very important for modern C# interviews.

A record is a type designed primarily for representing data and provides compiler-generated value-based equality and convenient syntax for immutable-style data.

Example:

public record Employee(string Name, int Age);

Now:

var e1 = new Employee("John", 30);
var e2 = new Employee("John", 30);

Console.WriteLine(e1 == e2);

Result:

True

Even though they are separate objects.

Records provide value-based equality, useful ToString(), and with expressions for nondestructive mutation. Microsoft Learn

Q14. Why were records introduced?

Before records, if you wanted value-based equality for a data-oriented class, you often had to write or generate:

Equals()
GetHashCode()
ToString()

Records provide this behavior automatically.

Example:

public record Product(
    int Id,
    string Name,
    decimal Price
);

Now two products with the same values compare equal.

Q15. What is the difference between a class and a record?

This is extremely important.

Class

public class Employee
{
    public string Name { get; set; }
}

By default, class equality is based on reference identity.

var e1 = new Employee { Name = "John" };
var e2 = new Employee { Name = "John" };

Console.WriteLine(e1 == e2);

Normally:

False

Record

public record Employee(string Name);
var e1 = new Employee("John");
var e2 = new Employee("John");

Console.WriteLine(e1 == e2);

Result:

True

Interview answer

A normal class is generally identity-oriented and uses reference equality by default, while a record is data-oriented and provides compiler-generated value-based equality. Microsoft Learn

Q16. Are records reference types or value types?

It depends.

record

public record Employee(string Name);

This is a record class, therefore a reference type.

record struct

public record struct Point(int X, int Y);

This is a value type.

So:

record class → reference type
record struct → value type

The record modifier adds data-oriented behavior, while class or struct determines the underlying reference/value semantics. Microsoft Learn

Q17. What is the with expression?

with creates a copy of a record while allowing selected properties to change.

public record Employee(string Name, string Department);
var employee1 =
    new Employee("John", "IT");

var employee2 =
    employee1 with { Department = "HR" };

Now:

employee1 → John, IT
employee2 → John, HR

The original record isn't modified.

This is called nondestructive mutation. Microsoft Learn

Q18. Are records always immutable?

Be careful with this interview question.

A better answer is:

Records are designed to support data-oriented, often immutable models, but record itself doesn't mean every property is automatically deeply immutable.

For example:

public record Product
{
    public string Name { get; init; }
    public decimal Price { get; set; }
}

Price is mutable because it has set.

Also, reference-type properties can still refer to mutable objects.

So don't simply say:

"Records are immutable."

Say:

"Records provide convenient syntax and semantics for immutable-style data, but immutability depends on how the members are defined and whether referenced objects are themselves mutable."

Q19. What is a positional record?

This:

public record Employee(
    int Id,
    string Name,
    string Department
);

is a positional record.

It provides concise syntax for declaring the data and generates corresponding members and useful equality/deconstruction behavior. Microsoft Learn

Part D — Enums

Q20. What is an enum?

An enum is a value type that defines a set of named constants.

Example:

public enum OrderStatus
{
    Pending,
    Approved,
    Shipped,
    Delivered,
    Cancelled
}

Usage:

OrderStatus status = OrderStatus.Approved;

This makes code much more readable than using arbitrary integers or strings.

Q21. What are the underlying values of enum members?

By default, enum values start at 0 and increment by 1.

public enum OrderStatus
{
    Pending,    // 0
    Approved,   // 1
    Shipped,    // 2
    Delivered   // 3
}

You can explicitly assign values:

public enum OrderStatus
{
    Pending = 1,
    Approved = 2,
    Shipped = 5
}

Q22. Can an enum have a different underlying type?

Yes.

By default, an enum uses int, but you can specify an integral type.

public enum Status : byte
{
    Pending = 1,
    Approved = 2,
    Rejected = 3
}

Valid underlying types include integral types such as:

byte
sbyte
short
ushort
int
uint
long
ulong

Q23. What is a [Flags] enum?

A flags enum allows multiple values to be combined using bitwise operations.

Example:

[Flags]
public enum Permission
{
    None   = 0,
    Read   = 1,
    Write  = 2,
    Delete = 4
}

Now:

Permission permission =
    Permission.Read | Permission.Write;

The user has:

Read + Write

You can check:

if ((permission & Permission.Write) != 0)
{
    Console.WriteLine("Can write");
}

Real-world scenario

Authorization:

Read
Write
Delete
Export
Admin

A flags enum can represent combinations efficiently.

Q24. How do you convert an enum to an integer?

OrderStatus status = OrderStatus.Approved;

int value = (int)status;

And integer to enum:

OrderStatus status =
    (OrderStatus)2;

But be careful: casting an integer doesn't necessarily guarantee that the value is a named enum member.

Q25. How do you safely parse an enum?

Use Enum.TryParse.

if (Enum.TryParse<OrderStatus>(
        "Approved",
        out var status))
{
    Console.WriteLine(status);
}

For external/user input, also consider validating that the resulting value is defined when appropriate.

🔥 The Most Important Comparison

Class vs Struct vs Record vs Enum

FeatureClassStructRecord ClassRecord StructEnum
Main purposeObjects/behaviorValue-like dataData + value equalityValue-like data + value equalityNamed constants
Type categoryReferenceValueReferenceValueValue
Reference equality by defaultYesNoNoNo
Value-based equalityCan implementYes via Equals behaviorBuilt inBuilt inValue-based
InheritanceYesNo class inheritanceYes between record classesNoNo
with supportNoModern structs have withYesYesNo
Good for mutable stateYesUsually avoid large mutable structsUsually data-orientedSmall value dataNo
ExampleOrderPointUserDtoCoordinateOrderStatus

The important distinction is that record is not itself a third category alongside class and struct: it modifies a class or struct to add record semantics. Microsoft Learn

🎯 Real-World .NET Scenario

Suppose you're building an order-management API.

Order → Class

public class Order
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public decimal Total { get; set; }

    public void CalculateTotal()
    {
        // Business logic
    }
}

Why?

The order has identity, mutable state, and behavior.

Address / DTO → Record

public record AddressDto(
    string City,
    string State,
    string Country
);

Why?

It's primarily data and value equality can be useful.

Coordinates → Struct

public readonly struct Coordinates
{
    public double Latitude { get; }
    public double Longitude { get; }

    public Coordinates(double latitude, double longitude)
    {
        Latitude = latitude;
        Longitude = longitude;
    }
}

Why?

It's a small value-like object.

OrderStatus → Enum

public enum OrderStatus
{
    Pending,
    Approved,
    Shipped,
    Delivered,
    Cancelled
}

Why?

The property represents one value from a fixed set of states.

This matches the general C# type-selection guidance: class for mutable state/behavior and identity, record class for immutable/value-based data, record struct for small copyable value data, and enum for named constant values. Microsoft Learn

↓

5. Memory in C# — Stack → Heap → Boxing → GC → IDisposable

This is a very high-priority C# interview topic, especially for your experience level. Interviewers often use it to distinguish someone who knows C# syntax from someone who understands how .NET actually works.

Important: Don't memorize the oversimplified rule “value types are always on the stack and reference types are always on the heap.” That's not accurate. We'll build the correct mental model below.

Part A — Stack and Heap

Q1. What is the stack and what is the heap?

Interview-ready answer

The stack is used for managing method execution, including call frames and local state, while the managed heap is where the CLR allocates objects that are managed by the garbage collector. The exact location of a particular value depends on its context and implementation details.

The .NET GC manages allocations on the managed heap and reclaims objects that are no longer reachable. Microsoft Learn

Conceptually:

STACK                         MANAGED HEAP

Method calls                  Objects
Local variables               Class instances
References                    Arrays
                              Strings
                              Other managed objects

Example

public void Calculate()
{
    int x = 10;

    Person person = new Person();

    person.Name = "John";
}

You should not simply say:

x → stack
person → stack
Person object → heap

A better explanation is:

person is a local reference, while the Person object is allocated on the managed heap. The precise storage details of locals are an implementation concern of the runtime/JIT.

Q2. What is the difference between stack and heap?

StackManaged Heap
Associated with method executionStores managed objects
Automatically managed as methods execute/returnManaged by GC
Per-thread execution stackShared managed heap within a process
Very fast allocation/deallocation for stack framesObject allocation + GC management
Limited in sizeGenerally much larger
Stack overflow possibleOut-of-memory can occur

Interview answer

The stack primarily manages execution state for threads, while the managed heap stores dynamically allocated managed objects and is managed by the garbage collector.

Q3. What is a stack frame?

Every method invocation has execution information associated with it.

For example:

void MethodA()
{
    MethodB();
}

void MethodB()
{
    int x = 10;
}

Conceptually:

Stack
┌──────────────────┐
│ MethodB frame    │
│ x = 10           │
├──────────────────┤
│ MethodA frame    │
├──────────────────┤
│ Main frame       │
└──────────────────┘

When MethodB() returns, its execution frame is removed.

Interview statement

A stack frame represents the execution context of a method invocation.

Q4. What happens when a method returns?

Consider:

void Calculate()
{
    int x = 100;
}

When Calculate() finishes, its method execution state is no longer needed.

The stack unwinds automatically as the method returns.

This is one reason stack-based execution is very efficient.

Part B — Value Types and Reference Types

Q5. Are value types stored on the stack and reference types on the heap?

This is a trap question.

Don't answer:

Yes, value types are on the stack and reference types are on the heap.

That's an oversimplification.

Better interview answer:

Value types and reference types describe their copying and type semantics, not a universal storage location. A value type can be stored on the stack, inside an object on the heap, in an array, or in other contexts. Reference-type objects are normally allocated on the managed heap, while a reference to those objects can itself be stored in different locations.

This is a much stronger Senior-level answer.

Q6. What happens when you copy a value type?

int a = 10;
int b = a;

b = 20;

Result:

a = 10
b = 20

The value is copied.

With a struct:

Point p1 = new Point(10, 20);
Point p2 = p1;

p2.X = 100;

p1 and p2 are independent value copies.

Q7. What happens when you copy a reference type?

Person p1 = new Person
{
    Name = "John"
};

Person p2 = p1;

p2.Name = "Mike";

Now:

p1.Name → Mike
p2.Name → Mike

because both references point to the same object.

p1 ─────┐
        ↓
      Person
      Name = Mike
        ↑
p2 ─────┘

Part C — Boxing

Q8. What is boxing?

Very important interview question.

Boxing is the conversion of a value type to object or to an interface type that it implements. It creates an object representation on the managed heap and copies the value into that object. Microsoft Learn

Example:

int number = 10;

object obj = number;

Here:

int
 ↓
boxing
 ↓
object on managed heap

The value 10 is copied into the boxed object. Microsoft Learn

Q9. What is unboxing?

Unboxing extracts the value from a boxed object.

object obj = 10;

int number = (int)obj;

Conceptually:

boxed object
     ↓
 unboxing
     ↓
    int

The cast must be compatible with the actual boxed value.

object obj = 10;

long number = (long)obj; // Invalid

Even though int can normally convert to long, the boxed object contains an int, not a boxed long.

Q10. Why is boxing expensive?

Boxing can involve:

  1. Allocating an object.
  1. Copying the value into it.
  1. Later unboxing/casting.

Microsoft specifically notes that boxing allocates an object on the heap and that boxing/unboxing can have performance costs. Microsoft Learn

Example:

int number = 10;

object obj = number; // Boxing
int result = (int)obj; // Unboxing

Interview answer

Boxing can cause heap allocation and copying, so excessive boxing can create additional allocations and GC pressure.

Q11. Give a real-world example where boxing can happen.

Consider a non-generic collection:

ArrayList numbers = new ArrayList();

numbers.Add(10);
numbers.Add(20);
numbers.Add(30);

ArrayList stores values as object, so the integers are boxed.

Modern C# generally prefers:

List<int> numbers = new List<int>();

This avoids boxing of each integer into object.

This leads to an important principle:

Generics help provide type safety and can avoid unnecessary boxing for value types.

We'll explore this deeply in Topic #7 — Generics.

Q12. Does assigning an int to object always mean boxing?

For normal value-type-to-object conversion, yes, that's boxing:

int x = 10;
object y = x;

But the exact runtime/JIT behavior can involve optimizations in some scenarios. For interview purposes, the correct conceptual model is:

Value type → object = boxing.

Part D — Garbage Collection

Q13. What is Garbage Collection?

Must know.

Garbage Collection, or GC, is the .NET runtime's automatic memory-management system. It identifies managed objects that are no longer reachable by the application and reclaims their memory. Microsoft Learn

Example:

void CreateUser()
{
    var user = new User();
}

After CreateUser() returns, if nothing else references that User object, it may eventually become eligible for garbage collection.

CreateUser()
     ↓
new User()
     ↓
No reachable references
     ↓
Eligible for GC
     ↓
GC reclaims memory

Q14. Does GC immediately remove an object when it becomes unreachable?

No.

This is an important distinction.

When an object becomes unreachable:

It becomes eligible for garbage collection.

The GC decides when collection occurs.

The runtime considers factors such as allocation activity and memory pressure when deciding when to perform a collection. Microsoft Learn

So:

Object becomes unreachable
        ↓
Eligible for GC
        ↓
GC runs later
        ↓
Memory reclaimed

Q15. How does the GC know whether an object is still being used?

The GC starts from GC roots and determines which objects remain reachable.

Examples of roots include:

  • Local variables on thread stacks
  • Static fields
  • CPU registers
  • GC handles
  • Finalization-related structures

Objects that cannot be reached from the roots can eventually be reclaimed. Microsoft Learn

Simplified example

GC Root
  ↓
Service
  ↓
Customer
  ↓
Address

All are reachable.

But:

SomeObject
    X

If nothing references SomeObject, it can become eligible for collection.

Q16. What are GC generations?

.NET's GC uses generations to optimize collection.

The main generations are:

Generation 0
Generation 1
Generation 2

Generation 0

Contains relatively new objects.

Short-lived objects are often collected here.

Generation 1

Acts as a buffer between short-lived and long-lived objects.

Generation 2

Contains longer-lived objects.

Interview answer

The generational GC is based on the observation that many objects are short-lived. Instead of examining the entire managed heap every time, the runtime can focus more frequently on younger generations and less frequently on older ones.

Q17. Why does .NET use generations?

Suppose your ASP.NET Core API creates thousands of temporary objects while processing requests.

Many of them become unused quickly.

Instead of repeatedly scanning every long-lived object, the GC can focus more frequently on younger objects.

Conceptually:

New objects
    ↓
Gen 0
    ↓ survive
Gen 1
    ↓ survive
Gen 2

This makes memory management more efficient.

Q18. What is Gen 0, Gen 1, and Gen 2 collection?

A collection can target different generations.

Generally:

Gen 0 collection
→ Gen 0

Gen 1 collection
→ Gen 0 + Gen 1

Gen 2 collection
→ Gen 0 + Gen 1 + Gen 2

A full collection is more expensive than a small young-generation collection.

Q19. What is the Large Object Heap (LOH)?

The Large Object Heap is used for sufficiently large allocations.

For example:

byte[] buffer = new byte[largeSize];

Large allocations are handled differently from ordinary small object allocations.

Why should you care?

In high-throughput applications, frequent large allocations can create memory pressure and affect GC performance.

This becomes especially relevant when you're dealing with:

  • Large arrays
  • Large JSON payloads
  • File processing
  • Image processing
  • Large response buffers

The .NET GC documentation treats the LOH as a distinct area of GC behavior. Microsoft Learn

Q20. What is a memory leak in a garbage-collected application?

A common misconception is:

"Garbage collection means memory leaks cannot happen."

That's false.

A managed memory leak can happen when an object is still reachable even though the application no longer logically needs it.

Example:

static List<object> cache = new List<object>();

void AddData()
{
    cache.Add(new LargeObject());
}

If cache keeps growing indefinitely, the objects remain reachable.

The GC cannot collect them because the application still has references to them.

Interview answer

GC prevents many manual-memory-management errors, but it doesn't prevent logical memory leaks. If unnecessary objects remain reachable through references such as static collections, caches, event subscriptions, or long-lived services, the GC cannot reclaim them.

Part E — GC.Collect()

Q21. Should we manually call GC.Collect()?

Generally, no.

GC.Collect();

The GC normally determines when collection is appropriate.

Microsoft notes that in almost all cases you don't need to call GC.Collect() manually; it is mainly useful in special scenarios and testing. Microsoft Learn

Interview answer

I generally avoid manually calling GC.Collect() because the runtime's GC is designed to make collection decisions based on allocation and memory conditions. Manually forcing collections can introduce unnecessary overhead.

Part F — IDisposable

Q22. What is IDisposable?

Extremely important for .NET interviews.

IDisposable provides a standard mechanism for deterministic cleanup of resources, especially unmanaged resources or managed objects that wrap resources requiring explicit release. Microsoft Learn

It defines:

public interface IDisposable
{
    void Dispose();
}

Example:

public class ResourceManager : IDisposable
{
    public void Dispose()
    {
        // Cleanup
    }
}

Q23. Why do we need IDisposable if we already have GC?

This is one of the most important questions.

GC handles:

Managed object memory.

Dispose() handles:

Resources that need deterministic cleanup, especially unmanaged resources and managed wrappers around such resources.

Examples:

File handles
Database connections
Network resources
Streams
OS handles

The GC doesn't know how to release an external OS resource just because the managed wrapper object is no longer reachable. Microsoft Learn

Interview answer

GC manages the memory of managed objects, but it doesn't deterministically release external resources. IDisposable gives us a way to explicitly release those resources when we're finished with them.

Q24. What is the using statement?

Instead of manually calling:

resource.Dispose();

you can use:

using (var stream = File.OpenRead("data.txt"))
{
    // Use stream
}

When execution leaves the using scope, Dispose() is called.

Microsoft recommends using the C# using construct or an equivalent try/finally pattern for objects implementing IDisposable. Microsoft Learn

Q25. What does using actually translate to conceptually?

Conceptually:

using (var resource = CreateResource())
{
    DoSomething(resource);
}

is roughly equivalent to:

var resource = CreateResource();

try
{
    DoSomething(resource);
}
finally
{
    resource?.Dispose();
}

So even if an exception occurs:

Create resource
      ↓
Use resource
      ↓
Exception?
      ↓
finally
      ↓
Dispose()

This is why using is important for reliable cleanup.

Q26. What is the difference between GC and Dispose?

GC

  • Automatic
  • Handles managed memory
  • Non-deterministic
  • Runtime controlled

Dispose

  • Explicit/deterministic
  • Releases owned resources
  • Called by code/consumer or language constructs like using
  • Commonly used for unmanaged resources and disposable wrappers

Excellent interview answer

GC answers "when can the memory of this managed object be reclaimed?"

Dispose() answers "when should this object release the resources it owns?"

That's a very good way to explain the difference.

Part G — Finalizers

Q27. What is a finalizer?

A finalizer is a mechanism associated with Object.Finalize that allows cleanup to be performed when an object is finalized by the GC.

In C# syntax:

~MyClass()
{
    // Cleanup
}

But don't confuse a finalizer with Dispose().

Important:

A finalizer is:

  • Non-deterministic
  • Controlled by the GC/finalization mechanism
  • Primarily relevant to unmanaged resource cleanup
  • More expensive than ordinary disposal

Microsoft notes that finalization is non-deterministic and recommends safe handles for unmanaged resources where applicable. Microsoft Learn

Q28. Dispose() vs Finalizer?

Dispose()Finalizer
Explicit/deterministicNon-deterministic
Called by consumer/codeInvoked through GC finalization
Usually preferredFallback mechanism
Can release resources immediatelyHappens later
using can call it automaticallyGC controls timing

Interview answer

Dispose() provides deterministic cleanup, while a finalizer provides a non-deterministic fallback for unmanaged resources. Modern .NET code should generally prefer IDisposable and safe handles rather than implementing finalizers unnecessarily. Microsoft Learn

Q29. What is GC.SuppressFinalize()?

If an object has a finalizer and Dispose() has already performed the required cleanup, you can prevent the finalizer from running later:

GC.SuppressFinalize(this);

Typical dispose pattern:

public void Dispose()
{
    Dispose(true);
    GC.SuppressFinalize(this);
}

The purpose is to tell the GC that finalization isn't needed because cleanup has already been performed. Microsoft Learn

Q30. What is the Dispose Pattern?

For a type that owns resources, the standard pattern can look like:

public class ResourceHolder : IDisposable
{
    private bool _disposed;

    public void Dispose()
    {
        Dispose(true);
        GC.SuppressFinalize(this);
    }

    protected virtual void Dispose(bool disposing)
    {
        if (_disposed)
            return;

        if (disposing)
        {
            // Dispose managed IDisposable resources
        }

        // Release unmanaged resources

        _disposed = true;
    }
}

For modern .NET development, you should also understand SafeHandle; Microsoft recommends safe handles as the preferred way to wrap unmanaged handles rather than writing raw finalizer logic yourself. Microsoft Learn

⭐ Real-World ASP.NET Core Scenario

Suppose your service works with a file:

public void ProcessFile(string path)
{
    using var stream = File.OpenRead(path);

    // Process file
}

What happens?

File.OpenRead()
      ↓
FileStream created
      ↓
Process file
      ↓
Method exits
      ↓
using calls Dispose()
      ↓
File handle released

The GC doesn't need to wait to release that resource.

This is especially important for scarce resources such as file handles and database/network resources. Microsoft Learn

🎯 The Most Important Interview Chain

Practice this sequence aloud:

What is the difference between stack and heap?

↓

Are value types always stored on the stack?

↓

What happens when a value type is boxed?

↓

What is Garbage Collection?

↓

↓

↓
