If you can answer that chain clearly, you're at a strong interview level for Topic #5.

One-page revision

STACK
→ Method execution / call frames
→ Per-thread
→ Fast automatic lifetime management

MANAGED HEAP
→ Managed objects
→ Controlled by GC

VALUE TYPE
→ Value semantics
→ Copying normally copies the value

REFERENCE TYPE
→ Reference semantics
→ Copying normally copies the reference

BOXING
→ Value type → object/interface
→ Creates boxed object
→ Can cause allocation + GC pressure

UNBOXING
→ Extract value from boxed object
→ Requires compatible type

GC
→ Automatic managed-memory management
→ Finds unreachable objects
→ Generational: Gen 0 → Gen 1 → Gen 2

IDISPOSABLE
→ Deterministic resource cleanup
→ Dispose()

USING
→ Ensures Dispose() is called

FINALIZER
→ Non-deterministic cleanup mechanism
→ Avoid unless actually needed

GC.SuppressFinalize()
→ Prevent unnecessary finalization after Dispose()

6. Collections — Basic → Advanced

6.1 What are Collections in C#?

Collections are classes/interfaces used to store and manage multiple objects.

Common generic collections:

CollectionBest use
List<T>Ordered items, index-based access
Dictionary<TKey,TValue>Key-value lookup
HashSet<T>Unique items
Queue<T>FIFO
Stack<T>LIFO
LinkedList<T>Linked-node scenarios
ConcurrentDictionary<TKey,TValue>Thread-safe key-value operations
ConcurrentQueue<T>Thread-safe FIFO

Interview answer

"C# provides generic collections such as List, Dictionary, HashSet, Queue and Stack for storing strongly typed data. The appropriate collection depends on requirements such as ordering, duplicate handling, lookup performance, and thread safety."

6.2 List<T>

List<T> is one of the most commonly used collections.

List<string> users = new List<string>();

users.Add("John");
users.Add("Mike");
users.Add("David");

Console.WriteLine(users[0]); // John

It provides index-based access and internally behaves like a dynamically sized array. Microsoft documents List<T> as a strongly typed collection accessible by index. Microsoft Learn

Q1. List vs Array?

Array

int[] numbers = new int[3];

numbers[0] = 10;
numbers[1] = 20;
numbers[2] = 30;

Size is fixed after creation.

List

List<int> numbers = new();

numbers.Add(10);
numbers.Add(20);
numbers.Add(30);
numbers.Add(40);

Can grow dynamically.

Interview answer

"An array has a fixed size, whereas List<T> is dynamically resizable. Both provide O(1) index-based access, but List<T> provides convenient methods such as Add, Remove and AddRange."

6.3 How does List<T> work internally?

A very common interview question.

Conceptually:

List<T>
   |
   +-- Internal array
          |
          +-- [A]
          +-- [B]
          +-- [C]
          +-- [ ]
          +-- [ ]

When the internal storage becomes full, the list allocates a larger array and copies the existing elements.

Therefore:

list.Add(item);

is amortized O(1), while resizing can temporarily cost O(n). Microsoft lists List<T>.Add as amortized O(1), with O(n) worst case. Microsoft Learn

Interview answer

"List<T> internally uses an array. When its capacity is insufficient, it expands its internal storage and copies the existing elements. Therefore Add is amortized O(1), although a resize operation itself can be O(n)."

6.4 Count vs Capacity

Very common follow-up.

List<int> numbers = new();

numbers.Add(10);
numbers.Add(20);
numbers.Add(30);

Console.WriteLine(numbers.Count);
Console.WriteLine(numbers.Capacity);

Count

Number of actual elements.

Capacity

Number of elements the internal storage can currently hold before resizing.

For example:

Count    = 3
Capacity = 4

There are 3 elements but space for 4.

Interview answer

"Count represents the number of elements currently stored, while Capacity represents the amount of storage currently allocated for the list."

6.5 Add() vs AddRange()

list.Add(10);

Adds one item.

list.AddRange(new[] { 20, 30, 40 });

Adds multiple items.

Example:

List<int> numbers = new() { 1, 2 };

numbers.Add(3);

numbers.AddRange(new[] { 4, 5, 6 });

Result:

1 2 3 4 5 6

6.6 Complexity of List

OperationComplexity
Access by indexO(1)
Add at endAmortized O(1)
Insert at beginningO(n)
Remove from beginningO(n)
Search/ContainsO(n)
SortO(n log n) generally
Remove at indexO(n)

The reason inserting/removing from the beginning is O(n) is that subsequent elements may need to be shifted.

6.7 Dictionary<TKey,TValue>

Dictionary stores:

Key → Value

Example:

Dictionary<int, string> users = new();

users.Add(101, "John");
users.Add(102, "David");
users.Add(103, "Mike");

Console.WriteLine(users[102]);

Output:

David

A dictionary provides very fast key-based lookup, close to O(1) on average, because it is implemented using hashing. Microsoft Learn

6.8 Why is Dictionary lookup O(1)?

This is a high-priority interview question.

Suppose:

Dictionary<int, string> users = new()
{
    { 101, "John" },
    { 102, "David" },
    { 103, "Mike" }
};

When we do:

users[102]

the dictionary uses the key's hash code to determine where to look.

Conceptually:

Key
 ↓
GetHashCode()
 ↓
Hash
 ↓
Bucket
 ↓
Find matching key
 ↓
Value

Interview answer

"Dictionary uses hashing for key-based lookup. It calculates a hash for the key and uses it to locate the appropriate bucket, then uses equality to identify the matching key. This gives approximately O(1) average lookup performance."

Microsoft notes that lookup performance depends partly on the quality of the key's hashing algorithm. Microsoft Learn

6.9 What is a hash collision?

Two different keys can produce the same hash code.

Key A ──> Hash 100
Key B ──> Hash 100

This is called a collision.

The dictionary handles collisions internally and uses equality comparison to determine the actual matching key.

Important interview statement:

"A hash code identifies a bucket, but it does not prove that two keys are equal."

6.10 Why are Equals() and GetHashCode() important?

Suppose you create:

class Employee
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
}

and use it as a dictionary key.

Dictionary needs to determine:

Are these two keys equal?

It uses equality semantics and hashing.

For custom key types, you should ensure that:

If A.Equals(B) == true
then
A.GetHashCode() == B.GetHashCode()

This is an extremely important rule.

Microsoft's Dictionary<TKey,TValue> documentation specifically notes that keys must remain consistent with their hash value while being used as dictionary keys. Microsoft Learn

6.11 Can Dictionary contain duplicate keys?

No.

Dictionary<int, string> users = new();

users.Add(1, "John");
users.Add(1, "David"); // Exception

Add() throws an exception when the key already exists.

But:

users[1] = "David";

updates/replaces the existing value.

Interview answer

"Dictionary keys must be unique. Add throws if the key already exists, while assigning through the indexer updates the existing value."

6.12 TryGetValue() vs ContainsKey()

You will very likely encounter this in interviews.

Less efficient pattern

if (users.ContainsKey(id))
{
    var user = users[id];
}

This performs the lookup twice conceptually.

Prefer:

if (users.TryGetValue(id, out var user))
{
    Console.WriteLine(user);
}

Interview answer

"TryGetValue is preferred when I need to check whether a key exists and retrieve its value because it combines the lookup and retrieval into one operation."

6.13 Dictionary vs Hashtable

DictionaryHashtable
GenericNon-generic
Strongly typedUses object
Better type safetyRequires casting
Avoids boxing for value types in the generic caseCan involve boxing/unboxing
Modern preferred choiceLegacy/non-generic scenarios

Example:

Dictionary<int, string> users = new();

versus:

Hashtable users = new();
users.Add(1, "John");

Microsoft specifically notes that generic Dictionary<TKey,TValue> avoids the boxing/unboxing typically involved when Hashtable stores value types. Microsoft Learn

Interview answer

"Dictionary<TKey,TValue> is generally preferred because it is generic, strongly typed, and avoids the boxing/unboxing overhead associated with storing value types in Hashtable."

6.14 HashSet<T>

HashSet<T> is designed to store unique elements.

HashSet<int> numbers = new();

numbers.Add(10);
numbers.Add(20);
numbers.Add(10);

Result:

10
20

The duplicate 10 is not added.

Microsoft describes HashSet<T> as an unordered collection of unique elements. Microsoft Learn

6.15 Why use HashSet instead of List?

Suppose:

List<int> ids = new();

You want to check:

ids.Contains(100);

A list generally searches sequentially:

10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 100

So lookup is O(n).

With:

HashSet<int> ids = new();

lookup is approximately O(1) on average.

Microsoft lists HashSet<T>.Add and lookup as O(1) average/amortized with O(n) worst-case complexity. Microsoft Learn

Interview answer

"I use HashSet when uniqueness is required and I frequently need membership checks. List is better when ordering and index-based access are important."

6.16 HashSet real-world example

Imagine a user has permissions:

Read
Write
Delete

You don't want:

Read
Read
Write
Delete

Use:

HashSet<string> permissions = new()
{
    "Read",
    "Write",
    "Delete"
};

Then:

if (permissions.Contains("Delete"))
{
    // Allow operation
}

This is a very realistic backend example.

6.17 Dictionary vs HashSet

This is another common interview question.

DictionaryHashSet
Key → ValueUnique values
Lookup by keyMembership check
Keys must be uniqueElements must be unique
dictionary[key]set.Contains(value)
Example: UserId → UserExample: Permission names

Simple rule

Need Key → Value?
       ↓
Dictionary

Need Unique Values?
       ↓
HashSet

6.18 Are List, Dictionary and HashSet thread-safe?

No, not for concurrent modification.

For example:

Dictionary<int, string> users = new();

If multiple threads simultaneously modify it, you need synchronization.

Microsoft states that generic collections such as List<T> and Dictionary<TKey,TValue> don't provide synchronization for concurrent modifications. Microsoft Learn

For concurrent scenarios, use collections from:

System.Collections.Concurrent

6.19 Concurrent Collections

Important collections:

ConcurrentDictionary<TKey,TValue>
ConcurrentQueue<T>
ConcurrentStack<T>
ConcurrentBag<T>

They are designed for concurrent access from multiple threads.

6.20 ConcurrentDictionary<TKey,TValue>

Example:

ConcurrentDictionary<int, string> users = new();

users.TryAdd(1, "John");
users.TryAdd(2, "David");

It is designed for scenarios where multiple threads access the dictionary concurrently. Microsoft Learn

Real-world scenario

Suppose your ASP.NET Core application has multiple requests updating an in-memory cache.

Instead of:

Dictionary<int, User> cache

with manually managed locks, you might use:

ConcurrentDictionary<int, User> cache

6.21 Why is this dangerous?

Consider:

if (!dictionary.ContainsKey(id))
{
    dictionary.Add(id, user);
}

Two threads could execute:

Thread 1                 Thread 2
   |                         |
ContainsKey = false       ContainsKey = false
   |                         |
Add                       Add
   |                         |
   ↓                         ↓
        Race condition

With ConcurrentDictionary, use atomic operations such as:

cache.TryAdd(id, user);

or:

cache.GetOrAdd(id, user);

depending on the required behavior.

The concurrent dictionary provides dedicated add/update methods for concurrent scenarios. Microsoft Learn

6.22 ConcurrentQueue

Used for FIFO processing.

ConcurrentQueue<string> queue = new();

queue.Enqueue("Job1");
queue.Enqueue("Job2");

queue.TryDequeue(out var job);

Conceptually:

Job1 → Job2 → Job3
 ↑
First in

Real-world scenario

Background job processing:

API Request
    ↓
ConcurrentQueue
    ↓
Background Worker
    ↓
Process Job

6.23 ConcurrentStack

LIFO behavior.

Job3 ← First removed
Job2
Job1

Useful when you specifically need stack semantics with concurrent access.

6.24 ConcurrentBag

Used when you need a thread-safe unordered collection and don't require FIFO/LIFO semantics.

Example scenario:

Multiple worker threads
       ↓
ConcurrentBag
       ↓
Collect results

Don't choose ConcurrentBag simply because "it's concurrent." Choose it based on the required access pattern.

6.25 Important Collection Interfaces

You should recognize these:

IEnumerable<T>
      ↓
ICollection<T>
      ↓
IList<T>

And:

IReadOnlyCollection<T>
IReadOnlyList<T>
IReadOnlyDictionary<TKey,TValue>
ISet<T>

For example:

public IReadOnlyList<User> GetUsers()
{
    return users;
}

This communicates that callers should consume the collection through a read-only interface.

We'll go much deeper into IEnumerable<T> and IQueryable<T> in Section #9 — LINQ, because that is where these become a major interview topic.

6.26 Most Important Interview Comparison

Memorize this table:

RequirementCollection
Fixed-size indexed dataArray
Dynamic indexed dataList<T>
Key → ValueDictionary<TKey,TValue>
Unique valuesHashSet<T>
FIFOQueue<T>
LIFOStack<T>
Concurrent key/valueConcurrentDictionary<TKey,TValue>
Concurrent FIFOConcurrentQueue<T>
Concurrent LIFOConcurrentStack<T>
Concurrent unordered collectionConcurrentBag<T>

🔥 Top Interview Questions for Your 3.9 YOE

You should be able to answer these without hesitation:

Basic

  1. What are collections in C#?
  1. List vs Array?
  1. What is List<T>?
  1. What is Dictionary<TKey,TValue>?
  1. What is HashSet<T>?
  1. Why use generic collections?
  1. Dictionary vs Hashtable?
  1. List vs HashSet?

Intermediate

  1. How does List<T> work internally?
  1. Count vs Capacity?
  1. What happens when List capacity is exceeded?
  1. Why is List index access O(1)?
  1. Why is List insertion at the beginning O(n)?
  1. How does Dictionary work internally?
  1. What is hashing?
  1. What is a hash collision?
  1. Why are Equals() and GetHashCode() important?
  1. Why must dictionary keys be unique?
  1. ContainsKey() vs TryGetValue()?
  1. What happens when duplicate key is added?
  1. What happens if a dictionary key is mutable?

Advanced

  1. Are List and Dictionary thread-safe?
  1. Why use ConcurrentDictionary?
  1. Dictionary vs ConcurrentDictionary?
  1. ConcurrentDictionary.GetOrAdd()?
  1. TryAdd() vs Add()?
  1. What is a race condition?
  1. ConcurrentDictionary vs locking Dictionary?
  1. ConcurrentQueue vs Queue?
  1. When would you use HashSet in a real application?

🎯 Real-World Scenario

Interviewer:

"You have 10,000 users and frequently need to find a user by UserId. Which collection would you use?"

Answer:

"I would use a Dictionary<int, User> because the requirement is key-based lookup by UserId. Dictionary provides approximately O(1) average lookup performance. If multiple threads need to concurrently update the collection, I would consider ConcurrentDictionary<int, User>." Microsoft Learn

Interviewer:

"You need to store unique permissions for a user. Which collection?"

Answer:

"I would use HashSet<string> because duplicate permissions aren't required and membership checks are efficient."

Interviewer:

"You need to process background jobs in FIFO order."

Answer:

"I would use Queue<T>. If multiple threads need to enqueue and dequeue concurrently, I would use ConcurrentQueue<T>."

🧠 Collection Selection Cheat Sheet

Think about the requirement first:

                    What do I need?
                           |
          ┌────────────────┼─────────────────┐
          ↓                ↓                 ↓
      Index access      Key lookup        Uniqueness
          |                |                 |
       List<T>       Dictionary<K,V>     HashSet<T>
          |
          ↓
     FIFO / LIFO?
       /       \
     FIFO      LIFO
      |          |
   Queue       Stack

And if multiple threads are modifying the collection:

ConcurrentDictionary
ConcurrentQueue
ConcurrentStack
ConcurrentBag

The major interview principle is:

Don't choose a collection by habit. Choose it based on access pattern, uniqueness, ordering, lookup requirements, complexity, and concurrency requirements.

7. Generics — Basic → Advanced

We’ll continue exactly in your roadmap order:

Generic Types → Generic Methods → Constraints → Variance

Generics are extremely important for your 3.9 YOE interviews because you use them constantly in List<T>, Dictionary<TKey,TValue>, Task<T>, IEnumerable<T>, repositories, services, and APIs. C# generics provide compile-time type safety and retain runtime type information. Microsoft Learn

7.1 What are Generics?

Generics allow us to write type-independent, reusable code.

Instead of:

public class IntRepository
{
    public void Add(int value) { }
}

and:

public class StringRepository
{
    public void Add(string value) { }
}

we can write:

public class Repository<T>
{
    public void Add(T value)
    {
        // Add value
    }
}

Then:

Repository<int> intRepository = new();

Repository<string> stringRepository = new();

T is called a type parameter.

The actual type (int, string, User, etc.) is the type argument. Microsoft Learn

Interview answer

"Generics allow us to write reusable and type-safe code that works with different data types without duplicating implementations or relying on runtime casting."

7.2 Why do we need Generics?

There are three major benefits:

1. Type safety

List<int> numbers = new();

numbers.Add(10);

// numbers.Add("Hello"); // Compile-time error

The compiler prevents invalid types.

2. Code reusability

One implementation works with many types.

3. Avoid unnecessary boxing/unboxing

For example:

List<int>

can work directly with int, unlike older non-generic collections such as ArrayList.

Microsoft specifically highlights type safety and avoiding runtime casts as major benefits of generics. Microsoft Learn

7.3 Generic Class

public class Repository<T>
{
    private readonly List<T> _items = new();

    public void Add(T item)
    {
        _items.Add(item);
    }

    public T Get(int index)
    {
        return _items[index];
    }
}

Usage:

Repository<string> names = new();

names.Add("John");
names.Add("David");

string name = names.Get(0);

Another type:

Repository<int> numbers = new();

numbers.Add(10);
numbers.Add(20);

int number = numbers.Get(0);

Same class, different types.

7.4 Generic Type vs Constructed Generic Type

This is terminology interviewers sometimes test.

Repository<T>

is a generic type definition.

While:

Repository<int>

is a constructed generic type.

Similarly:

Dictionary<TKey, TValue>

is the generic type definition.

Dictionary<int, string>

is a constructed generic type. Microsoft Learn

7.5 Generic Method

A generic method has its own type parameter.

public void Print<T>(T value)
{
    Console.WriteLine(value);
}

Usage:

Print<int>(10);
Print<string>("Hello");

C# can often infer the type:

Print(10);
Print("Hello");

Interview answer

"A generic method defines its own type parameter independently of whether the containing class is generic."

7.6 Generic Class vs Generic Method

Generic class

public class Repository<T>
{
    public void Add(T item)
    {
    }
}

The type parameter belongs to the class.

Generic method

public void Add<T>(T item)
{
}

The type parameter belongs to the method.

You can even have both:

public class Repository<T>
{
    public void Process<U>(U data)
    {
    }
}

Here:

T → class-level type parameter
U → method-level type parameter

7.7 Generic Method Real-World Example

Imagine logging:

public static void Log<T>(T data)
{
    Console.WriteLine(data);
}

Usage:

Log("User created");
Log(100);
Log(new User());

This avoids writing separate methods:

LogString()
LogInt()
LogUser()

7.8 Generic Interface

public interface IRepository<T>
{
    T GetById(int id);

    void Add(T entity);
}

Implementation:

public class UserRepository : IRepository<User>
{
    public User GetById(int id)
    {
        // database logic
        return new User();
    }

    public void Add(User entity)
    {
        // database logic
    }
}

This pattern is extremely common in .NET applications.

7.9 Generic Repository Example

In a backend application:

IRepository<User>
IRepository<Order>
IRepository<Product>

All can share the same generic abstraction.

public interface IRepository<T>
{
    Task<T?> GetByIdAsync(int id);

    Task AddAsync(T entity);

    Task DeleteAsync(T entity);
}

This is a practical example you can mention in a .NET interview.

7.10 Generic Constraints

Now we reach an important advanced area.

Without constraints:

public class Repository<T>
{
}

T could be almost anything.

A constraint restricts what types can be used as T.

Syntax:

where T : constraint

Microsoft describes constraints as limits placed on generic type parameters that tell the compiler what capabilities the type argument must provide. Microsoft Learn

7.11 where T : class

Means T must be a reference type.

public class Repository<T>
    where T : class
{
}

Valid:

Repository<User> repo = new();

Invalid:

Repository<int> repo = new();

because int is a value type.

7.12 where T : struct

Means T must be a non-nullable value type.

public class ValueProcessor<T>
    where T : struct
{
}

Valid:

ValueProcessor<int> processor = new();

Not valid:

ValueProcessor<string> processor = new();

The struct constraint also implies the new() constraint. Microsoft Learn

7.13 where T : new()

This is very commonly asked.

It means T must have a public parameterless constructor and must not be abstract. Microsoft Learn

Example:

public class Factory<T>
    where T : new()
{
    public T Create()
    {
        return new T();
    }
}

Now:

Factory<User> factory = new();

User user = factory.Create();

The compiler knows that:

new T()

is valid.

7.14 Multiple Generic Constraints

You can combine constraints:

public class Repository<T>
    where T : class, IEntity, new()
{
}

This means:

T must:
✔ Be a reference type
✔ Implement IEntity
✔ Have a public parameterless constructor

new() must appear last among ordinary constraints. Microsoft Learn

7.15 Interface Constraint

Very useful in real applications.

public interface IEntity
{
    int Id { get; }
}

Then:

public class Repository<T>
    where T : IEntity
{
    public int GetId(T entity)
    {
        return entity.Id;
    }
}

Why can we access:

entity.Id

?

Because the constraint guarantees that T implements IEntity.

Interview answer

"A constraint allows the compiler to know what operations are guaranteed to be available on the generic type parameter."

7.16 Base Class Constraint

public class Processor<T>
    where T : Employee
{
}

This means:

T must be Employee
or
T must derive from Employee

For example:

class Manager : Employee
{
}

Then:

Processor<Manager> processor = new();

is valid.

7.17 where T : notnull

Requires a non-nullable type.

public class Cache<TKey, TValue>
    where TKey : notnull
{
}

Useful when a generic parameter must safely act as a key.

Current C# also supports other constraints such as unmanaged, Enum, and Delegate for specialized scenarios. Microsoft Learn

7.18 Generic Constraint Cheat Sheet

Memorize this:

where T : class
        ↓
Reference type

where T : struct
        ↓
Non-nullable value type

where T : new()
        ↓
Public parameterless constructor

where T : BaseClass
        ↓
Base class or derived class

where T : IInterface
        ↓
Must implement interface

where T : notnull
        ↓
Non-nullable type

where T : unmanaged
        ↓
Unmanaged type

7.19 Why Use Constraints?

Consider:

public static T Max<T>(T a, T b)
{
    // How do I know T can be compared?
}

The compiler doesn't know that arbitrary T supports comparison.

So:

public static T Max<T>(T a, T b)
    where T : IComparable<T>
{
    return a.CompareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b;
}

Now the compiler knows:

T implements IComparable<T>
        ↓
CompareTo() is available

This is a very good interview example. Microsoft Learn

7.20 Generic Type Parameter vs object

Why not simply use:

public void Process(object value)
{
}

instead of:

public void Process<T>(T value)
{
}

With object

You lose compile-time specificity.

object value = 10;

int number = (int)value;

Potential runtime cast problems.

With generics

public T Process<T>(T value)
{
    return value;
}

The compiler preserves the type.

int result = Process(10);

No explicit cast required.

Interview answer

"Generics provide compile-time type safety and preserve the actual type, whereas object-based APIs often require casting and can introduce runtime errors and boxing for value types."

7.21 What is Generic Type Safety?

Example:

List<int> numbers = new();

numbers.Add(10);

// numbers.Add("Hello");

The compiler rejects the second statement.

This catches the problem before runtime.

That's one of the primary advantages of generics. Microsoft Learn

7.22 Generic Variance

This is where many Senior-level interviews become interesting.

There are three concepts:

Covariance
Contravariance
Invariance

7.23 Invariance

By default, generic types are invariant.

Suppose:

class Animal
{
}

class Dog : Animal
{
}

This does not mean:

List<Dog>

can be assigned to:

List<Animal>

This is invalid:

List<Dog> dogs = new();

List<Animal> animals = dogs; // ❌

Why?

Because if this were allowed:

animals.Add(new Cat());

the original List<Dog> would contain a Cat.

That would violate type safety.

Generic classes such as List<T> are therefore invariant. Microsoft Learn

7.24 Covariance

Covariance uses:

out

Think:

Producer → out

Example:

IEnumerable<Dog> dogs = new List<Dog>();

IEnumerable<Animal> animals = dogs;

This works because:

Dog → Animal
Derived → Base

IEnumerable<out T> is covariant. Microsoft Learn

Easy way to remember

out = produces data

For example:

IEnumerable<Dog>

produces Dog objects.

You can safely treat those dogs as animals.

7.25 Why can IEnumerable be Covariant?

Consider:

IEnumerable<Dog>

You can only read/enumerate from it.

You aren't allowed to add an arbitrary Cat.

Therefore:

IEnumerable<Dog>

can safely be viewed as:

IEnumerable<Animal>

7.26 Contravariance

Contravariance uses:

in

Think:

Consumer → in

Example:

Action<Animal> handleAnimal = animal =>
{
    Console.WriteLine(animal);
};

Action<Dog> handleDog = handleAnimal;

Why is this safe?

Because a method that can process any Animal can obviously process a Dog.

Action<Animal>
       ↓
Can process Animal
       ↓
Can process Dog

Action<T> is contravariant. Microsoft Learn

7.27 Covariance vs Contravariance

This table is worth memorizing:

ConceptKeywordDirectionExample
CovarianceoutDerived → BaseIEnumerable<Dog> → IEnumerable<Animal>
ContravarianceinBase → DerivedAction<Animal> → Action<Dog>
InvariancenoneNo conversionList<Dog> → List<Animal> ❌

Microsoft specifies that covariance uses type parameters in output positions, while contravariance uses them in input positions. Microsoft Learn

7.28 Why can't out T be used as a method parameter?

This is a common advanced question.

Incorrect:

interface IProcessor<out T>
{
    void Process(T value); // ❌
}

Why?

Because T is being used as an input.

For covariance:

out T

should be used in output positions.

Correct:

interface IProducer<out T>
{
    T Get();
}

For contravariance:

interface IConsumer<in T>
{
    void Process(T value);
}

These restrictions exist to preserve type safety. Microsoft Learn

7.29 Real-World .NET Example

Imagine:

class User
{
}

class AdminUser : User
{
}

A service produces users:

IEnumerable<AdminUser> admins;

You can consume them as:

IEnumerable<User> users = admins;

because IEnumerable<T> is covariant.

Now imagine a logger:

Action<User> logUser = user =>
{
    Console.WriteLine(user);
};

It can process:

Action<AdminUser> logAdmin = logUser;

because Action<T> is contravariant.

  1. What does out T mean?
  1. What does in T mean?
  1. Why is IEnumerable<T> covariant?
  1. Why is Action<T> contravariant?
  1. Why is List<T> invariant?
  1. Why can't out T be used as a method parameter?
  1. Can classes be declared covariant/contravariant?
  1. Which built-in .NET interfaces/delegates support variance?

Only generic interfaces and delegates can declare variant type parameters; classes and structs cannot use in/out variance annotations. Microsoft Learn

🎯 Most Important Interview Scenario

Interviewer:

"Why can't I assign List<Dog> to List<Animal>, but I can assign IEnumerable<Dog> to IEnumerable<Animal>?"

Strong 3.9 YOE answer:

"List<T> is invariant because it allows both reading and writing. If List<Dog> could be treated as List<Animal>, someone could add a Cat to it and violate the original list's type safety. IEnumerable<T>, on the other hand, is read-only from the consumer's perspective and is declared covariant using out T, so IEnumerable<Dog> can safely be assigned to IEnumerable<Animal>."

That's a very good Senior-level answer.

🧠 Final Generics Cheat Sheet

GENERIC
   │
   ├── Generic Class
   │      └── Repository<T>
   │
   ├── Generic Method
   │      └── Process<T>()
   │
   ├── Constraints
   │      ├── class
   │      ├── struct
   │      ├── new()
   │      ├── BaseClass
   │      ├── Interface
   │      ├── notnull
   │      └── unmanaged
   │
   └── Variance
          │
          ├── Covariance
          │      └── out
          │      └── Producer
          │      └── Derived → Base
          │
          ├── Contravariance
          │      └── in
          │      └── Consumer
          │      └── Base → Derived
          │
          └── Invariance
                 └── No conversion
                 └── List<Dog> ≠ List<Animal>

⭐ What I would memorize for interviews

Generics: reusable + type-safe code

where T : class: reference type

where T : struct: non-nullable value type

where T : new(): public parameterless constructor

where T : Interface: guarantees interface capabilities

Covariance: out → producer → derived to base

Contravariance: in → consumer → base to derived

Invariance: no implicit generic conversion

8. Delegates → Action → Func → Predicate → Lambda → Events

A delegate is a type-safe way to reference methods with a compatible signature. .NET also provides built-in generic delegates such as Action, Func, and Predicate. Microsoft Learn

8.1 What is a Delegate?

Interview-ready answer

"A delegate is a type-safe reference to a method. It defines the method's parameter list and return type, and allows a method to be passed as a parameter, stored in a variable, or invoked later."

Example:

public delegate int Calculator(int a, int b);

public int Add(int a, int b)
{
    return a + b;
}

Calculator calculator = Add;

int result = calculator(10, 20);

Here:

Calculator
     ↓
Delegate type

Add
     ↓
Method assigned to delegate

calculator(10, 20)
     ↓
Invokes Add()

A delegate can reference compatible static or instance methods. Microsoft Learn

8.2 Why Do We Need Delegates?

The main idea is:

Pass behavior as data.

Without delegates:

public int Calculate(int a, int b)
{
    return a + b;
}

You hard-code the operation.

With a delegate:

public int Calculate(
    int a,
    int b,
    Calculator operation)
{
    return operation(a, b);
}

Now:

Calculate(10, 20, Add);
Calculate(10, 20, Subtract);
Calculate(10, 20, Multiply);

The calculation method doesn't need to know which operation will be performed.

Real-world use

This concept appears in:

  • Callbacks
  • Event handlers
  • LINQ
  • Strategy-like behavior
  • Middleware/delegated processing
  • Async callbacks

8.3 Delegate Signature

Suppose:

public delegate string Formatter(int id);

A compatible method must have:

Input:
int

Return:
string

So this works:

public string FormatUser(int id)
{
    return $"User-{id}";
}

But this doesn't:

public int FormatUser(int id)
{
    return id;
}

because the return type doesn't match.

Key rule

Parameter types and return type must be compatible with the delegate signature.

8.4 Single-cast vs Multicast Delegate

A delegate can reference one or multiple methods.

Single method

Action action = Method1;

Multiple methods

Action action = Method1;
action += Method2;
action += Method3;

When:

action();

is executed, the subscribed methods are invoked according to the delegate's invocation list.

Delegates can therefore support multicast behavior. Microsoft Learn

8.5 What is Action?

Action is a built-in delegate that:

takes zero or more parameters and returns void.

Examples:

Action action = () =>
{
    Console.WriteLine("Hello");
};

With parameter:

Action<string> print = message =>
{
    Console.WriteLine(message);
};

With multiple parameters:

Action<int, int> addLog = (a, b) =>
{
    Console.WriteLine(a + b);
};

Conceptually:

Action
   ↓
Input → void

.NET provides Action<> so you don't need to create a custom void-returning delegate for common cases. Microsoft Learn

8.6 What is Func?

Func represents a delegate that returns a value.

Example:

Func<int, int> square = x => x * x;

int result = square(5);

Result:

25

Multiple parameters:

Func<int, int, int> add = (a, b) => a + b;

The last generic parameter is always the return type.

Func<int, string>

means:

int → string

And:

Func<int, int, string>

means:

int + int → string

Func supports up to 16 input parameters, with the final generic parameter representing the return type. Microsoft Learn

8.7 Action vs Func

Very common interview question.

ActionFunc
Returns voidReturns a value
Action<int>Func<int, string>
Used for actionsUsed for transformations/calculations

Example:

Action<string> print =
    message => Console.WriteLine(message);

versus:

Func<string, int> getLength =
    text => text.Length;

Easy memory trick

Action → performs an action → void

Func → performs a function → returns something

8.8 What is Predicate<T>?

Predicate<T> represents a method that:

takes one parameter and returns bool.

Example:

Predicate<int> isEven =
    number => number % 2 == 0;

Then:

bool result = isEven(10);

Result:

true

Conceptually:

Predicate<T>
       ↓
T → bool

Microsoft notes that Predicate<T> is structurally similar to Func<T,bool>, although they are distinct delegate types and aren't interchangeable simply because their signatures match. Microsoft Learn

8.9 Predicate vs Func<T, bool>

These look almost identical:

Predicate<int> p =
    x => x > 10;

and:

Func<int, bool> f =
    x => x > 10;

Both represent:

int → bool

But they are different delegate types.

Interview answer

"Predicate<T> specifically represents a single-input Boolean condition, while Func<T,bool> is the more general delegate that returns a Boolean. Their signatures are similar, but the delegate types themselves are different."

8.10 What is a Lambda Expression?

A lambda is a concise way of writing an anonymous function.

Instead of:

Func<int, int> square = delegate(int x)
{
    return x * x;
};

you can write:

Func<int, int> square = x => x * x;

Syntax:

(parameters) => expression

Example:

x => x * 2

Multiple parameters:

(a, b) => a + b

Statement body:

x =>
{
    int result = x * 2;
    return result;
}

Lambda expressions are commonly converted to delegate types and are heavily used with LINQ. Microsoft Learn

8.11 Anonymous Method vs Lambda

Older syntax:

Func<int, int> square = delegate(int x)
{
    return x * x;
};

Lambda:

Func<int, int> square = x => x * x;

Lambda expressions are generally the cleaner modern syntax.

8.12 Method Group

You don't always need to explicitly write a lambda.

Suppose:

public static bool IsAdult(int age)
{
    return age >= 18;
}

You can do:

Predicate<int> check = IsAdult;

IsAdult here is a method group that can be converted to a compatible delegate.

You could also write:

Predicate<int> check = age => IsAdult(age);

The first version is simpler when the signatures already match.

8.13 Delegate vs Lambda

This is an important distinction.

Delegate

A type representing a compatible method signature.

Func<int, int>

Lambda

An anonymous function expression.

x => x * 2

The lambda can be converted to a compatible delegate:

Func<int, int> square = x => x * x;

Interview answer

"A delegate is a type-safe method reference, whereas a lambda is an expression used to define an anonymous function. A lambda can be converted to a compatible delegate type."

8.14 What is an Event?

An event provides a notification mechanism.

One object publishes that something happened, and other objects subscribe to it.

Example:

public class OrderService
{
    public event EventHandler? OrderCreated;

    public void CreateOrder()
    {
        // Create order

        OrderCreated?.Invoke(this, EventArgs.Empty);
    }
}

Subscriber:

OrderService service = new();

service.OrderCreated += OnOrderCreated;

void OnOrderCreated(object? sender, EventArgs e)
{
    Console.WriteLine("Order created");
}

Events are built on delegates, but the event keyword restricts how external code can interact with the delegate. Outside the declaring type, subscribers can generally only += and -=; they can't raise the event directly. Microsoft Learn

8.15 Why use event instead of a public delegate?

Suppose you expose:

public Action? OrderCreated;

External code could potentially invoke it:

service.OrderCreated?.Invoke();

That's undesirable because subscribers shouldn't be able to raise the event.

With:

public event Action? OrderCreated;

external consumers can subscribe:

service.OrderCreated += Handler;

and unsubscribe:

service.OrderCreated -= Handler;

but they cannot normally invoke the event.

Strong interview answer

"An event provides controlled access to a delegate. Subscribers can add or remove handlers, but only the declaring type can raise the event. This preserves encapsulation between the publisher and subscribers."

This distinction is explicitly documented by Microsoft. Microsoft Learn

8.16 Publisher and Subscriber

Events normally have two sides.

Publisher

The object that raises the event.

OrderService

Subscriber

The object that listens.

NotificationService

Architecture:

OrderService
     |
     | OrderCreated event
     ↓
 ┌───────────────┐
 │               │
 ↓               ↓
EmailService   AuditService

The publisher doesn't need to know exactly which subscribers exist.

That's the main benefit of the event model. Microsoft Learn

8.17 Standard Event Pattern

.NET commonly uses:

EventHandler

or:

EventHandler<TEventArgs>

Example:

public event EventHandler<OrderCreatedEventArgs>? OrderCreated;

Custom event data:

public class OrderCreatedEventArgs : EventArgs
{
    public int OrderId { get; }

    public OrderCreatedEventArgs(int orderId)
    {
        OrderId = orderId;
    }
}

Raise:

OrderCreated?.Invoke(
    this,
    new OrderCreatedEventArgs(orderId));

Microsoft recommends EventHandler<TEventArgs> for events carrying event-specific data. Microsoft Learn

8.18 += and = with Events

Subscribe:

service.OrderCreated += HandleOrderCreated;

Unsubscribe:

service.OrderCreated -= HandleOrderCreated;

Why is unsubscription important?

Because if a long-lived publisher keeps references to subscribers, those subscriptions can contribute to objects staying reachable longer than intended.

So in long-lived event relationships, lifecycle management matters.

8.19 Can an Event Return a Value?

Typically, events use void-returning handlers.

For example:

EventHandler

returns void.

Why?

Because an event is primarily a notification mechanism, potentially with multiple subscribers. There's no natural single return value to represent all subscribers' results. Microsoft documents the standard event delegates as having no return value. Microsoft Learn

8.20 Delegate vs Event

This is one of the most important questions.

DelegateEvent
Represents method reference(s)Notification mechanism built on delegates
Can be invoked by whoever has access to itRaising is restricted to declaring type
Can be passed as parameterUsually used for publisher/subscriber
Can return a valueTypically void
Useful for callbacksUseful for notifications

Interview answer

"A delegate is a type-safe method reference and can be directly invoked. An event is built on a delegate and provides controlled publisher-subscriber semantics where external consumers can subscribe or unsubscribe but cannot raise the event." Microsoft Learn

8.21 Multicast Delegate

Example:

Action notify = SendEmail;

notify += SendSms;
notify += WriteAuditLog;

notify();

Conceptually:

notify()
   |
   ├── SendEmail()
   ├── SendSms()
   └── WriteAuditLog()

This is useful when multiple methods should be invoked through the same delegate.

8.22 What happens if a multicast delegate returns a value?

This is a common trap.

Suppose:

Func<int> getValue = Method1;

getValue += Method2;
getValue += Method3;

When invoked, multiple methods execute, but the caller doesn't receive a meaningful combined result from all methods. For a multicast delegate with a return value, the invocation result corresponds to the last delegate in the invocation list.

Therefore, multicast delegates are generally most natural for void operations such as notifications.

8.23 Delegate Covariance and Contravariance

This connects directly to the Generics topic we just completed.

For example:

Action<Animal>

is contravariant because Action<T> declares its parameter with in.

And:

Func<T>

is covariant in its return type because Func declares its result type with out. Microsoft Learn

So when interviewer asks:

"Where do you see variance in real C#?"

Good examples are:

IEnumerable<out T>
Func<..., out TResult>
Action<in T>
Predicate<in T>

8.24 Real-World .NET Scenario

Imagine your healthcare application processes an audit report.

Audit Report Generated
          |
          ↓
     ReportService
          |
          | event
          ↓
   ┌──────┼────────┐
   ↓      ↓        ↓
 Email   Audit    SignalR
Service  Logger   Notification

The report service doesn't need to know:

Who sends email?
Who writes audit logs?
Who sends SignalR notification?

It only publishes:

public event EventHandler<ReportGeneratedEventArgs>? ReportGenerated;

Subscribers decide what to do.

That's a clean example of loose coupling through publisher/subscriber behavior.

8.25 Delegate Real-World Scenario

Suppose you have a reusable filtering method:

public static List<T> Filter<T>(
    List<T> items,
    Predicate<T> condition)
{
    List<T> result = new();

    foreach (T item in items)
    {
        if (condition(item))
        {
            result.Add(item);
        }
    }

    return result;
}

Now:

var adults = Filter(
    users,
    user => user.Age >= 18);

Or:

var activeUsers = Filter(
    users,
    user => user.IsActive);

Same algorithm, different behavior.

That's the power of passing behavior through delegates.

🔥 Top Interview Questions

Basic

  1. What is a delegate?
  1. Why do we need delegates?
  1. How do you declare a delegate?
  1. How do you invoke a delegate?
  1. What is Action?
  1. What is Func?
  1. What is Predicate?
  1. What is a lambda expression?
  1. What is a method group?
  1. What is an anonymous method?

Intermediate

  1. Delegate vs lambda?
  1. Action vs Func?
  1. Func<T,bool> vs Predicate<T>?
  1. What is a multicast delegate?
  1. Can a delegate contain multiple methods?
  1. What is an event?
  1. Delegate vs event?
  1. Why use event?
  1. What are publisher and subscriber?
  1. What does += do with an event?
  1. What does = do?
  1. What is EventHandler?
  1. What is EventHandler<TEventArgs>?
  1. Why do events normally use void?

Advanced

  1. How are delegates implemented conceptually?
  1. Single-cast vs multicast delegates?
  1. What happens when a multicast delegate has a return value?
  1. Delegate covariance and contravariance?
  1. Why is Action<T> contravariant?
  1. Why is Func<T,TResult> covariant in TResult?
  1. Why can't external code raise a normal event?
  1. How can event subscriptions contribute to object lifetime issues?
  1. Delegate vs interface-based strategy?
  1. When would you choose a delegate instead of an interface?
  1. What is closure/captured variable behavior with lambdas?

⭐ Very Important: Closure

This is an excellent Senior-level follow-up.

Consider:

int multiplier = 10;

Func<int, int> multiply =
    x => x * multiplier;

The lambda accesses:

multiplier

even though multiplier isn't a parameter of the lambda.

The lambda captures the surrounding variable.

This is called a closure.

Example:

int multiplier = 10;

Func<int, int> calculate =
    x => x * multiplier;

multiplier = 20;

Console.WriteLine(calculate(5));

The result is:

100

The lambda captures the variable, not simply a frozen copy of its original value.

This becomes particularly important with loops, asynchronous code, and deferred execution.

🎯 Interview Scenario

Interviewer:

"You need to notify multiple components when an order is created. Would you use a delegate or event?"

Strong answer:

"I would generally use an event because this is a publisher-subscriber notification scenario. The OrderService can publish an OrderCreated event, while email, audit, or notification components can subscribe independently. The event also prevents external subscribers from directly raising the notification, which preserves encapsulation."

🧠 Final Cheat Sheet

DELEGATE
   ↓
Type-safe method reference
   ↓
Callbacks / behavior

ACTION
   ↓
Input → void

FUNC
   ↓
Input → Return value

PREDICATE
   ↓
Input → bool

LAMBDA
   ↓
Anonymous function
   ↓
x => x * 2

EVENT
   ↓
Notification mechanism
   ↓
Publisher → Subscribers

EventHandler
   ↓
Standard .NET event pattern

+=
   ↓
Subscribe / add handler

-=
   ↓
Unsubscribe / remove handler

⭐ Memorize these five lines

Delegate = type-safe method reference.

Action = delegate returning void.

Func = delegate returning a value.

Predicate = delegate returning bool for a condition.

Event = controlled publisher-subscriber mechanism built on delegates.

Next in the roadmap is #9 LINQ — IEnumerable, IQueryable, deferred execution, projection, filtering, grouping, joining, Select, Where, SelectMany, Any, All, First, Single, and performance traps.

9. LINQ — Basic → Advanced

This is one of the highest-priority C# topics for your interviews because LINQ appears everywhere in .NET: collections, EF Core, APIs, data transformation, filtering, grouping, and querying databases.

We’ll follow the roadmap exactly:

IEnumerable → IQueryable → Deferred Execution → Projection → Filtering → Grouping → Joining → Advanced LINQ → Performance

LINQ provides a consistent way to query different data sources, but IEnumerable<T> and IQueryable<T> have important behavioral differences. Microsoft Learn

9.1 What is LINQ?

LINQ stands for:

Language Integrated Query

It allows you to query collections and other data sources using C# syntax.

Without LINQ:

List<int> numbers = new() { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 };

List<int> evenNumbers = new();

foreach (int number in numbers)
{
    if (number % 2 == 0)
    {
        evenNumbers.Add(number);
    }
}

With LINQ:

var evenNumbers = numbers
    .Where(x => x % 2 == 0)
    .ToList();

Interview answer

"LINQ is a set of C# language and .NET APIs that allows us to query and transform data using a consistent syntax. It can work with in-memory collections as well as query providers such as Entity Framework."

9.2 Two Types of LINQ Syntax

There are two common styles.

Method syntax

var result = users
    .Where(u => u.IsActive)
    .Select(u => u.Name)
    .ToList();

Query syntax

var result =
    from u in users
    where u.IsActive
    select u.Name;

Both can represent LINQ queries.

Interview tip

For real-world .NET development, method syntax is more commonly encountered, especially when chaining operations.

9.3 IEnumerable<T>

IEnumerable<T> represents a sequence that can be enumerated.

Example:

IEnumerable<int> numbers =
    new List<int> { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 };

You can enumerate it:

foreach (var number in numbers)
{
    Console.WriteLine(number);
}

LINQ's Enumerable methods operate on IEnumerable<T>.

For example:

IEnumerable<int> result =
    numbers.Where(x => x > 2);

Enumerable.Where takes a Func<T,bool> and returns an IEnumerable<T>. Microsoft Learn

9.4 IQueryable<T>

IQueryable<T> is designed for querying data sources that can provide their own query provider.

Common example:

DbSet<User>

from EF Core can participate in LINQ queries.

Example:

IQueryable<User> users = dbContext.Users;

var result = users
    .Where(u => u.IsActive)
    .Select(u => u.Name);

Queryable.Where uses an:

Expression<Func<T,bool>>

rather than a normal:

Func<T,bool>

The expression can be represented as an expression tree and interpreted by the query provider. Microsoft Learn

9.5 IEnumerable vs IQueryable

This is a must-know interview question.

IEnumerable<T>IQueryable<T>
Usually in-memory queryingDesigned for queryable data sources
Uses delegates such as Func<>Uses expression trees
LINQ-to-ObjectsProvider translates query
Filtering generally occurs in application memoryProvider may translate operations to source query
Enumerable methodsQueryable methods

Example

IEnumerable<User> users = db.Users;

versus:

IQueryable<User> users = db.Users;

With IQueryable, EF Core can translate supported LINQ expressions into SQL.

Interview answer

"IEnumerable<T> is generally used for in-memory enumeration and LINQ-to-Objects, while IQueryable<T> represents a query that can be translated by a query provider. In EF Core, IQueryable allows supported LINQ expressions to be translated into SQL and executed by the database."

9.6 Important Trap: IQueryable Doesn't Automatically Mean "Database"

Don't memorize:

IQueryable = SQL

That's too simplistic.

IQueryable<T> represents a queryable abstraction backed by an IQueryProvider.

EF Core is one important implementation.

So the better statement is:

"IQueryable<T> allows a query provider to interpret an expression tree and execute or translate the query according to that provider."

Microsoft's Queryable.Where documentation explicitly describes building an expression tree and passing it to the provider represented by IQueryProvider. Microsoft Learn

9.7 Where()

Where() filters elements.

var activeUsers = users
    .Where(u => u.IsActive)
    .ToList();

Conceptually:

Input
 ↓
User 1 → active
User 2 → inactive
User 3 → active
 ↓
Where(IsActive)
 ↓
User 1
User 3

Enumerable.Where filters an IEnumerable<T> using a predicate. Microsoft Learn

Interview answer

"Where filters a sequence based on a Boolean condition."

9.8 Select()

Select() performs projection.

This is a very important LINQ concept.

Suppose:

class User
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Name { get; set; } = "";
    public string Email { get; set; } = "";
}

Instead of returning the complete user:

var result = users;

you can select only what you need:

var result = users
    .Select(u => u.Name)
    .ToList();

Now:

User
 ↓
Select(Name)
 ↓
string

Microsoft describes Select as projecting each element into a new form. Microsoft Learn

9.9 Select into DTO

This is extremely common in your .NET backend work.

var result = users
    .Select(u => new UserDto
    {
        Id = u.Id,
        Name = u.Name
    })
    .ToList();

You're transforming:

User
 ↓
UserDto

Interview answer

"Select is used for projection. I commonly use it to map entities to DTOs and return only the fields required by an API."

9.10 Where vs Select

Very common question.

Where

answers:

Which elements do I want?
Select

answers:

What shape should those elements have?

Example:

var result = users
    .Where(u => u.IsActive)
    .Select(u => u.Name);

Meaning:

Where
 ↓
Keep active users

Select
 ↓
Return their names

9.11 SelectMany()

Another high-priority question.

Suppose:

class Department
{
    public List<Employee> Employees { get; set; } = new();
}

You have:

Department 1
 ├── Employee A
 └── Employee B

Department 2
 ├── Employee C
 └── Employee D

Using:

Select(d => d.Employees)

gives:

List<Employee>
List<Employee>

So you have nested collections.

Using:

SelectMany(d => d.Employees)

flattens them:

Employee A
Employee B
Employee C
Employee D

Microsoft specifically describes SelectMany as flattening sequences when the selector returns collections. Microsoft Learn

Interview answer

"Select transforms each element, while SelectMany transforms and flattens nested collections into a single sequence."

9.12 OrderBy() / ThenBy()

var users = usersList
    .OrderBy(u => u.Name)
    .ToList();

Descending:

var users = usersList
    .OrderByDescending(u => u.Name)
    .ToList();

Multiple sort conditions:

var result = users
    .OrderBy(u => u.Department)
    .ThenBy(u => u.Name)
    .ToList();

Think:

OrderBy
   ↓
Primary sorting

ThenBy
   ↓
Secondary sorting

9.13 First() vs FirstOrDefault()

Very common interview question.

First

var user = users.First();

If no element exists, it throws an exception.

FirstOrDefault

var user = users.FirstOrDefault();

If no element exists, it returns the default value.

For a reference type:

null

Interview answer

"First expects at least one matching element and throws if none exists. FirstOrDefault returns the first matching element or the default value when the sequence is empty."

9.14 Single() vs SingleOrDefault()

Single() means:

I expect exactly one element.
var user = users.Single(u => u.Id == id);

It throws if:

  • zero elements match
  • more than one element matches

SingleOrDefault() allows zero or one, but still throws if multiple elements match.

Important distinction

First
↓
I only care about the first match

Single
↓
I expect exactly one match

For example, if UserId is guaranteed unique:

users.Single(u => u.Id == id);

can express that expectation.

9.15 Any() vs Count() > 0

Prefer:

users.Any()

when you only need to know whether at least one item exists.

Instead of:

users.Count() > 0

Why?

Any() communicates intent and can stop once it finds a matching element.

Example:

bool hasActiveUsers =
    users.Any(u => u.IsActive);

Interview answer

"If I only need to know whether a matching element exists, I prefer Any because it expresses the intent directly and can short-circuit once a match is found."

9.16 All()

Checks whether every element satisfies a condition.

bool allActive =
    users.All(u => u.IsActive);

Conceptually:

User 1 → true
User 2 → true
User 3 → true

All → true

But if one is false:

User 1 → true
User 2 → false
User 3 → true

All → false

All() can short-circuit when it finds a failing element.

9.17 Contains()

Checks whether an element exists.

bool exists =
    userIds.Contains(100);

For objects, the result depends on equality semantics.

For example:

List<User> users;

then:

users.Contains(user);

uses the relevant equality comparer/equality semantics.

This connects directly to the Equals() / GetHashCode() discussion from Collections.

9.18 Distinct()

Removes duplicates according to equality semantics.

var ids = new[] { 1, 2, 2, 3, 3 };

var uniqueIds = ids
    .Distinct()
    .ToList();

Result:

1
2
3

For custom objects, be aware of how equality is defined.

9.19 GroupBy()

Very important for interviews.

Suppose:

class Employee
{
    public string Department { get; set; } = "";
    public string Name { get; set; } = "";
}

Group employees by department:

var groups = employees
    .GroupBy(e => e.Department);

Conceptually:

IT
 ├── John
 ├── Mike
 └── David

HR
 ├── Sarah
 └── Emma

9.20 GroupBy + Select

A common real-world pattern:

var result = employees
    .GroupBy(e => e.Department)
    .Select(g => new
    {
        Department = g.Key,
        Count = g.Count()
    })
    .ToList();

Result conceptually:

IT  → 3
HR  → 2

This pattern is very common in reporting APIs.

9.21 Join()

LINQ can join sequences similar to SQL joins.

Suppose:

class User
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Name { get; set; } = "";
}

class Order
{
    public int UserId { get; set; }
    public decimal Amount { get; set; }
}

Join:

var result = users.Join(
    orders,
    user => user.Id,
    order => order.UserId,
    (user, order) => new
    {
        UserName = user.Name,
        order.Amount
    });

Conceptually:

Users
  Id
   ↓
Orders
 UserId

matching:

user.Id == order.UserId

9.22 Join vs GroupJoin

Join produces matching combinations.

GroupJoin associates each outer element with a collection of matching inner elements.

Conceptually:

Join
User → Order
User → Order
User → Order

Whereas:

GroupJoin

User A
 ├── Order 1
 ├── Order 2

User B
 ├── Order 3
 └── Order 4

This becomes useful when you need parent-child relationships.

9.23 Deferred Execution

Extremely important.

Consider:

var query = numbers
    .Where(x => x > 10);

At this point, the query generally hasn't enumerated the source yet.

Then:

foreach (var number in query)
{
    Console.WriteLine(number);
}

The query executes during enumeration.

Microsoft documents Enumerable.Where as using deferred execution: the returned object stores the information needed for the operation and execution occurs when the sequence is enumerated. Microsoft Learn

9.24 Example of Deferred Execution

var numbers = new List<int>
{
    1, 2, 3
};

var query = numbers.Where(x => x > 1);

numbers.Add(4);

foreach (var number in query)
{
    Console.WriteLine(number);
}

The result includes:

2
3
4

because the query is evaluated during enumeration.

Interview answer

"Deferred execution means the LINQ query is constructed first but the operation isn't executed until the sequence is enumerated, such as through foreach or another terminal operation."

9.25 How to Force Immediate Execution?

Use materialization methods:

ToList()
ToArray()
ToDictionary()
ToHashSet()

Example:

var result = numbers
    .Where(x => x > 1)
    .ToList();

Now the results are materialized into a list.

9.26 Deferred vs Immediate Execution

DeferredImmediate
WhereToList
SelectToArray
OrderByToDictionary
GroupByToHashSet
Query evaluated laterQuery/materialization occurs now

Important nuance: not every LINQ operator has identical execution characteristics, so don't memorize a simplistic "all LINQ is deferred" rule.

9.27 Why ToList() Matters in EF Core

Consider:

var query = db.Users
    .Where(u => u.IsActive);

This is still queryable.

Then:

var users = await query.ToListAsync();

Now the query is executed and results are materialized.

A common API pattern is:

var users = await db.Users
    .Where(u => u.IsActive)
    .Select(u => new UserDto
    {
        Id = u.Id,
        Name = u.Name
    })
    .ToListAsync();

This allows the database query provider to translate the supported expression before materialization.

9.28 Why Projection Before ToList()?

Compare:

var users = await db.Users
    .ToListAsync();

var result = users
    .Select(u => new UserDto
    {
        Id = u.Id,
        Name = u.Name
    })
    .ToList();

versus:

var result = await db.Users
    .Select(u => new UserDto
    {
        Id = u.Id,
        Name = u.Name
    })
    .ToListAsync();

In an EF Core scenario, the second form allows the provider to translate the projection and retrieve only the required data when supported.

Interview answer

"When querying a database through EF Core, I generally keep the query as IQueryable and project to the required DTO before materialization. This can reduce the amount of data retrieved and processed by the application."

9.29 IEnumerable Trap

Suppose:

var query = db.Users
    .AsEnumerable()
    .Where(u => SomeCustomMethod(u));

After:

AsEnumerable()

the subsequent Where is LINQ-to-Objects.

That means the filtering happens in application memory rather than being translated by the provider.

This is an important performance consideration.

9.30 ToList() vs AsEnumerable()

Very common interview question.

ToList()

var users = query.ToList();

Actually materializes the results into a list.

AsEnumerable()

var users = query.AsEnumerable();

changes the interface used for subsequent LINQ operations to IEnumerable<T>; it does not itself create a list.

Interview answer

"ToList materializes the query and creates a list, whereas AsEnumerable switches subsequent operations to IEnumerable semantics without itself materializing the entire result into a list."

9.31 AsQueryable()

var query = users.AsQueryable();

This allows the source to be exposed as IQueryable<T>.

But don't assume that simply calling AsQueryable() magically converts an in-memory list into a database query.

For an in-memory collection, you still have an in-memory source.

9.32 Select vs SelectMany

Memorize this:

Select
 ↓
One input → One output

SelectMany
 ↓
One input → Multiple outputs
 ↓
Flatten

Example:

departments.Select(d => d.Employees)

→ nested sequences.

departments.SelectMany(d => d.Employees)

→ one flattened employee sequence.

9.33 First vs Single

Memorize this table:

Method0 matches1 matchMultiple
FirstExceptionFirstFirst
FirstOrDefaultDefaultFirstFirst
SingleExceptionValueException
SingleOrDefaultDefaultValueException

Rule

First
→ I need the first one.

Single
→ There must be exactly one.

9.34 Any vs All

users.Any(u => u.IsActive)

means:

At least one active user exists.
users.All(u => u.IsActive)

means:

Every user is active.

9.35 Common LINQ Performance Trap

Bad:

var users = db.Users.ToList();

var activeUsers = users
    .Where(u => u.IsActive)
    .ToList();

Potential issue:

Database
   ↓
ALL users
   ↓
Application memory
   ↓
Filter

Prefer, when the provider can translate the query:

var activeUsers = await db.Users
    .Where(u => u.IsActive)
    .ToListAsync();

Conceptually:

Database
   ↓
WHERE IsActive = ...
   ↓
Only required rows
   ↓
Application

This distinction is especially important in EF Core interviews.

9.36 Multiple Enumeration

Consider:

var query = users.Where(u => u.IsActive);

var count = query.Count();

var first = query.First();

Depending on the source, you've potentially enumerated/executed the query more than once.

If the result is reused and materialization makes sense:

var usersList = query.ToList();

var count = usersList.Count;
var first = usersList.First();

But don't blindly call ToList() everywhere. Materialization itself has memory and execution costs.

Senior-level principle

Understand the lifetime and cost of the sequence before materializing or enumerating it repeatedly.

9.37 LINQ Method Categories

You should recognize these groups.

Filtering

Where
OfType

Projection

Select
SelectMany

Sorting

OrderBy
OrderByDescending
ThenBy
ThenByDescending
Reverse

Aggregation

Count
LongCount
Sum
Average
Min
Max
Aggregate

Quantifiers

Any
All
Contains

Element operators

First
FirstOrDefault
Single
SingleOrDefault
Last
LastOrDefault
ElementAt

Set operations

Distinct
Union
Intersect
Except

Grouping

GroupBy
ToLookup

Joining

Join
GroupJoin

Materialization

ToList
ToArray
ToDictionary
ToHashSet

  1. What is Select()?

  1. What is GroupBy()?

Intermediate

  1. IEnumerable vs IQueryable?
