⭐ 10 Lines to Memorize

  1. Reflection allows .NET applications to inspect and interact with types at runtime.
  1. Main namespaces/APIs are System.Reflection and System.Type.
  1. typeof(T) gets a Type for a compile-time-known type.
  1. GetType() gets the runtime type of an object.
  1. MethodInfo represents method metadata.
  1. PropertyInfo represents property metadata.
  1. FieldInfo represents field metadata.
  1. Activator.CreateInstance() can dynamically create an object.
  1. MethodInfo.Invoke() can dynamically invoke a method.
  1. Reflection provides flexibility but usually has more overhead than strongly typed direct access, so metadata/delegates should be cached when appropriate. Microsoft Learn

🎯 30-second interview answer

"Reflection in C# allows us to inspect and interact with types at runtime. Using System.Type and System.Reflection, we can discover assemblies, types, methods, properties, fields, constructors and attributes. We can also dynamically create objects using Activator.CreateInstance and invoke methods using MethodInfo.Invoke. Common use cases include plugin systems, serialization, framework infrastructure and runtime type discovery. The trade-off is additional runtime overhead compared with strongly typed code, so I would avoid reflection in hot paths or cache the metadata when necessary."

17. Attributes

The most important concept is:

An attribute is declarative metadata that you attach to program elements such as classes, methods, properties, parameters, or assemblies. It can later be inspected at runtime, commonly through reflection. Microsoft Learn

For your interviews, focus on:

Attribute
   ↓
Metadata
   ↓
AttributeUsage
   ↓
Custom Attribute
   ↓
Reflection
   ↓
Read Attribute
   ↓
Framework/Application behavior

1. What is an Attribute?

Interview-ready answer

"An attribute in C# is a declarative piece of metadata that provides additional information about a program element. Attributes can be applied to classes, methods, properties, parameters and other supported elements, and that metadata can be retrieved at runtime using reflection."

Example:

[Obsolete("Use NewMethod instead")]
public void OldMethod()
{
}

Here:

[Obsolete(...)]

is an attribute.

Attributes are stored as metadata associated with program elements. Microsoft Learn

2. Why do we use Attributes?

Attributes allow us to add declarative information without changing the main implementation logic.

Common uses include:

  • Validation
  • Serialization
  • Authorization/metadata
  • Routing
  • Testing
  • Documentation
  • ORM mapping
  • Framework configuration
  • Compiler behavior
  • Custom application metadata

For example:

[Serializable]
public class Customer
{
}

The attribute communicates metadata about the type.

3. Common Built-in Attributes

You should recognize these in interviews.

[Obsolete]

Marks something as obsolete:

[Obsolete("Use GetCustomerAsync instead")]
public Customer GetCustomer()
{
    ...
}

The compiler can warn when this member is used.

[Conditional]

Controls whether calls to a method are included based on a compilation symbol.

[Conditional("DEBUG")]
public void LogDebug()
{
}

[AttributeUsage]

Controls where and how a custom attribute can be applied.

[AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Class)]
public class MyAttribute : Attribute
{
}

These are examples of attributes that have language/compiler/runtime significance. Microsoft Learn

4. What is a Custom Attribute?

A custom attribute is an attribute you create yourself.

It must derive directly or indirectly from:

System.Attribute

Example:

public class AuthorAttribute : Attribute
{
    public string Name { get; }

    public AuthorAttribute(string name)
    {
        Name = name;
    }
}

Then use it:

[Author("Saurabh")]
public class CustomerService
{
}

By convention, attribute classes use the Attribute suffix, but when applying the attribute, the suffix can be omitted:

[Author]

instead of:

[AuthorAttribute]

Microsoft documents this naming convention explicitly. Microsoft Learn

5. Why does an Attribute inherit from System.Attribute?

Interview answer

"Custom attributes derive from System.Attribute, which identifies the class as an attribute type and allows the compiler/runtime to treat instances of that class as attribute metadata."

Example:

public class AuditAttribute : Attribute
{
}

Then:

[Audit]
public class OrderService
{
}

6. What is AttributeUsage?

🔥 Very important interview question.

AttributeUsage specifies where and how a custom attribute can be used.

Example:

[AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Class)]
public class AuditAttribute : Attribute
{
}

Now:

[Audit]
public class OrderService
{
}

is valid.

But applying [Audit] to a method would not be valid because we restricted it to classes.

AttributeUsage controls three important things:

AttributeTargets
AllowMultiple
Inherited
``` :chatgpt-content-reference{index="4"}


---

# 7. `AttributeTargets`

You can specify where an attribute is allowed.

Examples include:

```csharp
AttributeTargets.Class
AttributeTargets.Method
AttributeTargets.Property
AttributeTargets.Field
AttributeTargets.Parameter
AttributeTargets.Interface
AttributeTargets.Struct
AttributeTargets.Enum
AttributeTargets.ReturnValue

You can combine them using |.

Example:

[AttributeUsage(
    AttributeTargets.Class |
    AttributeTargets.Method |
    AttributeTargets.Property)]
public class AuditAttribute : Attribute
{
}

This allows:

[Audit]
public class OrderService
{
    [Audit]
    public void CreateOrder()
    {
    }
}

The C# specification defines the supported attribute targets, including type, method, property, field, parameter, return, event, and others. Microsoft Learn

8. What is AllowMultiple?

By default, an attribute generally cannot be applied multiple times to the same target.

Example:

[AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Class)]
public class RoleAttribute : Attribute
{
}

This:

[Role]
[Role]   // ❌
public class UserService
{
}

is not allowed.

But:

[AttributeUsage(
    AttributeTargets.Class,
    AllowMultiple = true)]
public class RoleAttribute : Attribute
{
}

allows:

[Role]
[Role]
public class UserService
{
}

Microsoft specifically documents AllowMultiple as the setting that controls whether an attribute can be applied more than once. Microsoft Learn

9. What is Inherited?

Inherited controls whether an attribute applied to a base class can be inherited by derived classes when the relevant reflection APIs consider inherited attributes.

Example:

[AttributeUsage(
    AttributeTargets.Class,
    Inherited = true)]
public class AuditableAttribute : Attribute
{
}

Then:

[Auditable]
public class BaseService
{
}

public class OrderService : BaseService
{
}

The attribute can be inherited according to the attribute's usage configuration.

Default AttributeUsage behavior includes Inherited = true and AllowMultiple = false when those settings aren't explicitly changed. Microsoft Learn

10. Positional vs Named Parameters

This is a good intermediate question.

Consider:

public class AuthorAttribute : Attribute
{
    public string Name { get; }

    public string Version { get; set; }

    public AuthorAttribute(string name)
    {
        Name = name;
    }
}

Usage:

[Author("Saurabh", Version = "2.0")]
public class CustomerService
{
}

Here:

"Saurabh"

is a positional argument.

And:

Version = "2.0"

is a named argument.

Microsoft describes constructor parameters as positional parameters and public read/write fields/properties as named parameters. Microsoft Learn

11. Complete Custom Attribute Example

Let's build a practical one.

[AttributeUsage(
    AttributeTargets.Method,
    AllowMultiple = false)]
public class AuditAttribute : Attribute
{
    public string Action { get; }

    public AuditAttribute(string action)
    {
        Action = action;
    }
}

Apply it:

public class OrderService
{
    [Audit("CreateOrder")]
    public void CreateOrder()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Order created");
    }
}

Now the method contains metadata:

CreateOrder()
     |
     +--- AuditAttribute
              |
              +--- Action = "CreateOrder"

12. How do you read an Attribute?

This is where Reflection from the previous topic connects.

MethodInfo method =
    typeof(OrderService)
        .GetMethod("CreateOrder");

var attribute =
    method.GetCustomAttribute<AuditAttribute>();

Console.WriteLine(attribute?.Action);

Output:

CreateOrder

The relationship is:

Attribute
   ↓
Metadata
   ↓
Reflection
   ↓
GetCustomAttribute()
   ↓
Attribute instance

Attributes can be queried at runtime using reflection. Microsoft Learn

13. GetCustomAttribute<T>() vs GetCustomAttributes()

One attribute

var attribute =
    method.GetCustomAttribute<AuditAttribute>();

Useful when you expect a single attribute.

Multiple attributes

var attributes =
    method.GetCustomAttributes();

This returns the attributes associated with the member.

You can also filter:

var attributes =
    method.GetCustomAttributes<AuditAttribute>();

This becomes especially useful when:

AllowMultiple = true

14. Attributes don't automatically execute business logic

🔥 Important interview trap.

Suppose:

[Audit]
public void CreateOrder()
{
}

Don't say:

"The Audit attribute automatically logs the method."

The attribute itself is primarily metadata.

Something else must read that metadata and act on it.

For example:

[Audit]
   ↓
Metadata
   ↓
Framework / Reflection / Interceptor
   ↓
Read attribute
   ↓
Perform audit behavior

Interview answer

"An attribute by itself mainly provides metadata. Some framework or application code must interpret that metadata and perform the corresponding behavior."

That's an important distinction.

15. Attribute vs Annotation

If you've worked with Java, you may hear:

Annotation

In C#, the equivalent concept is generally called an:

Attribute

For example:

[Serializable]

C# calls this an attribute.

16. Attribute vs Comment

Why not just use comments?

Comment

// This method creates an order

Primarily for developers/readability.

Attribute

[Audit("CreateOrder")]

Structured metadata that can be retrieved programmatically.

Comment
   ↓
Human-readable

Attribute
   ↓
Structured metadata
   ↓
Can be inspected programmatically

17. Attribute vs Configuration File

Suppose you have:

[Route("api/orders")]
public class OrderController
{
}

The routing metadata is close to the code it describes.

Attributes are useful when configuration is tightly associated with a program element.

External configuration is often preferable when values need to change without recompiling.

Interview answer

"Attributes are useful for metadata that naturally belongs to a code element, while external configuration is generally more appropriate for environment-specific or frequently changing values."

18. Attribute Targets

You can apply attributes to many things.

For example:

Class

[Audit]
public class OrderService
{
}

Method

[Audit]
public void CreateOrder()
{
}

Property

[Required]
public string CustomerName { get; set; }

Parameter

public void CreateOrder(
    [SomeAttribute] int orderId)
{
}

Assembly

Attributes can also be applied at assembly level:

[assembly: SomeAssemblyAttribute]

The C# specification supports attribute application to assemblies, modules, types, members, parameters, type parameters and other program elements. Microsoft Learn

19. Attribute Targets with |

A common interview coding question:

[AttributeUsage(
    AttributeTargets.Class |
    AttributeTargets.Method |
    AttributeTargets.Property)]
public class LogAttribute : Attribute
{
}

The | means:

Allow this attribute on any of these targets.

It is a flags-style combination of AttributeTargets values.

20. Can an Attribute have constructor parameters?

Yes.

Example:

public class ApiVersionAttribute : Attribute
{
    public string Version { get; }

    public ApiVersionAttribute(string version)
    {
        Version = version;
    }
}

Usage:

[ApiVersion("v2")]
public class OrderController
{
}

21. Can an Attribute have properties?

Yes.

public class ApiAttribute : Attribute
{
    public string Version { get; }

    public bool Deprecated { get; set; }

    public ApiAttribute(string version)
    {
        Version = version;
    }
}

Usage:

[Api("v2", Deprecated = false)]
public class OrderController
{
}

22. Can an Attribute have fields?

Yes, but public read/write fields can participate as named arguments.

For example:

public class AuthorAttribute : Attribute
{
    public string Name;

    public AuthorAttribute(string name)
    {
        Name = name;
    }
}

Usage:

[Author("Saurabh")]
public class Customer
{
}

For modern application design, properties are often preferable for named configuration values.

23. Attribute Constructor Restrictions

Attribute arguments aren't arbitrary runtime expressions.

Typical attribute arguments include values that can be represented in attribute metadata, such as:

primitive values
string
Type
enum
arrays of supported attribute argument types

For example:

[MyAttribute(
    "Customer",
    typeof(Customer),
    SomeEnum.Active)]

is valid when the attribute constructor/property signatures support those types.

This is why you can't simply pass arbitrary objects:

[MyAttribute(new Customer())] // ❌

24. Real-World ASP.NET Core Example

Since your stack includes ASP.NET Core, this is especially important.

You have likely seen:

[ApiController]
[Route("api/[controller]")]
public class OrdersController : ControllerBase
{
}

Here:

[ApiController]

and:

[Route(...)]

are attributes.

They provide metadata that ASP.NET Core's framework infrastructure can interpret.

Conceptually:

Controller
   ↓
Attributes
   ↓
ASP.NET Core infrastructure
   ↓
Routing / API behavior

This is one of the most useful real-world connections for your interviews.

25. Validation Example

You've probably seen:

public class CreateUserRequest
{
    [Required]
    public string Name { get; set; }

    [EmailAddress]
    public string Email { get; set; }
}

The attributes describe validation metadata.

Framework/application infrastructure can inspect this metadata and apply validation behavior.

Conceptually:

[Required]
    ↓
Metadata
    ↓
Validation system
    ↓
Validate property

26. Serialization Example

Attributes can also influence serialization behavior.

Conceptually:

[SomeSerializationAttribute]
public string InternalCode { get; set; }

A serializer can inspect that metadata and determine how the member should be represented.

This is one of the documented uses of attributes in .NET. Microsoft Learn

27. Reflection + Attributes + ASP.NET Core

This is a strong interview connection:

Attribute
   ↓
Metadata
   ↓
Reflection / framework infrastructure
   ↓
Interpret metadata
   ↓
Application behavior

For example:

[HttpGet]
public IActionResult GetOrders()
{
}

Conceptually, the framework needs to understand that the method has HTTP GET metadata.

You don't need to claim that every framework operation is implemented through a simple direct GetCustomAttribute() call—the internal implementation can be more sophisticated.

28. AttributeUsage Example — Full Interview Code

[AttributeUsage(
    AttributeTargets.Method,
    AllowMultiple = true,
    Inherited = false)]
public class PermissionAttribute : Attribute
{
    public string Permission { get; }

    public PermissionAttribute(string permission)
    {
        Permission = permission;
    }
}

Usage:

public class OrderController
{
    [Permission("Order.Read")]
    [Permission("Order.Export")]
    public void ExportOrders()
    {
    }
}

Because:

AllowMultiple = true

multiple [Permission] attributes are allowed.

29. Reading Multiple Custom Attributes

MethodInfo method =
    typeof(OrderController)
        .GetMethod("ExportOrders");

var permissions =
    method.GetCustomAttributes<PermissionAttribute>();

foreach (var permission in permissions)
{
    Console.WriteLine(permission.Permission);
}

Output:

Order.Read
Order.Export

This demonstrates:

Attribute
   ↓
AllowMultiple
   ↓
Reflection
   ↓
GetCustomAttributes<T>()

30. Important Interview Question: Are Attributes Objects?

The nuanced answer:

Attribute declarations are metadata associated with program elements. When you retrieve them through APIs such as GetCustomAttributes, you can obtain attribute instances representing that metadata.

So don't oversimplify this as:

"Attributes are just normal objects stored on the class."

Their primary purpose is declarative metadata. The runtime/compiler stores the relevant attribute information in metadata, and reflection APIs expose it. Microsoft Learn

31. Attributes vs Reflection

Very important distinction:

Attribute

Provides metadata.

[Audit]
public void Save()
{
}

Reflection

Reads/inspects metadata.

method.GetCustomAttribute<AuditAttribute>();

Therefore:

Attribute → writes/describes metadata

Reflection → reads/inspects metadata

This connects directly to your previous topic.

32. Attributes vs Expression Trees

Another useful Senior-level comparison:

AttributesExpression Trees
Declarative metadataRepresentation of code
Describe program elementsRepresent expressions
[Route(...)]x => x.Age > 18
Read using reflectionInspect/translate/compile
Common in framework configurationCommon in LINQ/query providers

33. Scenario-Based Question

Interviewer:

"How would you implement a custom authorization mechanism using attributes?"

Strong answer

"I could define a custom attribute such as PermissionAttribute containing the required permission. I would apply it to controller actions or service methods. Then an authorization component or framework integration could inspect that metadata and check the current user's permissions before executing the operation. I would use AttributeUsage to control where the attribute can be applied and whether multiple permissions are allowed."

Flow:

[Permission("Order.Read")]
          ↓
Metadata
          ↓
Authorization component
          ↓
Read attribute
          ↓
Check user permission
          ↓
Allow / deny operation

34. Common Interview Traps

❌ "Attributes execute automatically."

Not necessarily.

They provide metadata; something has to interpret them.

❌ "Reflection and attributes are the same."

No.

Attribute = metadata

Reflection = mechanism to inspect metadata

❌ "Every attribute must be inherited."

No.

Inherited is configurable through AttributeUsage.

❌ "You can apply any attribute anywhere."

No.

AttributeUsage can restrict targets.

❌ "Multiple copies of an attribute are always allowed."

No.

AllowMultiple controls this.

🔥 Top Interview Questions

Basic

  1. What is an attribute in C#?
  1. Why do we use attributes?
  1. What is a custom attribute?
  1. What is System.Attribute?
  1. Give examples of built-in attributes.
  1. What is [Obsolete]?
  1. What is [AttributeUsage]?

Intermediate

  1. How do you create a custom attribute?
  1. What is AttributeTargets?
  1. What is AllowMultiple?
  1. What is Inherited?
  1. What are positional parameters?
  1. What are named parameters?
  1. Can attributes have constructors?
  1. Can attributes have properties?
  1. How do you retrieve an attribute using reflection?
  1. GetCustomAttribute() vs GetCustomAttributes()?
  1. Can attributes be applied to methods/properties/parameters?

Advanced

  1. How are attributes stored?
  1. How does reflection retrieve attributes?
  1. Attribute vs Reflection?
  1. Attribute vs Expression Tree?
  1. How would you create a custom authorization attribute?
  1. How would you create a custom validation attribute?
  1. How can multiple custom attributes be supported?
  1. What are attribute constructor argument restrictions?
  1. How are attributes used by ASP.NET Core?
  1. How would you build an attribute-driven plugin/processing system?
  1. What does Inherited = true mean?
  1. What happens if AllowMultiple = false?

⭐ 10 Lines to Memorize

  1. An attribute is declarative metadata attached to a program element.
  1. Custom attributes derive from System.Attribute.
  1. Attributes can be applied to classes, methods, properties, parameters, assemblies and other supported targets.
  1. AttributeUsage controls where an attribute can be applied.
  1. AllowMultiple controls whether the same attribute can be applied multiple times.
  1. Inherited controls attribute inheritance behavior.
  1. Constructor arguments are commonly positional parameters.
  1. Public writable properties/fields can be named parameters.
  1. Reflection can retrieve attributes at runtime.
  1. Attributes provide metadata; reflection or framework infrastructure interprets that metadata. Microsoft Learn

🎯 30-second interview answer

"Attributes in C# provide declarative metadata that can be attached to classes, methods, properties, parameters and other program elements. Built-in examples include Obsolete, while we can create custom attributes by inheriting from System.Attribute. AttributeUsage controls where the attribute can be applied, whether multiple instances are allowed, and whether it can be inherited. At runtime, reflection can retrieve the attribute metadata and frameworks such as ASP.NET Core can use that metadata to implement behavior such as routing, validation or authorization."

18. dynamic

dynamic is an important advanced C# interview topic, especially around runtime binding, reflection, COM/interoperability, and dynamic APIs.

Microsoft describes dynamic as bypassing normal compile-time type checking for operations and resolving those operations at runtime. At runtime, dynamic is effectively represented as object; dynamic is primarily a compile-time construct. Microsoft Learn

1. What is dynamic?

Interview-ready answer

"dynamic is a C# type that enables late binding. Unlike normal statically typed variables, operations performed on a dynamic value are resolved at runtime instead of compile time. This provides flexibility but moves certain errors from compile time to runtime."

Example:

dynamic value = 10;

Console.WriteLine(value + 20);   // 30
Console.WriteLine(value.Length); // Runtime exception

The compiler allows value.Length because value is dynamic.

The runtime then discovers that int doesn't have a Length property and throws an exception. Microsoft Learn

2. var vs object vs dynamic

This is very commonly asked.

Featurevarobjectdynamic
Type determinedCompile timeobjectRuntime operation
Static type checking✅✅❌ for dynamic operations
IntelliSenseUsually strongBased on object membersLimited
Runtime errorsLess likelyCompile-time casting neededMore likely
Can hold any typeYesYesYes
Use caseNormal type inferenceGeneral base typeRuntime/dynamic scenarios

Example

var a = 10;
a = "hello";       // ❌ Compile error

Because var means:

int a = 10;
object b = 10;

Console.WriteLine(b + 10); // ❌

You need casting/unboxing as appropriate:

Console.WriteLine((int)b + 10);
dynamic c = 10;

Console.WriteLine(c + 10); // ✅

The operation is dynamically bound.

3. Is dynamic actually a runtime type?

Interview trap ⚠️

No.

A strong answer:

"dynamic is primarily a compile-time feature. At runtime, a variable declared as dynamic is represented similarly to object; what changes is how operations involving it are bound."

Microsoft's C# specification explicitly states that dynamic is indistinguishable from object at runtime. Microsoft Learn

dynamic x = 100;

Console.WriteLine(x.GetType());

Output:

System.Int32

There is no runtime type called dynamic.

4. Static binding vs dynamic binding

Static binding

Normal C# code:

string name = "Saurabh";

Console.WriteLine(name.Length);

The compiler knows:

name → string → Length

So the operation is resolved at compile time.

Dynamic binding

dynamic name = "Saurabh";

Console.WriteLine(name.Length);

The compiler doesn't perform the normal member lookup.

The runtime determines:

runtime value → String → Length

This is called late binding / dynamic binding. Microsoft Learn

5. What happens if the operation is invalid?

dynamic employee = "Saurabh";

Console.WriteLine(employee.Age);

This compiles.

But at runtime:

RuntimeBinderException

because string doesn't have an Age property.

Interview point

"dynamic trades compile-time safety for runtime flexibility."

6. Dynamic method invocation

dynamic calculator = new Calculator();

var result = calculator.Add(10, 20);

If the method exists:

class Calculator
{
    public int Add(int a, int b)
    {
        return a + b;
    }
}

Result:

30

But:

calculator.UnknownMethod();

will fail at runtime.

7. Dynamic overload resolution

This is a good advanced interview question.

class Calculator
{
    public void Print(int value)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("int");
    }

    public void Print(string value)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("string");
    }
}

Now:

dynamic value = "Hello";

var calculator = new Calculator();

calculator.Print(value);

The overload resolution happens at runtime, based on the runtime type of value.

Output:

string

Microsoft specifically notes that overload resolution occurs at runtime when a dynamic argument or receiver is involved. Microsoft Learn

8. dynamic and DLR

What is DLR?

DLR = Dynamic Language Runtime

It provides infrastructure for dynamic operations in .NET.

Think:

C# code
   ↓
dynamic
   ↓
Dynamic Language Runtime
   ↓
Runtime binding
   ↓
Actual operation

The DLR supports dynamic programming scenarios and dynamic features in statically typed languages such as C#. Microsoft Learn

Interview answer

"The Dynamic Language Runtime provides the infrastructure that enables dynamic binding and dynamic object behavior in .NET."

9. ExpandoObject

This is another important topic.

ExpandoObject allows you to dynamically add and remove members at runtime. Microsoft Learn

dynamic employee = new ExpandoObject();

employee.Name = "Saurabh";
employee.Age = 27;

Console.WriteLine(employee.Name);
Console.WriteLine(employee.Age);

You dynamically created:

Name
Age

without defining a traditional class.

You can also add methods:

dynamic employee = new ExpandoObject();

employee.Name = "Saurabh";

employee.Greet = (Action)(() =>
{
    Console.WriteLine("Hello!");
});

employee.Greet();

10. dynamic vs ExpandoObject

Very common follow-up.

dynamic

Keyword that enables dynamic binding.

dynamic obj = GetSomething();

ExpandoObject

A concrete .NET class whose members can be dynamically added/removed.

dynamic obj = new ExpandoObject();

Think:

dynamic
   ↓
How you access the object

ExpandoObject
   ↓
One type of object that supports dynamic members

Microsoft describes ExpandoObject as an object whose members can be dynamically added and removed at runtime. Microsoft Learn

11. DynamicObject

DynamicObject is a base class that allows you to define your own dynamic behavior. Microsoft Learn

Example:

public class MyDynamicObject : DynamicObject
{
    public override bool TryGetMember(
        GetMemberBinder binder,
        out object? result)
    {
        result = $"You requested {binder.Name}";
        return true;
    }
}

Usage:

dynamic obj = new MyDynamicObject();

Console.WriteLine(obj.Name);

The custom TryGetMember() controls what happens.

Difference

ExpandoObject
    ↓
Simple dynamic properties

DynamicObject
    ↓
Custom dynamic behavior

12. dynamic vs Reflection

This is especially relevant given your roadmap.

Reflection

You explicitly inspect types/members:

Type type = obj.GetType();

PropertyInfo? property =
    type.GetProperty("Name");

var value = property?.GetValue(obj);

Dynamic

dynamic d = obj;

var value = d.Name;

Interview answer

"Reflection gives explicit programmatic access to metadata and members, while dynamic provides more natural syntax for late-bound operations. Dynamic can internally use runtime binding infrastructure, whereas reflection requires me to explicitly inspect and invoke members."

13. dynamic vs Generics

Generics

Prefer when the type relationship is known at compile time.

public T GetValue<T>(T value)
{
    return value;
}

Advantages:

  • Type safety
  • Compile-time checking
  • Better tooling
  • Usually preferable for application business logic

Dynamic

Use when the structure/type isn't known until runtime.

dynamic data = GetExternalData();

Console.WriteLine(data.Name);

Interview rule

Known type relationship → Generics.

Runtime structure/binding requirement → Dynamic.

14. Real-world scenario

Imagine an application receives data from multiple external systems.

System A:

{
    "name": "Saurabh",
    "age": 27
}

System B:

{
    "customerName": "Saurabh",
    "customerId": 101
}

If the structure is genuinely variable and you don't want strongly typed models for every shape, you might encounter dynamic JSON/data handling.

Conceptually:

dynamic data = GetExternalData();

Console.WriteLine(data.name);

However, for a normal production .NET API where the schema is known, strongly typed DTOs are generally preferable because they provide compile-time safety and clearer contracts.

That's an important interview distinction.

15. When should you use dynamic?

Good scenarios:

1. COM interoperability

Microsoft specifically identifies COM interop as a use case for dynamic. Microsoft Learn

2. Dynamic language interoperability

For example, interacting with dynamic-language environments.

3. Truly dynamic object structures

dynamic data = ...

4. ExpandoObject

When properties need to be added/removed dynamically.

5. Legacy APIs

When you're interacting with APIs that expose loosely typed objects.

16. When should you avoid dynamic?

For normal business application code:

dynamic user = GetUser();

is usually less desirable than:

User user = GetUser();

Why?

  • Less compile-time safety
  • Runtime errors
  • Weaker refactoring support
  • Less predictable contracts
  • Debugging can be harder
  • Tooling/IntelliSense is weaker

Microsoft also recommends concrete types where compile-time type information is needed, such as declarations, constraints, inheritance, and reflection operations. Microsoft Learn

17. Important interview traps

❌ Trap 1

"dynamic is a runtime type."

Not exactly.

Better:

"dynamic changes binding behavior so operations are resolved at runtime; at runtime the value is represented as object."

❌ Trap 2

"var and dynamic are basically the same."

No.

var x = 10;
// x is statically int

dynamic y = 10;
// y is dynamically bound

❌ Trap 3

"Dynamic makes C# dynamically typed."

Not exactly.

C# remains a statically typed language; dynamic provides dynamic binding for specific expressions/operations.

❌ Trap 4

"Dynamic is always slower."

Too absolute.

Better:

"Dynamic introduces runtime binding overhead and removes compile-time checking, so I wouldn't use it unnecessarily, especially in performance-sensitive or strongly typed business logic."

18. Top interview questions

For your 3.9 YOE Senior/.NET Full Stack interviews, prepare these particularly well:

Basic

  1. What is dynamic?
  1. var vs dynamic?
  1. object vs dynamic?
  1. Is dynamic compile-time or runtime?
  1. What is late binding?
  1. What happens when an invalid operation is performed on dynamic?

Intermediate

  1. How does dynamic binding work?
  1. What is DLR?
  1. What is ExpandoObject?
  1. ExpandoObject vs DynamicObject?
  1. dynamic vs reflection?
  1. Can you use dynamic with methods?
  1. How does overload resolution work with dynamic?

Advanced

  1. Why is dynamic represented as object at runtime?
  1. What are the disadvantages of dynamic?
  1. When would you use dynamic in a production application?
  1. Dynamic vs generics?
  1. Dynamic vs expression trees?
  1. How does dynamic interact with extension methods?
  1. Why shouldn't dynamic be used everywhere?

19. 30-second interview answer

If the interviewer simply asks:

"What is dynamic in C#?"

Say:

"dynamic is a C# feature that enables late binding. With normal C# code, member access and overload resolution are generally checked at compile time, but operations involving dynamic are resolved at runtime. This provides flexibility when working with dynamic objects, COM APIs, or interoperability scenarios, but it sacrifices compile-time type safety. ExpandoObject and DynamicObject are related mechanisms for working with dynamically shaped or dynamically behaving objects."

That is a strong 3.9 YOE-level answer. Microsoft Learn

🔥 #18 Cheat Sheet

dynamic
   ↓
Late / runtime binding
   ↓
Compile-time checking bypassed
   ↓
Runtime determines operation
var
→ compile-time inferred type

object
→ strongly typed as object

dynamic
→ runtime binding
ExpandoObject
→ dynamically add/remove members

DynamicObject
→ customize dynamic behavior

DLR
→ infrastructure for dynamic binding

10 lines to memorize

  1. dynamic enables late binding.
  1. Dynamic operations are resolved at runtime.
  1. dynamic is a compile-time language feature.
  1. At runtime, dynamic is represented like object.
  1. Invalid dynamic operations fail at runtime.
  1. DLR provides infrastructure for dynamic binding.
  1. ExpandoObject supports dynamically added/removed members.
  1. DynamicObject allows custom dynamic behavior.
  1. Reflection explicitly inspects/invokes members; dynamic provides late-bound syntax.
  1. Prefer strongly typed models/generics when the type is known.

19. Pattern Matching in C#

Pattern matching is a high-value modern C# topic for your interviews because it combines is, switch, type checking, null checking, relational conditions, property matching, and modern C# syntax.

1. What is Pattern Matching?

Interview-ready answer

"Pattern matching in C# allows us to test an expression against a specific type, value, property structure, or condition and execute logic when the pattern matches. It provides concise and type-safe alternatives to traditional type checks and complex if-else chains."

Example:

object value = "Hello";

if (value is string text)
{
    Console.WriteLine(text.Length);
}

Here:

value is string text

does two things:

  1. Checks whether value is a string
  1. If it is, assigns the value to text

2. is with Type Pattern

The basic pattern is:

if (obj is string)
{
    // obj is a string
}

But normally you want the matched value:

if (obj is string text)
{
    Console.WriteLine(text.Length);
}

This is called a declaration pattern.

Microsoft describes this as testing the runtime type and declaring a variable containing the matched value. Microsoft Learn

Traditional approach

if (obj is string)
{
    string text = (string)obj;
    Console.WriteLine(text.Length);
}

Pattern matching

if (obj is string text)
{
    Console.WriteLine(text.Length);
}

The second approach is cleaner and avoids the separate cast.

3. is vs as

This is a common interview question.

is

Returns a Boolean and can perform pattern matching:

if (employee is Manager manager)
{
    manager.ApproveLeave();
}

as

Attempts a reference/nullable conversion:

Manager? manager = employee as Manager;

if (manager != null)
{
    manager.ApproveLeave();
}

Interview answer

"is is useful when I want to test a type and optionally capture the value using pattern matching. as attempts a compatible reference or nullable conversion and returns null if it can't convert."

For modern C#, I would generally prefer:

if (employee is Manager manager)

when performing a type test and using the result.

4. Constant Pattern

You can match a specific constant:

int status = 200;

if (status is 200)
{
    Console.WriteLine("Success");
}

You can also use it with switch:

string GetMessage(int status) =>
    status switch
    {
        200 => "Success",
        404 => "Not Found",
        500 => "Server Error",
        _ => "Unknown"
    };

The 200, 404, and 500 are constant patterns.

5. switch Expression

This is one of the most important modern C# features.

Traditional:

string GetStatus(int status)
{
    switch (status)
    {
        case 200:
            return "Success";

        case 404:
            return "Not Found";

        case 500:
            return "Server Error";

        default:
            return "Unknown";
    }
}

Modern:

string GetStatus(int status) =>
    status switch
    {
        200 => "Success",
        404 => "Not Found",
        500 => "Server Error",
        _ => "Unknown"
    };

Interview answer

"A switch expression evaluates an input and returns a value based on the first matching pattern. It's particularly useful when each branch produces a result."

Microsoft recommends a switch expression when the branches calculate one result, while a switch statement is more appropriate when branches perform multiple statements/actions. Microsoft Learn

6. Discard Pattern _

The _ pattern means:

Match anything that hasn't already matched.
string GetRole(string role) =>
    role switch
    {
        "Admin" => "Full Access",
        "Manager" => "Management Access",
        "User" => "Standard Access",
        _ => "Unknown Role"
    };

Here:

_ => "Unknown Role"

acts as the fallback.

Important interview trap

The discard pattern should generally be last because it matches everything. A later pattern after _ can become unreachable/subsumed. Microsoft Learn

7. Relational Patterns

Modern C# allows:

<
<=
>
>=

Example:

string GetGrade(int marks) =>
    marks switch
    {
        >= 90 => "A",
        >= 75 => "B",
        >= 60 => "C",
        >= 40 => "D",
        _ => "Fail"
    };

This is much cleaner than:

if (marks >= 90)
{
}
else if (marks >= 75)
{
}

Microsoft defines relational patterns for comparisons such as <, <=, >, and >=. Microsoft Learn

8. Logical Patterns: and, or, not

Very important for interviews.

and

Both conditions must match:

if (age is >= 18 and <= 60)
{
    Console.WriteLine("Eligible");
}

Equivalent idea:

if (age >= 18 && age <= 60)

or

Either condition can match:

if (status is 200 or 201)
{
    Console.WriteLine("Successful response");
}

not

Negates a pattern:

if (user is not null)
{
    Console.WriteLine("User exists");
}

Microsoft documents and, or, and not as logical patterns for combining or negating patterns. Microsoft Learn

9. Property Pattern

This is a very important Senior-level pattern.

Suppose:

class Employee
{
    public string Department { get; set; }
    public int Experience { get; set; }
}

Instead of:

if (employee != null &&
    employee.Department == "IT" &&
    employee.Experience >= 3)
{
}

You can write:

if (employee is
    {
        Department: "IT",
        Experience: >= 3
    })
{
    Console.WriteLine("Experienced IT employee");
}

This is called a property pattern.

Property patterns can inspect properties and nest other patterns. Microsoft Learn

10. Property Pattern with switch

This is where pattern matching becomes really powerful.

string GetEmployeeLevel(Employee employee) =>
    employee switch
    {
        { Experience: >= 10 } => "Architect",
        { Experience: >= 5 } => "Senior",
        { Experience: >= 3 } => "Mid-Level",
        _ => "Junior"
    };

The input is:

employee

and the patterns inspect:

employee.Experience

11. Type + Property Pattern

You can combine type matching and property matching.

object employee = new Manager
{
    Experience = 8
};

string result = employee switch
{
    Manager { Experience: >= 5 } => "Experienced Manager",

    Developer { Experience: >= 5 } => "Experienced Developer",

    _ => "Other"
};

This allows you to match:

Type
+
Properties
+
Conditions

in a single expression.

12. when Guard

A when clause provides an additional Boolean condition.

Example:

string GetDiscount(Customer customer) =>
    customer switch
    {
        { IsPremium: true } when customer.TotalAmount >= 10000
            => "20% Discount",

        { IsPremium: true }
            => "10% Discount",

        _ => "No Discount"
    };

Here:

{ IsPremium: true }

is the pattern.

And:

when customer.TotalAmount >= 10000

is the additional guard.

Important distinction

Use a pattern for the shape/value of the input.

Use when when an additional Boolean condition is needed, particularly when it depends on other information or is clearer as a Boolean expression. Microsoft Learn

13. Pattern Matching for Null

Instead of:

if (user == null)
{
}

you can write:

if (user is null)
{
}

And:

if (user is not null)
{
}

Why is this useful?

is null and is not null perform pattern matching and don't invoke a user-defined == or != operator. Microsoft Learn

This makes them particularly useful for reliable null checks.

14. Positional Pattern

Suppose we have:

public record Point(int X, int Y);

You can match:

Point point = new(10, 20);

if (point is (10, 20))
{
    Console.WriteLine("Point is 10,20");
}

Or:

string GetPosition(Point point) =>
    point switch
    {
        (0, 0) => "Origin",
        (0, _) => "Y axis",
        (_, 0) => "X axis",
        _ => "Other"
    };

Positional patterns work with values that expose positional/deconstruction information. Pattern matching supports both property and positional patterns. Microsoft Learn

15. List Patterns

Modern C# also supports list patterns.

Example:

int[] numbers = { 1, 2, 3 };

if (numbers is [1, 2, 3])
{
    Console.WriteLine("Exact match");
}

You can use:

_

for an individual element:

if (numbers is [1, _, 3])
{
    Console.WriteLine("First and last match");
}

And:

..

for a slice:

if (numbers is [1, ..])
{
    Console.WriteLine("Starts with 1");
}

List and slice patterns allow matching both the values and shape of supported sequences. Microsoft Learn

16. Nested / Recursive Patterns

Patterns can contain other patterns.

Example:

if (order is
    {
        Customer: { IsPremium: true },
        TotalAmount: >= 10000
    })
{
    Console.WriteLine("Premium high-value order");
}

Here you're matching:

Order
 ├── Customer
 │    └── IsPremium == true
 │
 └── TotalAmount >= 10000

This is called recursive/nested pattern matching.

17. Pattern Matching vs Traditional if

Traditional

if (employee != null &&
    employee is Manager &&
    ((Manager)employee).Experience >= 5)
{
    ...
}

Pattern matching

if (employee is Manager { Experience: >= 5 })
{
    ...
}

The second version expresses the data shape being matched directly.

18. Pattern Matching vs switch

A common interview question:

if + is

Use when you have a smaller number of conditions:

if (value is string text)
{
}

switch statement

Use when branches perform actions:

switch (value)
{
    case string text:
        Console.WriteLine(text);
        break;

    case int number:
        Console.WriteLine(number);
        break;
}

switch expression

Use when branches produce a value:

string result = value switch
{
    string text => text,
    int number => number.ToString(),
    _ => "Unknown"
};

This distinction is explicitly reflected in Microsoft's guidance. Microsoft Learn

19. Exhaustiveness

This is a good Senior-level interview question.

Consider:

string GetResult(int status) =>
    status switch
    {
        200 => "Success",
        404 => "Not Found"
    };

What about:

500
201
400
...

Not every possible input is handled.

The compiler can warn about a non-exhaustive switch expression.

You can provide:

_ => "Unknown"

to handle everything else.

Microsoft notes that if no switch-expression arm matches at runtime, .NET Core 3.0+ throws SwitchExpressionException; the compiler generally warns when it detects non-exhaustive handling. Microsoft Learn

20. Pattern Order Matters

Consider:

int GetLevel(int experience) =>
    experience switch
    {
        >= 3 =>  "Experienced",
        >= 10 => "Senior",
        _ => "Junior"
    };

This is wrong logically.

Why?

For:

experience = 10

the first pattern:

>= 3

already matches.

Therefore:

>= 10

will never be reached.

Correct:

int GetLevel(int experience) =>
    experience switch
    {
        >= 10 => "Senior",
        >= 3 => "Experienced",
        _ => "Junior"
    };

The first matching switch arm wins, and the compiler can report subsumed/unreachable patterns in cases it can determine. Microsoft Learn

21. Real-World .NET API Scenario

Suppose your API receives different payment types:

public abstract record Payment;

public record CreditCardPayment(
    string CardNumber,
    decimal Amount) : Payment;

public record UpiPayment(
    string UpiId,
    decimal Amount) : Payment;

public record CashPayment(
    decimal Amount) : Payment;

Instead of:

if (payment is CreditCardPayment)
{
    ...
}
else if (payment is UpiPayment)
{
    ...
}

you can write:

string ProcessPayment(Payment payment) =>
    payment switch
    {
        CreditCardPayment { Amount: >= 10000 }
            => "Credit card high-value payment",

        CreditCardPayment
            => "Credit card payment",

        UpiPayment { Amount: >= 5000 }
            => "UPI high-value payment",

        UpiPayment
            => "UPI payment",

        CashPayment
            => "Cash payment",

        _ => "Unknown payment"
    };

This is a very realistic example of where pattern matching improves readability in a .NET application.

22. Advanced Interview Question: What is the difference between a type pattern and declaration pattern?

Type pattern

if (obj is string)
{
}

You're checking the type.

Declaration pattern

if (obj is string text)
{
}

You're checking the type and capturing the value.

Interview answer

"A type pattern checks whether the runtime value is compatible with a specified type, while a declaration pattern additionally introduces a variable containing the matched value."

23. Advanced Interview Question: What is a property pattern?

Answer

"A property pattern matches an object's properties against nested patterns. It allows me to check multiple properties and conditions without manually accessing each property."

Example:

if (employee is
    {
        Department: "IT",
        Experience: >= 3
    })
{
    ...
}

24. Advanced Interview Question: What is pattern subsumption?

This is worth remembering for Senior interviews.

Suppose:

int GetLevel(int experience) =>
    experience switch
    {
        _ => "Anything",
        >= 10 => "Senior"
    };

The first pattern:

_

matches everything.

Therefore:

>= 10

can never be selected.

This is called subsumption: an earlier pattern covers all values that a later pattern could match. The compiler reports an error when it can determine that a later switch arm is subsumed by earlier unguarded patterns. Microsoft Learn

  1. Why does pattern order matter?
  1. is pattern vs as?
  1. How can pattern matching simplify polymorphic code?
  1. Where would you use pattern matching in a real ASP.NET Core application?

🔥 30-Second Interview Answer

If the interviewer asks:

"Explain pattern matching in C#."

Say:

"Pattern matching allows us to test an expression against a type, value, or object shape and execute logic when the pattern matches. In C#, we can use patterns with is, switch statements, and switch expressions. Common patterns include type or declaration patterns, constant patterns, relational patterns, property patterns, positional patterns, logical patterns like and, or, not, and discard patterns. I commonly use it for type-based processing, null checks, status handling, and replacing complex if-else chains with readable switch expressions." Microsoft Learn

🧠 Pattern Matching Cheat Sheet

is
│
├── Type
│   └── value is string
│
├── Declaration
│   └── value is string text
│
├── Constant
│   └── status is 200
│
├── Relational
│   └── age is >= 18
│
├── Logical
│   ├── and
│   ├── or
│   └── not
│
├── Property
│   └── employee is { Experience: >= 3 }
│
├── Positional
│   └── point is (0, 0)
│
├── List
│   └── numbers is [1, 2, ..]
│
└── Discard
    └── _

Memorize these 10 lines

  1. Pattern matching tests an expression against a pattern.
  1. is supports pattern matching.
  1. Declaration patterns test a type and capture the value.
  1. switch expressions return a value.
  1. _ is the discard/catch-all pattern.
  1. Relational patterns use <, <=, >, >=.
  1. and, or, not combine patterns.
  1. Property patterns inspect object properties.
  1. when adds an additional Boolean guard.
  1. Pattern order matters because the first matching switch arm wins. Microsoft Learn

20. Modern C# Features: Interview Preparation

1. Nullable Reference Types

One of the most important modern C# features.

Before nullable reference types:

string name = null;

The compiler doesn't warn you about the possibility of null.

With nullable reference types enabled:

string name = "Saurabh";

string? nullableName = null;

? explicitly communicates:

This reference is allowed to contain null.

Then:

Console.WriteLine(nullableName.Length);

can produce a compiler warning because nullableName might be null.

You can handle it:

Console.WriteLine(nullableName?.Length);

Interview answer

"Nullable reference types provide compile-time analysis to help prevent null-reference errors. string represents a non-nullable reference by default when nullable analysis is enabled, while string? explicitly allows null."

Important trap

Nullable reference types are primarily a compile-time analysis feature. They don't magically prevent null values at runtime.

2. Null-Coalescing Operators

You've likely already used these, but they're commonly included in modern C# discussions.

??

string name = inputName ?? "Unknown";

Meaning:

If inputName != null
    use inputName
else
    use "Unknown"

??=

name ??= "Unknown";

Equivalent conceptually to:

if (name == null)
{
    name = "Unknown";
}

3. Null-Conditional Operators

var length = user?.Name?.Length;

Instead of:

int? length = null;

if (user != null &&
    user.Name != null)
{
    length = user.Name.Length;
}

You can also use:

user?.GetAddress()?.City

4. initOnly Setters

init was introduced to support immutable-style initialization.

public class Employee
{
    public string Name { get; init; }
    public int Experience { get; init; }
}

You can initialize:

var employee = new Employee
{
    Name = "Saurabh",
    Experience = 3
};

But after initialization:

employee.Name = "John";

is not allowed.

Interview answer

"init allows a property to be assigned during object initialization but prevents modification afterward, which is useful for immutable or immutable-style objects."

5. required Members

required ensures callers initialize particular members.

public class Employee
{
    public required string Name { get; init; }

    public int Experience { get; init; }
}

Now:

var employee = new Employee
{
    Name = "Saurabh"
};

is valid.

But:

var employee = new Employee();

causes a compiler error because Name wasn't initialized.

Microsoft documents required as a way to force callers to set members during initialization. Microsoft Learn

required vs init

Very common interview question.

required string Name { get; init; }

means:

  • required → must be initialized
  • init → can only be assigned during initialization

They solve different problems and can be used together.

6. Records

You already covered records in #4 Types, but they're one of the most important modern C# features.

public record Employee(
    int Id,
    string Name,
    string Department);

Records are designed for data-centric models and provide value-based equality semantics.

var e1 = new Employee(1, "Saurabh", "IT");
var e2 = new Employee(1, "Saurabh", "IT");

Console.WriteLine(e1 == e2);

Result:

True

Unlike normal classes where equality by default is reference-based.

7. with Expressions

Records work especially well with with.

var employee1 =
    new Employee(1, "Saurabh", "IT");

var employee2 =
    employee1 with
    {
        Department = "Engineering"
    };

This creates a new record value based on the original with the specified changes.

Interview answer

"with provides nondestructive mutation. It creates a new record instance based on an existing instance while changing selected properties."

8. File-Scoped Namespaces

Traditional:

namespace MyApp.Services
{
    public class UserService
    {
    }
}

Modern:

namespace MyApp.Services;

public class UserService
{
}

Advantages:

  • Less indentation
  • Less boilerplate
  • Cleaner files

This is simple but frequently encountered in modern .NET projects.

9. Global using

Instead of putting:

using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Linq;

in every file, you can define:

global using System;
global using System.Collections.Generic;
global using System.Linq;

Those namespaces then apply throughout the project.

Real-world use

ASP.NET Core projects commonly centralize frequently used namespaces.

10. Top-Level Statements

Traditional:

class Program
{
    static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Hello");
    }
}

Modern:

Console.WriteLine("Hello");

The compiler generates the necessary entry-point infrastructure.

Important interview point

"Top-level statements reduce boilerplate for application entry points; they don't remove the underlying program entry point."

11. Target-Typed new

Instead of:

Employee employee =
    new Employee();

you can write:

Employee employee = new();

The compiler knows the target type.

It can also make collections cleaner:

Dictionary<int, string> users = new();

12. Target-Typed Conditional Expressions

Modern C# can infer the target type in conditional expressions.

Employee employee = condition
    ? new Manager()
    : new Developer();

The target type helps determine the resulting type.

This is another example of modern C# reducing redundant type information.

13. Raw String Literals

Extremely useful for JSON, SQL, HTML, regex, prompts, etc.

Traditional:

string json =
    "{ \"name\": \"Saurabh\", \"role\": \"Developer\" }";

Raw string:

string json = """
{
    "name": "Saurabh",
    "role": "Developer"
}
""";

Much easier to read.

Microsoft's C# coding conventions recommend raw string literals for suitable multiline strings. Microsoft Learn

ASP.NET Core example

string json = """
{
    "id": 101,
    "name": "Saurabh",
    "skills": [
        "C#",
        ".NET",
        "React"
    ]
}
""";

14. String Interpolation

Modern C# heavily uses:

string message =
    $"Employee {name} has {experience} years of experience.";

Instead of:

string message =
    "Employee " + name +
    " has " + experience +
    " years of experience.";

For large repeated concatenation in loops, StringBuilder remains appropriate. Microsoft Learn

15. Primary Constructors — C# 12

This is very important for current .NET interviews.

Before:

public class UserService
{
    private readonly IUserRepository _repository;

    public UserService(IUserRepository repository)
    {
        _repository = repository;
    }
}

With a primary constructor:

public class UserService(IUserRepository repository)
{
    public async Task<User?> GetUser(int id)
    {
        return await repository.GetByIdAsync(id);
    }
}

The constructor parameter is available throughout the class body.

C# 12 extended primary constructors beyond records to ordinary classes and structs. Microsoft Learn

Important trap

Primary constructor parameters are not automatically properties in ordinary classes.

This:

public class UserService(IUserRepository repository)
{
}

doesn't automatically create:

public IUserRepository Repository { get; }

That's different from record behavior.

16. Primary Constructors with ASP.NET Core DI

This is highly relevant to your resume.

Traditional:

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly IOrderRepository _repository;

    public OrderService(IOrderRepository repository)
    {
        _repository = repository;
    }
}

Modern:

public class OrderService(
    IOrderRepository repository,
    ILogger<OrderService> logger)
{
    public async Task ProcessAsync(int orderId)
    {
        logger.LogInformation(
            "Processing order {OrderId}",
            orderId);

        await repository.ProcessAsync(orderId);
    }
}

Interview answer

"Primary constructors reduce constructor boilerplate and work well with dependency injection because constructor parameters can be directly used throughout the class."

17. Collection Expressions — C# 12

Instead of:

int[] numbers = new[] { 1, 2, 3 };

you can write:

int[] numbers = [1, 2, 3];

For a list:

List<string> names =
[
    "Saurabh",
    "Rahul",
    "Amit"
];

You can also spread another collection:

int[] first = [1, 2, 3];

int[] second =
[
    0,
    ..first,
    4
];

The .. is the spread element.

C# 12 introduced collection expressions for arrays, spans, lists and other collection-like types. Microsoft Learn

18. Pattern Matching

You just completed #19, so remember that modern C# includes powerful patterns:

if (employee is
    {
        Department: "IT",
        Experience: >= 3
    })
{
}

And:

string result = status switch
{
    >= 200 and < 300 => "Success",
    >= 400 and < 500 => "Client Error",
    >= 500 => "Server Error",
    _ => "Unknown"
};

For interviews, connect:

Modern C#
    ↓
Pattern Matching
    ↓
Readable business rules

19. await using

For asynchronous resource disposal:

await using var resource =
    new AsyncResource();

The resource implements:

IAsyncDisposable

and disposal occurs asynchronously.

This is particularly relevant when cleanup itself involves asynchronous operations.

20. IAsyncEnumerable<T> and await foreach

For asynchronous streaming:

await foreach (var user in GetUsersAsync())
{
    Console.WriteLine(user.Name);
}

The method can return:

IAsyncEnumerable<User>

This is useful when data arrives progressively rather than all at once.

For example:

Database / API
      ↓
stream data
      ↓
await foreach
      ↓
process each item

This connects directly with your earlier #14 Iterators topic.

21. Lambda Improvements

Modern C# continues to expand lambda capabilities.

For example, C# 12 added optional/default parameters to lambdas. Microsoft Learn

var calculate =
    (int value, int multiplier = 2)
        => value * multiplier;

Then:

calculate(10);

returns:

20

And:

calculate(10, 5);

returns:

50

22. C# 13 Features — Know the Names

For your interviews, you don't need to deeply memorize every C# 13 compiler feature, but know the major additions:

  • params collections
  • New lock type/semantics
  • \e escape sequence
  • Improved method-group handling
  • ^ in object initializers
  • ref/unsafe in iterators and async methods
  • ref struct interfaces
  • ref struct generic support
  • Partial properties/indexers
  • Overload resolution priority

These are part of C# 13, supported by .NET 9. Microsoft Learn

Interview priority

For you:

Know conceptually:

params collections
new lock semantics
ref struct improvements
partial members

Don't spend hours memorizing syntax unless the job specifically requires recent C# features.

23. C# 14 — Current Released Version

As of 2026, C# 14 is the latest released C# version and is supported by .NET 10. Microsoft Learn

Important C# 14 additions include:

Extension members

C# 14 expands extension functionality beyond traditional extension methods, including extension properties and other extension members. Microsoft Learn

Null-conditional assignment

A newer syntax allows:

customer?.Order = order;

instead of:

if (customer is not null)
{
    customer.Order = order;
}

The right side is evaluated only when the receiver isn't null. Microsoft Learn

field keyword

C# 14 introduces the field contextual keyword for accessing a compiler-generated backing field:

public string Name
{
    get;
    set => field = value ?? throw
        new ArgumentNullException(nameof(value));
}

This can remove the need to manually declare a backing field for some property implementations. Microsoft Learn

Other C# 14 features include:

  • nameof support for unbound generic types
  • More implicit conversions for Span<T> / ReadOnlySpan<T>
  • Modifiers on simple lambda parameters
  • Partial constructors
  • Partial events
  • User-defined compound assignment operators Microsoft Learn

24. C# 15 — Don't Confuse Preview with Released

This is an important current-version interview trap.

Microsoft currently lists C# 15 as a preview release associated with .NET 11 preview, not the latest stable release. Microsoft Learn

So if an interviewer asks:

"What is the latest released C# version?"

For the current date:

C# 14.

Don't answer C# 15 unless you explicitly qualify it as the preview version.

27. 🔥 Very Important Interview Comparisons

set vs init

set
↓
Can assign after construction

init
↓
Can assign only during initialization

init vs required

init
↓
Controls WHEN assignment is allowed

required
↓
Controls WHETHER caller MUST initialize it

class vs record

class
↓
Usually identity-based equality

record
↓
Value-based equality
Data-oriented modeling

IEnumerable vs IAsyncEnumerable

IEnumerable<T>
↓
Synchronous iteration

IAsyncEnumerable<T>
↓
Asynchronous iteration
await foreach

Normal constructor vs primary constructor

Normal
↓
Explicit constructor body

Primary
↓
Less boilerplate
Parameters available throughout type

28. Real-World ASP.NET Core Example

Here's a modern-style service combining several concepts:

public record UserDto(
    int Id,
    string Name,
    string Email);

public class UserService(
    IUserRepository repository,
    ILogger<UserService> logger)
{
    public async IAsyncEnumerable<UserDto> GetUsersAsync()
    {
        await foreach (var user in repository.GetUsersAsync())
        {
            yield return new UserDto(
                user.Id,
                user.Name,
                user.Email);
        }
    }
}

This demonstrates:

record
   +
primary constructor
   +
dependency injection
   +
async iteration
   +
IAsyncEnumerable

That's exactly the type of connection you should be able to explain in a Senior .NET interview.

🎯 30-Second Interview Answer

If asked:

"What modern C# features have you used?"

You can answer:

"I've worked with several modern C# features including nullable reference types, records, init-only properties, required members, pattern matching, switch expressions, file-scoped namespaces, global usings, raw string literals, async streams with IAsyncEnumerable, and primary constructors. I also understand newer C# features such as collection expressions and the recent C# 13 and C# 14 additions. I generally use these features where they improve type safety, readability, immutability, or reduce boilerplate."

For a 3.9 YOE interview, that's a much better answer than simply listing 20 language features.
