10 lines to memorize

  1. init allows assignment only during initialization.
  1. required forces callers to initialize a member.
  1. Records provide value-based equality and data-oriented semantics.
  1. with creates a modified copy of a record.
  1. Nullable reference types provide compile-time nullability analysis.
  1. Primary constructors reduce constructor boilerplate.
  1. Collection expressions provide concise collection creation syntax.
  1. IAsyncEnumerable<T> enables asynchronous streaming with await foreach.
  1. C# 14 is currently the latest released C# version; C# 15 is currently preview. Microsoft Learn
  1. Modern C# should be used to improve readability, safety, maintainability, and appropriate performance—not simply because the syntax is newer.

21. Compiler / CLR Internals in C#

This is the “what happens after I write C#?” section of your roadmap.

For your ~3.9 YOE interviews, you don't need to become a CLR engineer. But you should confidently explain:

C# Source Code
      ↓
Roslyn Compiler
      ↓
CIL / IL + Metadata
      ↓
Assembly (.dll / .exe)
      ↓
CLR / CoreCLR
      ↓
JIT Compiler
      ↓
Native Machine Code
      ↓
CPU

Microsoft's managed-execution model describes the core flow as: compiler → CIL + metadata → JIT → native code → execution under the CLR. Microsoft Learn

1. What is Roslyn?

Roslyn is the .NET compiler platform used for C# and Visual Basic.

For C#:

Your C# code
     ↓
Roslyn
     ↓
IL/CIL + Metadata

For example:

int Add(int a, int b)
{
    return a + b;
}

Roslyn analyzes and compiles the source code into an intermediate representation that ultimately becomes CIL/IL in the assembly.

Interview answer

"Roslyn is Microsoft's compiler platform for C# and Visual Basic. It parses source code, performs semantic analysis and compilation, and produces assemblies containing IL and metadata."

2. What does the C# compiler actually produce?

A common interview misconception is:

"C# gets directly compiled into machine code."

❌ Not normally in the traditional JIT execution model.

Instead:

C#
 ↓
CIL / IL
 ↓
JIT
 ↓
Machine Code

Microsoft describes CIL as CPU-independent instructions that are converted to CPU-specific native code at execution time. Microsoft Learn

3. What is IL / CIL?

IL = Intermediate Language

Microsoft documentation commonly calls it:

CIL = Common Intermediate Language

It is CPU-independent intermediate code.

Example conceptually:

int result = a + b;

may become IL instructions conceptually resembling:

load a
load b
add
store result

You don't need to memorize individual IL instructions for normal interviews.

Interview answer

"IL or CIL is CPU-independent intermediate code generated by the compiler. The .NET runtime later converts it into native machine code appropriate for the target architecture." Microsoft Learn

4. What is Metadata?

When the compiler generates an assembly, it doesn't produce only IL.

It also generates metadata.

Metadata describes things such as:

  • Types
  • Methods
  • Method signatures
  • Fields
  • Properties
  • Referenced members
  • Other type information

Microsoft explains that CIL and metadata are contained in the PE-based assembly format and are used by the runtime during execution. Microsoft Learn

Think:

Assembly
│
├── IL
│
└── Metadata
      ├── Classes
      ├── Methods
      ├── Fields
      └── Type information

This metadata is also fundamental to features such as reflection.

5. What is an Assembly?

An assembly is a compiled .NET unit.

Common examples:

MyApplication.dll
MyApplication.exe

An assembly can contain:

IL
+
Metadata
+
Manifest
+
Resources

The important interview point is:

A DLL is not simply a native machine-code library. A normal managed .NET assembly contains IL and metadata that the runtime can load and execute.

6. .dll vs .exe

In modern .NET, both can contain managed assemblies.

Conceptually:

.dll
→ library

.exe
→ executable application

But don't confuse .exe with:

"It's already machine code."

A managed .NET executable can still contain IL that is JIT-compiled when executed.

7. What is CLR?

CLR = Common Language Runtime

It provides the runtime environment for managed .NET code.

Responsibilities include services such as:

  • JIT compilation
  • Garbage collection
  • Exception handling
  • Type system/runtime support
  • Threading/runtime services
  • Interoperability
  • Debugging/profiling support

Microsoft describes the CLR as the runtime environment that executes managed code and provides these runtime services. Microsoft Learn

Interview answer

"CLR is the runtime environment responsible for executing managed .NET code and providing services such as JIT compilation, garbage collection, exception handling, and interoperability."

8. CLR vs .NET

This is frequently asked.

.NET

The broader development platform:

.NET
├── Runtime
├── Libraries
├── SDK
├── Compiler
├── Tools
└── Frameworks

CLR

The runtime execution environment.

In modern .NET terminology, the runtime implementation is CoreCLR.

Simple interview answer

".NET is the overall platform, while the CLR is the runtime component responsible for executing managed code and providing runtime services."

9. What is JIT?

JIT = Just-In-Time compiler

It converts IL/CIL into native machine code at runtime.

IL
 ↓
JIT
 ↓
Native machine code

Microsoft explains that JIT compilation occurs when methods are loaded/executed and the generated native code can subsequently be reused within that process. Microsoft Learn

10. Does JIT compile the entire application at startup?

❌ No.

A common simplified explanation is:

"The JIT compiles the application."

That's too broad.

JIT compilation is performed as methods need to execute.

Conceptually:

Application starts
      ↓
Method A called
      ↓
JIT compiles A
      ↓
A executes

Later:
Method B called
      ↓
JIT compiles B
      ↓
B executes

This avoids compiling code that may never actually be executed.

Microsoft explicitly describes JIT as compiling CIL on demand rather than converting all CIL ahead of time. Microsoft Learn

11. What happens when a method is called for the first time?

Conceptually:

Method call
    ↓
Is native code available?
    ↓
No
    ↓
JIT compiles IL
    ↓
Native machine code
    ↓
Execute

Subsequent calls can use the generated native code within that process. Microsoft Learn

12. Why doesn't every method get JIT-compiled immediately?

Imagine your application has:

1000 methods

but only:

200 methods

are actually used during a particular execution.

Compiling all 1000 immediately would waste:

  • Startup time
  • CPU
  • Memory

JIT can compile methods as needed.

That's one reason JIT is useful.

13. What is Tiered Compilation?

This is a Senior-level interview topic.

Modern .NET uses tiered compilation.

Conceptually:

Method
 ↓
Tier 0
 ↓
Quick compilation
 ↓
Run
 ↓
Collect runtime information
 ↓
Tier 1
 ↓
More optimized code

Microsoft documents tiered compilation as transitioning methods through tiers, with an initial fast compilation followed by more optimized compilation. Microsoft Learn

Why?

The runtime balances:

Startup speed
       vs
Long-term performance

You don't want to spend a lot of time optimizing code that barely runs.

14. What is Quick JIT?

Quick JIT prioritizes faster compilation over maximum optimization.

So:

Quick JIT
↓
Compile faster
↓
Application starts faster

but the generated code may initially be less optimized.

Microsoft documents Quick JIT as a startup-oriented optimization and notes that it can produce code with weaker performance characteristics than fully optimized code. Microsoft Learn

15. What is PGO?

PGO = Profile-Guided Optimization

The runtime observes how the application actually behaves and uses that information to optimize frequently executed paths.

Conceptually:

Application runs
      ↓
Runtime gathers execution profile
      ↓
Which methods/types/paths are hot?
      ↓
JIT optimization

Modern .NET supports dynamic PGO, which works with tiered compilation. Microsoft Learn

Interview answer

"Profile-guided optimization uses runtime execution information to optimize code based on the paths and types that are actually used frequently."

16. What is ReadyToRun?

This is important for deeper .NET interviews.

ReadyToRun (R2R) provides precompiled native code in assemblies to reduce the amount of work required at startup.

Conceptually:

Normal:
IL → JIT → Native Code

ReadyToRun:
Precompiled code available
       ↓
Less JIT work

However, JIT still remains part of the runtime story for code that needs further compilation/optimization.

Microsoft documents ReadyToRun as precompiled code that can be used by the runtime and notes that disabling it forces more JIT compilation. Microsoft Learn

17. JIT vs AOT

Very important modern .NET interview question.

JIT

IL
 ↓
Runtime
 ↓
JIT
 ↓
Machine Code

Compilation happens at runtime.

AOT

Ahead-of-Time compilation generates native code ahead of execution.

Conceptually:

Source
 ↓
Build
 ↓
Native code
 ↓
Run

Trade-off

JIT:

+ Runtime optimization
+ Flexible runtime behavior
+ Dynamic compilation
- Some startup compilation cost

AOT:

+ Potentially faster startup
+ Smaller runtime requirements in suitable scenarios
- More restrictions in some scenarios
- Less runtime compilation flexibility

For your interviews, know the concept rather than memorizing implementation details.

18. What is the difference between IL and machine code?

IL

CPU-independent

Example:

CIL
 ↓
x86
x64
ARM64

Machine code

CPU-specific

For example:

x64 machine code
ARM64 machine code

This is why the same IL assembly can be executed on different supported architectures through appropriate runtime/JIT compilation. Microsoft Learn

19. What is Managed Code?

Code compiled for and executed under the .NET runtime is generally called managed code.

Example:

public class OrderService
{
    public void Process()
    {
    }
}

The CLR provides runtime services for this code.

Unmanaged code

Native code that isn't managed by the CLR in the same way.

Examples include:

Native C/C++ libraries
Operating system APIs
Native system resources

.NET supports interoperability between managed and unmanaged code. Microsoft Learn

20. Managed vs Unmanaged Code

ManagedUnmanaged
Runs under .NET runtimeRuns outside CLR management
GC availableResource management often manual/explicit
Runtime type systemNative type/runtime rules
JIT/AOT .NET execution modelNative compilation
C# typical codeNative C/C++ code

Important

Don't say:

"Unmanaged code doesn't have memory management."

It does. It just isn't managed by the .NET GC.

21. What is the CTS?

CTS = Common Type System

It defines how types are represented and used within the .NET environment.

Examples:

int
string
class
struct
interface
enum
delegate

The CTS enables languages targeting .NET to share a common type system.

22. What is CLS?

CLS = Common Language Specification

CLS defines a set of rules that .NET languages can follow for interoperability.

Think:

CTS
 ↓
Complete .NET type system

CLS
 ↓
Common subset/rules for language interoperability

Interview answer

"CTS defines the common type system used by .NET, while CLS defines a set of language-interoperability rules that .NET components can follow."

23. CTS vs CLS

Very common interview question.

CTS
→ What types and type rules exist?

CLS
→ Which subset/rules should languages follow
  for broad interoperability?

Example:

A language may support a type or feature that another .NET language doesn't naturally understand.

CLS compliance helps expose APIs in a language-neutral way.

Microsoft's managed-execution documentation notes that exported types intended for broad cross-language use should expose features within the CLS. Microsoft Learn

24. What is ILDASM / ILSpy?

For interview understanding, tools such as:

  • ILSpy
  • ildasm
  • dotnet tools

can help inspect compiled assemblies and IL.

For example:

int Add(int a, int b)
{
    return a + b;
}

You can inspect the generated IL to understand how the compiler represents the method.

Interview point

"IL inspection tools are useful for understanding compiler output, metadata, and runtime behavior."

25. What happens when you run an ASP.NET Core API?

This is the real-world question you should be able to answer.

Suppose you have:

[HttpGet]
public async Task<User> GetUser(int id)
{
    return await service.GetUserAsync(id);
}

Conceptually:

C# Source
   ↓
Roslyn Compiler
   ↓
IL + Metadata
   ↓
Assembly
   ↓
ASP.NET Core starts
   ↓
.NET Runtime / CoreCLR
   ↓
Methods execute
   ↓
JIT compiles required methods
   ↓
Native machine code
   ↓
CPU executes

During execution, the runtime also provides services such as:

GC
Exception handling
Threading
Type/runtime services
Interop
``` :chatgpt-content-reference{index="15"}


---

# 26. How does this relate to your performance work?

You mentioned performance optimization in your experience.

Suppose:

```csharp
public async Task<User> GetUserAsync(int id)
{
    return await repository.GetUserAsync(id);
}

There are multiple layers involved:

Your C# code
     ↓
Compiler
     ↓
IL
     ↓
JIT
     ↓
Native code
     ↓
CPU
     ↓
Database/API/etc.

If an API is slow, the problem isn't necessarily JIT.

It could be:

SQL query
Database indexes
Network
Serialization
Allocations
GC
Lock contention
Async bottleneck
Algorithm
External API

That's an important Senior-level mindset:

Don't automatically blame the runtime; measure the actual bottleneck.

27. Common Interview Question: Is C# compiled or interpreted?

Best answer

"C# is a compiled language. The C# compiler compiles source code into IL/CIL and metadata. At runtime, the .NET runtime uses mechanisms such as JIT to compile IL into native machine code for execution. Depending on the deployment model, precompiled/AOT code can also be involved."

This is much better than simply saying:

"C# is compiled."

28. Common Interview Question: Why does .NET use IL?

Answer

"IL provides a CPU-independent intermediate representation. It allows the same managed assembly to be used across supported architectures, with the runtime producing appropriate native code for the target environment." Microsoft Learn

29. Common Interview Question: Why use JIT?

Answer

"JIT allows the runtime to compile methods for the actual target architecture and execution environment. It can also use runtime information for optimization, while avoiding compilation of methods that are never executed."

This is particularly relevant to tiered compilation and dynamic PGO. Microsoft Learn

30. Common Interview Question: What happens to JIT-generated code?

The generated native code can be kept in memory and reused for subsequent calls during that process. When the process ends, that process-specific generated code doesn't simply become a permanent replacement for the original assembly. Microsoft Learn

31. Common Interview Question: Does CLR execute IL directly?

❌ Usually no.

The normal flow is:

IL
 ↓
JIT
 ↓
Native code
 ↓
CPU

The CLR provides the runtime infrastructure and coordinates execution; the CPU ultimately executes native instructions. Microsoft Learn

32. Common Interview Question: What is the difference between JIT and Roslyn?

This is very important.

Roslyn

C# Source
    ↓
Roslyn
    ↓
IL + Metadata

JIT

IL
 ↓
JIT
 ↓
Native Machine Code

So:

Roslyn = source → IL

JIT = IL → native code

Do not confuse them.

33. Common Interview Question: What is CLR responsible for?

A strong answer:

"The CLR provides the runtime environment for managed .NET code. It handles execution services including JIT compilation, garbage collection, exception handling, type/runtime services, interoperability, and other runtime infrastructure." Microsoft Learn

34. 🔥 Most Important Interview Questions

Basic

  1. What happens when C# code is compiled?
  1. What is IL/CIL?
  1. What is CLR?
  1. What is JIT?
  1. What is an assembly?
  1. What is metadata?
  1. What is managed code?
  1. Is C# compiled or interpreted?

Intermediate

  1. Roslyn vs CLR?
  1. Roslyn vs JIT?
  1. IL vs machine code?
  1. Why does .NET use IL?
  1. What happens when a method is called?
  1. Why isn't all code JIT-compiled immediately?
  1. What is CTS?
  1. What is CLS?
  1. CTS vs CLS?
  1. Managed vs unmanaged code?

Advanced / Senior

  1. What is tiered compilation?
  1. What is Quick JIT?
  1. What is dynamic PGO?
  1. What is ReadyToRun?
  1. JIT vs AOT?
  1. How does runtime optimization work?
  1. How does JIT affect startup performance?
  1. How does CLR provide garbage collection?
  1. How would you investigate JIT/runtime-related performance issues?

🎯 35-Second Interview Answer

If the interviewer asks:

"Explain how C# code executes."

Say:

"When I write C# code, the Roslyn compiler compiles it into CIL/IL along with metadata, which is packaged into a .NET assembly. When the application runs, the .NET runtime, through CoreCLR, loads the assembly and the JIT compiler converts required IL methods into native machine code for the target architecture. Modern .NET also uses mechanisms such as tiered compilation and profile-guided optimization to improve runtime performance. The CLR additionally provides services such as garbage collection, exception handling, and interoperability." Microsoft Learn

🧠 Final Mental Model

Memorize this diagram:

                 DEVELOPMENT TIME
                       │
                       ▼
              ┌─────────────────┐
              │   C# Source     │
              │   Program.cs    │
              └────────┬────────┘
                       │
                       ▼
              ┌─────────────────┐
              │     Roslyn      │
              │    Compiler     │
              └────────┬────────┘
                       │
                       ▼
              ┌─────────────────┐
              │   IL / CIL      │
              │   + Metadata    │
              └────────┬────────┘
                       │
                       ▼
              ┌─────────────────┐
              │    Assembly     │
              │  .dll / .exe    │
              └────────┬────────┘
                       │
═══════════════════════╪════════════════════
                       │
                 RUNTIME
                       │
                       ▼
              ┌─────────────────┐
              │  CLR/CoreCLR    │
              └────────┬────────┘
                       │
                       ▼
              ┌─────────────────┐
              │      JIT        │
              │  Tiered / PGO   │
              └────────┬────────┘
                       │
                       ▼
              ┌─────────────────┐
              │ Native Machine  │
              │      Code       │
              └────────┬────────┘
                       │
                       ▼
                    CPU

Microsoft's managed execution documentation describes this overall progression from compiler output to CIL, JIT compilation, and execution under the CLR. Microsoft Learn

🔥 10 lines to memorize

  1. Roslyn compiles C# source code.
  1. C# normally compiles to IL/CIL + metadata.
  1. IL is CPU-independent intermediate code.
  1. An assembly contains IL, metadata, and other assembly information.
  1. CLR/CoreCLR provides the runtime environment.
  1. JIT converts IL into native machine code.
  1. JIT generally compiles methods when needed, rather than compiling everything immediately.
  1. Tiered compilation allows faster initial compilation followed by optimized code.
  1. PGO uses runtime behavior to improve optimization.
  1. Roslyn = C# → IL; JIT = IL → native code. Microsoft Learn

22. Performance — Allocation, GC, Pooling, Strings, Span & Benchmarking

22.1 What does performance optimization mean in .NET?

Interview-ready answer

“In .NET, performance optimization means reducing unnecessary CPU work, memory allocations, I/O latency, database calls, and contention while maintaining correctness and maintainability. I would first measure the bottleneck using profiling or metrics, then optimize the actual hot path rather than making assumptions.”

Typical areas:

Performance
│
├── CPU
│   ├── Algorithms
│   ├── LINQ
│   └── unnecessary computation
│
├── Memory
│   ├── Allocations
│   ├── GC pressure
│   ├── Boxing
│   └── Large objects
│
├── I/O
│   ├── Database
│   ├── HTTP
│   └── File operations
│
├── Concurrency
│   ├── Lock contention
│   └── Thread pool starvation
│
└── Data processing
    ├── Strings
    ├── Arrays
    ├── Span<T>
    └── Pooling

Golden rule:

Measure → Identify bottleneck → Optimize → Measure again.

Microsoft specifically recommends measuring realistic scenarios before introducing mechanisms such as object pooling because pooling can itself have overhead. Microsoft Learn

22.2 What is an allocation?

When you create an object that requires memory on the managed heap, an allocation occurs.

var user = new User();

Conceptually:

new User()
    ↓
Managed heap allocation
    ↓
Object initialized
    ↓
Reference returned

Example:

for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++)
{
    var user = new User();
}

This creates a very large number of temporary objects.

Eventually the GC has to clean up objects that are no longer reachable.

Why are excessive allocations bad?

Because they can increase:

  • memory usage
  • GC frequency
  • CPU consumed by GC
  • latency
  • Gen 2 collections in some cases

Microsoft notes that increased allocation rates can cause GC to happen more frequently. Microsoft Learn

22.3 What is GC pressure?

Interview-ready answer

“GC pressure means creating enough temporary managed objects that the garbage collector has to work more frequently to reclaim memory.”

Example:

for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++)
{
    var result = new SomeObject();
}

If those objects quickly become unreachable:

Many allocations
      ↓
More garbage
      ↓
More GC work
      ↓
More CPU usage
      ↓
Potential latency

How do you reduce GC pressure?

Common techniques:

  • reduce unnecessary object creation
  • reuse objects where appropriate
  • avoid unnecessary boxing
  • avoid unnecessary string allocations
  • use StringBuilder for repeated string construction
  • use ArrayPool<T> for reusable buffers
  • use Span<T>/ReadOnlySpan<T> where appropriate
  • avoid materializing unnecessary LINQ results
  • avoid creating large temporary objects

22.4 What is the Large Object Heap?

The Large Object Heap (LOH) stores sufficiently large objects. Microsoft documents the commonly used threshold as approximately 85,000 bytes for large-object allocations. Microsoft Learn

Typical examples:

byte[] buffer = new byte[100_000];

Large arrays are a common LOH scenario.

Why can LOH be expensive?

Frequent temporary large allocations can cause expensive Gen 2 collections and affect application responsiveness. Microsoft Learn

Example:

Request
   ↓
Create 10 MB buffer
   ↓
Process file
   ↓
Buffer becomes unreachable
   ↓
Another request creates 10 MB
   ↓
Repeated large allocations
   ↓
LOH pressure
   ↓
More expensive GC

Practical solution

Instead of repeatedly creating large buffers:

var buffer = new byte[1_000_000];

consider:

ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Rent(1_000_000);

when the workload actually benefits from pooling.

22.5 What is object pooling?

Interview-ready answer

“Object pooling means keeping reusable objects in a pool instead of repeatedly allocating and garbage-collecting them.”

Conceptually:

           ┌───────────────┐
           │ Object Pool   │
           │               │
           │ Object 1      │
           │ Object 2      │
           │ Object 3      │
           └───────┬───────┘
                   │
              Get object
                   ↓
              Use object
                   ↓
             Reset object
                   ↓
             Return object

ASP.NET Core provides Microsoft.Extensions.ObjectPool for this purpose. Microsoft notes that pooling is particularly useful for objects that are expensive to initialize and are used frequently and predictably. Microsoft Learn

22.6 When should you use ObjectPool?

Good candidate:

Expensive initialization
        +
Frequent reuse
        +
Predictable usage
        ↓
Potential pooling candidate

Example:

var builder = pool.Get();

try
{
    builder.Append("Hello");
    builder.Append(" World");

    return builder.ToString();
}
finally
{
    builder.Clear();
    pool.Return(builder);
}

Important interview point

Don't say:

“Pooling always improves performance.”

Instead:

“Pooling can reduce allocation and GC overhead, but it introduces management overhead and retains objects, so I would use it only when profiling shows that allocation/reinitialization is a real bottleneck.”

Microsoft explicitly warns that object pooling doesn't always improve performance. Microsoft Learn

22.7 What is ArrayPool<T>?

ArrayPool<T> allows arrays to be rented and returned instead of allocating new arrays repeatedly.

using System.Buffers;

byte[] buffer = ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Rent(4096);

try
{
    // Use the buffer
}
finally
{
    ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Return(buffer);
}

Important

The returned array can be larger than requested.

Rent(4096)

doesn't guarantee:

buffer.Length == 4096

Therefore always use your actual required length separately.

Also, clear sensitive data when appropriate before returning buffers, depending on the data and security requirements.

Real-world example

File processing:

10,000 requests
       ↓
Each request needs temporary byte buffer
       ↓
new byte[] repeatedly
       ↓
many allocations
       ↓
GC pressure

ArrayPool<byte>
       ↓
reuse buffers
       ↓
fewer allocations

Microsoft specifically recommends ArrayPool<T> for pooling large buffers in ASP.NET Core performance scenarios. Microsoft Learn

22.8 String performance

This is a very common interview topic.

Strings in C# are immutable.

string name = "Saurabh";

name += " Kedar";

Conceptually, a new string is created rather than modifying the original string.

Bad approach for repeated concatenation

string result = "";

for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++)
{
    result += i;
}

Repeated concatenation can generate many intermediate strings.

Better approach

var builder = new StringBuilder();

for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++)
{
    builder.Append(i);
}

string result = builder.ToString();

Interview answer

“Because strings are immutable, repeated concatenation in a loop can create many intermediate strings. For substantial repeated construction, I would consider StringBuilder.”

22.9 String vs StringBuilder

ScenarioPrefer
Simple concatenationstring
Few concatenationsstring
Large repeated constructionStringBuilder
Loop-based constructionOften StringBuilder
Read-only textstring

Don't say:

“Always use StringBuilder.”

The compiler can optimize some simple concatenation scenarios.

22.10 Boxing and performance

You already learned boxing in Section #5.

Recall:

int number = 10;

object obj = number;

The value gets boxed into an object.

This can create an allocation.

Bad example

ArrayList list = new ArrayList();

for (int i = 0; i < 100000; i++)
{
    list.Add(i);
}

The integers are boxed.

Better

List<int> list = new List<int>();

for (int i = 0; i < 100000; i++)
{
    list.Add(i);
}

Generic collections preserve type information and avoid this boxing scenario.

Interview answer

“Boxing can introduce allocations and CPU overhead, so in performance-sensitive code I prefer generics and strongly typed APIs over object-based APIs.”

22.11 LINQ and performance

LINQ is powerful, but it can introduce unnecessary work or allocations depending on the scenario.

Example

var users = db.Users
    .ToList()
    .Where(x => x.IsActive)
    .ToList();

Potential problem:

Database
   ↓
Load ALL users
   ↓
Create List
   ↓
Filter in memory

Better:

var users = await db.Users
    .Where(x => x.IsActive)
    .ToListAsync();

Now filtering can be translated to SQL by EF Core.

Even better when you only need a few fields

var users = await db.Users
    .Where(x => x.IsActive)
    .Select(x => new UserDto
    {
        Id = x.Id,
        Name = x.Name
    })
    .ToListAsync();
Bad:
DB → all rows → all columns → application filtering

Better:
DB → filtered rows → required columns → application

This is one of the most useful performance optimizations for your .NET interviews because it connects C# + LINQ + EF Core + SQL.

22.12 Span<T> and performance

You covered Span<T> in Section #13.

From a performance perspective:

Span<T> allows you to work with contiguous memory without necessarily creating another copy.

Example:

int[] numbers = { 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 };

Span<int> middle = numbers.AsSpan(1, 3);

middle represents:

Original array

[10][20][30][40][50]
     └───────┘
       Span

No new integer array needs to be created for the slice.

Microsoft's C# performance guidance specifically discusses using span-related types to avoid allocations and unnecessary data copies. Microsoft Learn

22.13 Span vs substring

A traditional approach:

string part = text.Substring(0, 10);

creates a separate string containing the selected characters.

For performance-sensitive parsing, a span can represent a slice:

ReadOnlySpan<char> part = text.AsSpan(0, 10);

The span is a view over existing memory.

Interview answer

“A span is useful when I need to process a slice of contiguous memory without creating another copy. It is especially useful in high-performance parsing and serialization scenarios.”

22.14 ReadOnlySpan<T>

Use:

ReadOnlySpan<char>

when you only need to read the data.

Example:

ReadOnlySpan<char> input = "12345";

if (input.StartsWith("123"))
{
    // Process input
}

You communicate:

“This code can read the memory but shouldn't modify it.”

22.15 Span<T> vs Memory<T>

This is a Senior-level interview question.

Span<T>Memory<T>
Memory viewYesYes
Allocation-free viewYesYes
Stack-onlyYesNo
Can live on heapNoYes
Across awaitNoYes
Async scenariosLimitedGood
High-performance synchronous processingExcellentGood

Interview answer

“Span<T> is a stack-only ref struct and is ideal for synchronous high-performance memory processing. Memory<T> is heap-friendly and can be stored and used across asynchronous boundaries.”

22.16 What is benchmarking?

Don't optimize based only on intuition.

You should measure.

A popular .NET benchmarking library is BenchmarkDotNet.

Example:

[Benchmark]
public string UsingStringBuilder()
{
    var builder = new StringBuilder();

    for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++)
    {
        builder.Append(i);
    }

    return builder.ToString();
}

You can compare:

Implementation A
      vs
Implementation B

and measure things such as:

  • execution time
  • allocations
  • memory usage
  • throughput

Interview answer

“For micro-level performance comparisons, I would use BenchmarkDotNet rather than relying on a simple Stopwatch test, because proper benchmarking needs repeated measurements and controlled execution.”

22.17 Profiling vs Benchmarking

Very important distinction.

Profiling

Used to understand where the application spends resources.

Application
    ↓
Profiler
    ↓
CPU / memory / allocations / call stacks

Example:

“Why is my API slow?”

Benchmarking

Used to compare specific implementations.

Method A
    VS
Method B
    ↓
Benchmark
    ↓
Which implementation behaves better?

Interview answer

“Profiling helps me find the bottleneck in a real application, while benchmarking helps me compare specific pieces of code under controlled conditions.”

22.18 How would you troubleshoot a slow ASP.NET Core API?

This is one of the most important scenario questions for you.

Interview-ready answer

“I would first measure where the latency is coming from instead of immediately changing code. I would check API telemetry, database query duration, external API calls, CPU, memory allocation and GC activity. Then I would identify whether the bottleneck is database, CPU, memory, I/O, locking, or network related.”

Then investigate:

API slow
  │
  ├── Database?
  │     ├── Slow query
  │     ├── Missing index
  │     ├── Too many rows
  │     └── N+1 queries
  │
  ├── CPU?
  │     ├── Expensive algorithm
  │     └── Excessive processing
  │
  ├── Memory?
  │     ├── Excessive allocations
  │     ├── Large objects
  │     └── GC pressure
  │
  ├── External service?
  │     └── HTTP latency
  │
  └── Concurrency?
        ├── Lock contention
        └── Thread pool issues

Then:

Measure
 ↓
Find bottleneck
 ↓
Optimize
 ↓
Benchmark/load test
 ↓
Measure again

22.19 Your real-world .NET performance answer

Based on the experience you've been preparing for interviews, you can explain performance work like this:

“In my .NET applications, I look at performance across the API, database and application layers. For example, if an API is processing a high number of transactions, I would use asynchronous operations for I/O-bound work, optimize SQL queries and indexes, project only the required fields through EF Core, avoid unnecessary allocations and materialization, and measure the result using application monitoring and profiling.”

If asked about a specific optimization, you can discuss your SQL indexing + async/await performance work from your resume, but be precise about what you actually measured.

22.20 Common performance mistakes

❌ 1. Calling GC.Collect() everywhere

GC.Collect();

Don't use this as a normal optimization strategy.

❌ 2. Pooling everything

Pooling has overhead and retains objects.

❌ 3. Using Span<T> everywhere

Span is useful for particular high-performance memory scenarios, not ordinary business logic.

❌ 4. Assuming LINQ is always slow

Don't make blanket statements.

The question is:

What does the query do, where does it execute, and what does it allocate?

❌ 5. Optimizing without measuring

This is perhaps the biggest mistake.

❌ 6. Saying “struct is always faster than class”

Incorrect.

Large structs can introduce copying costs, and changing class → struct also changes semantics. Microsoft explicitly cautions that copying larger structs can impact performance. Microsoft Learn

For your level, make sure you can answer these without hesitation:

  1. What is memory allocation?
  1. What is GC pressure?
  1. How does excessive allocation affect performance?
  1. What is LOH?
  1. Why can LOH allocations be expensive?
  1. How can you reduce GC pressure?
  1. What is object pooling?
  1. When would you use ObjectPool<T>?
  1. What is ArrayPool<T>?
  1. Why is repeated string concatenation potentially expensive?
  1. string vs StringBuilder?
  1. What is boxing and why can it hurt performance?
  1. How can LINQ affect performance?
  1. How can you optimize an EF Core query?
  1. What is Span<T>?
  1. Span<T> vs Memory<T>?
  1. Why can't Span<T> cross an await boundary?
  1. Profiling vs benchmarking?
  1. How would you troubleshoot a slow API?
  1. What is your approach to performance optimization?

🧠 10 Lines to Memorize

  1. Measure first; don't optimize based on assumptions.
  1. Excessive allocations can increase GC work.
  1. Short-lived allocations primarily create Gen 0 pressure.
  1. Large temporary allocations can cause expensive LOH/Gen 2 GC activity. Microsoft Learn
  1. Object pooling reuses expensive/frequently used objects.
  1. ArrayPool<T> is useful for reusable buffers.
  1. StringBuilder is useful for substantial repeated string construction.
  1. Boxing can introduce allocations and overhead.
  1. Span<T> provides a high-performance view over contiguous memory without requiring a copy.
  1. Profiling finds bottlenecks; benchmarking compares implementations.

🎯 Your #22 Interview Priority

For your 3.9 YOE Senior/.NET Full Stack interviews, prioritize:

Must know deeply

  • Allocations
  • GC pressure
  • Gen 0/1/2
  • LOH
  • Boxing
  • String performance
  • LINQ/EF Core performance
  • Span<T>
  • ReadOnlySpan<T>
  • Memory<T>
  • ArrayPool<T>
  • Object pooling
  • Profiling vs benchmarking
  • Slow API troubleshooting

Senior-level

  • Allocation rate
  • LOH fragmentation
  • ref/ref struct

23. Design — SOLID, Immutability & Design Patterns

23.1 What is SOLID?

SOLID represents five object-oriented design principles:

S → Single Responsibility Principle
O → Open/Closed Principle
L → Liskov Substitution Principle
I → Interface Segregation Principle
D → Dependency Inversion Principle

Interview-ready answer

“SOLID is a set of object-oriented design principles that help us build code that is maintainable, extensible, testable and less tightly coupled.”

Important:

SOLID is not a collection of rules that must be applied mechanically.

You should use these principles where they solve actual design problems.

23.2 S — Single Responsibility Principle

Definition

A class should have one reason to change.

Don't interpret this as:

“A class can have only one method.”

That's incorrect.

Bad example

public class UserService
{
    public void CreateUser()
    {
    }

    public void SendEmail()
    {
    }

    public void GeneratePdf()
    {
    }

    public void SaveToDatabase()
    {
    }
}

This class has several responsibilities.

UserService
 ├── User management
 ├── Email
 ├── PDF generation
 └── Database persistence

Changes to any of these areas can affect the same class.

Better

public class UserService
{
    private readonly IUserRepository _repository;
    private readonly IEmailService _emailService;

    public UserService(
        IUserRepository repository,
        IEmailService emailService)
    {
        _repository = repository;
        _emailService = emailService;
    }
}

Separate responsibilities:

UserService
     ↓
IUserRepository

     +

IEmailService

Interview answer

“SRP means a class should have one reason to change. For example, I wouldn't make a user service responsible for database persistence, email delivery and PDF generation. I would separate those responsibilities.”

23.3 O — Open/Closed Principle

Definition

Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification.

Suppose you support:

Credit Card
PayPal
UPI

Bad design

public decimal CalculateFee(string paymentType)
{
    if (paymentType == "Card")
    {
        // ...
    }
    else if (paymentType == "UPI")
    {
        // ...
    }
    else if (paymentType == "PayPal")
    {
        // ...
    }

    return 0;
}

Every new payment method requires modifying the existing class.

Better

public interface IPaymentProcessor
{
    decimal CalculateFee(decimal amount);
}

Implementations:

public class CardPaymentProcessor : IPaymentProcessor
{
    public decimal CalculateFee(decimal amount)
    {
        return amount * 0.02m;
    }
}
public class UpiPaymentProcessor : IPaymentProcessor
{
    public decimal CalculateFee(decimal amount)
    {
        return amount * 0.01m;
    }
}

Now a new payment processor can be added without changing existing processors.

Interview answer

“OCP means existing behavior should not need to be modified every time we introduce a new variation. We can use abstractions and polymorphism to extend behavior.”

23.4 L — Liskov Substitution Principle

This is often considered the hardest SOLID principle to explain.

Definition

Objects of a derived type should be usable wherever the base type is expected without breaking the correctness of the program.

Classic example:

public class Bird
{
    public virtual void Fly()
    {
    }
}

Then:

public class Penguin : Bird
{
    public override void Fly()
    {
        throw new NotSupportedException();
    }
}

Now:

void MakeBirdFly(Bird bird)
{
    bird.Fly();
}

Passing:

MakeBirdFly(new Penguin());

breaks the expected contract.

The inheritance hierarchy is poorly modeled.

Better design

Separate capabilities:

public interface IBird
{
}
public interface IFlyingBird
{
    void Fly();
}

Then:

public class Eagle : IBird, IFlyingBird
{
    public void Fly()
    {
    }
}
public class Penguin : IBird
{
}

Interview answer

“LSP means a derived implementation should honor the behavioral contract of its abstraction. If substituting the derived class causes unexpected behavior or exceptions, the abstraction is probably wrong.”

23.5 I — Interface Segregation Principle

Definition

Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they don't use.

Bad

public interface IEmployee
{
    void Work();
    void Eat();
    void GenerateReport();
    void Drive();
}

A developer may need only:

Work();

but must depend on the entire interface.

Better

public interface IWorker
{
    void Work();
}
public interface IReportGenerator
{
    void GenerateReport();
}
public interface IDriver
{
    void Drive();
}

Now classes depend only on the capabilities they require.

Interview answer

“ISP means interfaces should be small and focused so that consumers don't depend on methods they don't need.”

23.6 D — Dependency Inversion Principle

Definition

High-level modules should not depend directly on low-level implementations. Both should depend on abstractions.

Bad

public class OrderService
{
    private SqlOrderRepository _repository =
        new SqlOrderRepository();
}

Now OrderService is tightly coupled to SQL implementation.

Better

public interface IOrderRepository
{
    Order GetById(int id);
}
public class OrderService
{
    private readonly IOrderRepository _repository;

    public OrderService(IOrderRepository repository)
    {
        _repository = repository;
    }
}

ASP.NET Core/.NET's built-in DI system supports exactly this style: dependencies are registered and injected rather than hard-coded inside the consuming class. Microsoft Learn

23.7 Dependency Inversion vs Dependency Injection

Very common interview question.

DIP

A design principle.

High-level
    ↓
Abstraction
    ↑
Low-level implementation

DI

A technique for supplying dependencies.

public OrderService(IOrderRepository repository)
{
    _repository = repository;
}

Interview answer

“Dependency Inversion is the principle of depending on abstractions instead of concrete implementations. Dependency Injection is one technique used to implement that principle by providing dependencies from outside the class.”

23.8 Dependency Injection in ASP.NET Core

Typical registration:

builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, OrderRepository>();

Then:

public class OrderController : ControllerBase
{
    private readonly IOrderService _service;

    public OrderController(IOrderService service)
    {
        _service = service;
    }
}

Flow:

Controller
    ↓
IOrderService
    ↓
OrderService
    ↓
IOrderRepository
    ↓
OrderRepository

The container creates/resolves the required implementations.

Microsoft documents IServiceCollection for registration and IServiceProvider for resolving registered services. Microsoft Learn

23.9 DI Lifetimes

You should absolutely know these.

LifetimeMeaning
SingletonOne instance for application/container lifetime
ScopedOne instance per scope; in ASP.NET Core commonly per request
TransientNew instance each time requested

Example:

builder.Services.AddSingleton<IMyService, MyService>();

builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();

builder.Services.AddTransient<IEmailService, EmailService>();

Important interview trap

Don't say:

“Singleton means one instance globally forever.”

More accurately, it is one instance within the relevant DI container lifetime.

Also, Singleton services must be designed carefully if they hold mutable shared state because the DI container's thread safety does not automatically make the service itself thread-safe. Microsoft Learn

23.10 What is immutability?

An immutable object cannot have its observable state changed after creation.

Example:

public sealed class Money
{
    public decimal Amount { get; }
    public string Currency { get; }

    public Money(decimal amount, string currency)
    {
        Amount = amount;
        Currency = currency;
    }
}

After creation:

var money = new Money(100, "USD");

You cannot do:

money.Amount = 200;

because the state is immutable.

23.11 Why is immutability useful?

Benefits include:

  • easier reasoning
  • fewer accidental state changes
  • safer sharing
  • easier concurrency
  • easier testing
  • fewer side effects

For example:

Mutable object

Thread A ──┐
           ├──> shared object
Thread B ──┘
       ↓
possible race condition

Immutable:

Thread A ──> object
Thread B ──> same object
              ↓
        state cannot change

This doesn't mean immutability automatically makes every system thread-safe, but it significantly reduces one class of shared-state problems.

23.12 Records and immutability

You already covered records.

Example:

public record User(
    int Id,
    string Name);

Records provide value-oriented equality and convenient non-destructive mutation through with.

var user1 = new User(1, "Saurabh");

var user2 = user1 with
{
    Name = "Rahul"
};

Conceptually:

user1
 Id = 1
 Name = Saurabh

        ↓ with

user2
 Id = 1
 Name = Rahul

Important interview nuance:

Records encourage immutable/data-oriented design, but record alone does not guarantee deep immutability.

For example, a record containing a mutable List<T> can still expose mutable state.

23.13 What is a design pattern?

Interview answer

“A design pattern is a reusable solution template for a recurring software design problem. It is not a copy-paste implementation; it describes a structure or approach that can be adapted to the problem.”

Examples:

Creational
 ├── Singleton
 ├── Factory
 └── Builder

Structural
 ├── Adapter
 ├── Decorator
 └── Facade

Behavioral
 ├── Strategy
 ├── Observer
 ├── Command
 └── Template Method

Microsoft's design-pattern guidance describes patterns as reusable approaches/templates for recurring object-design problems. Microsoft Learn

23.14 Factory Pattern

Problem

You need to create different implementations based on some input.

Payment type
     ↓
Factory
 ├── CardProcessor
 ├── UpiProcessor
 └── PaypalProcessor

Example:

public interface IPaymentProcessor
{
    void Process(decimal amount);
}
public class PaymentFactory
{
    public IPaymentProcessor Create(string type)
    {
        return type switch
        {
            "Card" => new CardPaymentProcessor(),
            "UPI" => new UpiPaymentProcessor(),
            _ => throw new ArgumentException("Invalid type")
        };
    }
}

Interview use

“I use Factory when object creation involves selecting between multiple implementations or encapsulating creation logic.”

23.15 Strategy Pattern

This is very important for interviews.

Problem

You have multiple algorithms/behaviors that can be exchanged.

IPricingStrategy
      │
 ┌────┼─────┐
 ↓    ↓     ↓
Regular Premium Festival

Example:

public interface IDiscountStrategy
{
    decimal CalculateDiscount(decimal amount);
}
public class RegularDiscount : IDiscountStrategy
{
    public decimal CalculateDiscount(decimal amount)
        => amount * 0.05m;
}
public class PremiumDiscount : IDiscountStrategy
{
    public decimal CalculateDiscount(decimal amount)
        => amount * 0.15m;
}

Then:

public class CheckoutService
{
    private readonly IDiscountStrategy _strategy;

    public CheckoutService(IDiscountStrategy strategy)
    {
        _strategy = strategy;
    }

    public decimal CalculateDiscount(decimal amount)
    {
        return _strategy.CalculateDiscount(amount);
    }
}

Key idea

Strategy = interchangeable behavior/algorithm.

23.16 Factory vs Strategy

Extremely common.

FactoryStrategy
Focuses on creationFocuses on behavior
Creates/selects objectExecutes interchangeable algorithm
Create()Calculate()/Execute()
CreationalBehavioral

Example:

Factory
"What object should I create?"

Strategy
"Which algorithm should I use?"

23.17 Repository Pattern

Very common in .NET interviews.

Repository abstracts data access.

public interface IUserRepository
{
    Task<User?> GetByIdAsync(int id);
}

Implementation:

public class UserRepository : IUserRepository
{
    private readonly AppDbContext _context;

    public UserRepository(AppDbContext context)
    {
        _context = context;
    }

    public Task<User?> GetByIdAsync(int id)
    {
        return _context.Users
            .FirstOrDefaultAsync(x => x.Id == id);
    }
}

Service:

public class UserService
{
    private readonly IUserRepository _repository;

    public UserService(IUserRepository repository)
    {
        _repository = repository;
    }
}

Interview nuance

Don't say:

“Every EF Core application must use Repository.”

EF Core's DbContext/DbSet already provide data-access abstractions, so adding another repository layer should solve a specific architectural/testing concern rather than being automatic boilerplate.

23.18 Unit of Work

Concept

Coordinates multiple changes as one logical transaction.

OrderService
    │
    ├── OrderRepository
    ├── PaymentRepository
    └── InventoryRepository
             ↓
       Unit of Work
             ↓
          Commit

In EF Core, DbContext already acts in many scenarios as a unit-of-work-like abstraction by tracking changes and coordinating SaveChanges().

Interview answer

“Unit of Work coordinates changes across multiple repositories or aggregates and commits them as one unit. EF Core's DbContext already provides much of this behavior.”

23.19 Adapter Pattern

Problem

Your application expects one interface, but an external system exposes another.

Your Application
      ↓
ITaxService
      ↓
   Adapter
      ↓
ExternalTaxApi

Example:

public interface ITaxService
{
    decimal Calculate(decimal amount);
}

External API:

public class ExternalTaxClient
{
    public decimal GetTax(decimal value)
    {
        return value * 0.18m;
    }
}

Adapter:

public class TaxAdapter : ITaxService
{
    private readonly ExternalTaxClient _client;

    public TaxAdapter(ExternalTaxClient client)
    {
        _client = client;
    }

    public decimal Calculate(decimal amount)
    {
        return _client.GetTax(amount);
    }
}

Key phrase

Adapter makes incompatible interfaces work together.

23.20 Decorator Pattern

Decorator adds behavior without modifying the original class.

IOrderService
      ↓
LoggingDecorator
      ↓
CachingDecorator
      ↓
OrderService

Example:

public interface IOrderService
{
    Task<Order> GetOrderAsync(int id);
}

Decorator:

public class LoggingOrderService : IOrderService
{
    private readonly IOrderService _inner;

    public LoggingOrderService(IOrderService inner)
    {
        _inner = inner;
    }

    public async Task<Order> GetOrderAsync(int id)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Getting order {id}");

        return await _inner.GetOrderAsync(id);
    }
}

Key phrase

Decorator adds behavior around an existing object without changing its core implementation.

23.21 Facade Pattern

Facade provides a simplified interface over a complex subsystem.

Client
  ↓
OrderFacade
  ├── InventoryService
  ├── PaymentService
  ├── ShippingService
  └── NotificationService

Example:

public class OrderFacade
{
    public async Task PlaceOrderAsync(Order order)
    {
        // inventory
        // payment
        // shipping
        // notification
    }
}

Client doesn't need to know the complexity underneath.

Key phrase

Facade simplifies access to a complex subsystem.

23.22 Observer Pattern

You already have a practical example from your background: notifications/events.

Order Created
      ↓
   Event
 ┌────┼───────┐
 ↓    ↓       ↓
Email Audit Notification

C# events naturally support this publisher/subscriber style.

public event EventHandler? OrderCreated;

Subscribers:

orderService.OrderCreated += SendEmail;
orderService.OrderCreated += WriteAudit;

Key phrase

Observer allows subscribers to react when the publisher's state/event changes.

23.23 Singleton Pattern

Concept

Ensure one instance of a service within a defined scope/context.

Classic implementation:

public sealed class Singleton
{
    private static readonly Singleton _instance = new();

    private Singleton()
    {
    }

    public static Singleton Instance => _instance;
}

But in modern ASP.NET Core:

builder.Services.AddSingleton<IMyService, MyService>();

is generally preferable when what you need is an application-level DI singleton.

Microsoft's DI guidance also recommends avoiding unnecessary static/global state and direct dependency instantiation. Microsoft Learn

Interview trap

Don't automatically say:

“Singleton is always good for caching.”

Singleton introduces shared state/lifetime concerns. If it has mutable state, thread safety becomes important.

23.24 Command Pattern

Encapsulates an operation/request as an object.

CreateOrderCommand
UpdateOrderCommand
CancelOrderCommand

Useful for:

  • queues
  • undo/redo
  • command processing
  • CQRS-style architectures

Example:

public interface ICommand
{
    Task ExecuteAsync();
}

23.25 CQRS

Senior-level architecture concept.

CQRS = Command Query Responsibility Segregation

Separate:

Commands
  ↓
Change state

Queries
  ↓
Read state

Example:

CreateOrderCommand
UpdateOrderCommand
CancelOrderCommand

        VS

GetOrderQuery
GetOrdersQuery

Important:

CQRS does not automatically mean microservices, event sourcing, or separate databases.

It can be implemented simply within one application.

23.26 Composition over Inheritance

Very important design principle.

Inheritance

Car
 ↑
SportsCar

Composition

Car
 ├── Engine
 ├── Transmission
 └── Navigation

Instead of creating deep inheritance hierarchies, compose behavior from smaller components.

Interview answer

“I prefer composition when behavior can be assembled from independent components because it generally reduces coupling and avoids rigid inheritance hierarchies. Inheritance is still appropriate when there is a genuine substitutable type relationship.”

23.27 Design Patterns You Should Know

For your interviews:

🔥 Must know deeply

1. Factory
2. Strategy
3. Repository
4. Dependency Injection
5. Singleton
6. Adapter
7. Decorator
8. Facade
9. Observer

🟡 Senior-level

10. Unit of Work
11. Command
12. CQRS
13. Builder
14. Template Method
15. Chain of Responsibility

🟢 Awareness

16. Prototype
17. Composite
18. Mediator
19. State
20. Proxy

23.28 SOLID + Design Patterns Together

This is where interviews become practical.

Imagine:

                    OrderController
                          │
                          ↓
                    OrderService
                          │
              ┌───────────┴───────────┐
              ↓                       ↓
      IOrderRepository          IPaymentStrategy
              │                       │
       OrderRepository          ┌─────┼─────┐
                                ↓     ↓     ↓
                              Card   UPI   PayPal

Here:

Dependency Injection → supplies dependencies
DIP                 → depend on abstractions
SRP                 → separate responsibilities
OCP                 → add payment implementations
Strategy            → interchangeable payment behavior
Repository          → abstracts persistence

This is exactly the kind of connection you should be able to explain in a Senior .NET interview.

23.29 Real-world Scenario: Design an Order API

Suppose interviewer asks:

“Design an Order Processing Service using SOLID principles.”

You could answer:

Step 1 — Controller

public class OrdersController : ControllerBase
{
    private readonly IOrderService _service;

    public OrdersController(IOrderService service)
    {
        _service = service;
    }
}

Step 2 — Service

public interface IOrderService
{
    Task<OrderResult> CreateOrderAsync(CreateOrderRequest request);
}

Step 3 — Repository

public interface IOrderRepository
{
    Task SaveAsync(Order order);
}

Step 4 — Payment abstraction

public interface IPaymentProcessor
{
    Task ProcessAsync(Order order);
}

Implementations:

CardPaymentProcessor
UpiPaymentProcessor
WalletPaymentProcessor

Step 5 — DI

builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, OrderRepository>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IPaymentProcessor, CardPaymentProcessor>();

The exact registration strategy would depend on how the payment implementation is selected; a keyed service, factory, or strategy resolver may be appropriate.

Architecture

             HTTP Request
                  ↓
          OrdersController
                  ↓
            IOrderService
                  ↓
        ┌─────────┴──────────┐
        ↓                    ↓
 IOrderRepository      IPaymentProcessor
        ↓                    ↓
    EF Core DB          Payment Provider

This gives you:

  • separation of responsibilities
  • testability
  • dependency inversion
  • replaceable implementations
  • easier extension
